About the Author

作者简介

Susanna Abse has been a psychoanalytic psychotherapist for over 30 years. She specialises in helping couples and was CEO of the charity Tavistock Relationships from 2006 to 2016 and Chair of the British Psychoanalytic Council from 2018 to 2021.

苏珊娜·阿布斯从事精神分析心理治疗已有 30 多年。她专长于帮助夫妻，曾于 2006 年至 2016 年担任慈善机构塔维斯托克关系中心的首席执行官，并于 2018 年至 2021 年担任英国精神分析委员会主席。

Alongside her professional writing on couples therapy, she has contributed articles on wider social and political issues to the Guardian , the New Statesman and Open Democracy . In 2019, she presented a series of films called Britain on the Couch for Channel 4 News. She is co-editor of The Library of Couple and Family Psychoanalysis for Routledge Books and is a trustee of the Freud Museum, London.

除了撰写有关伴侣治疗的专业文章外，她还为《卫报》、《新政治家》和《开放民主》等媒体撰写有关更广泛的社会和政治议题的文章。2019年，她为英国第四频道新闻制作了一系列名为《沙发上的英国》的纪录片。她是劳特利奇出版社出版的《伴侣与家庭精神分析文库》的联合编辑，也是伦敦弗洛伊德博物馆的理事。

Introduction

介绍

The couple relationship is at the centre of this book, just as it is at the centre of our lives. We are born wanting to reach out and relate to others, and each of us, whilst not necessarily growing up with two parents, has a deep internal structure rooted in the idea of intimate connection. Despite technological advances, there is always a sperm and an egg, a nipple and a mouth – two bodies and two minds coming together. For humans, we cannot make babies single-handed and even if we could, the drive for ‘intercourse’ and human interaction would remain. We are hardwired for love.

伴侣关系是本书的核心，正如它在我们生活中的核心一样。我们生来就渴望与他人建立联系，每个人，即便未必都成长于双亲家庭，内心深处也根植着对亲密联结的渴望。尽管科技进步，但生命依然离不开精子和卵子、乳头和嘴巴——两个身体和两个心灵的结合。对人类而言，我们无法单枪匹马地孕育生命，即便可以，对“性交”和人际互动的渴望依然存在。我们天生渴望爱。

This sense of connection lies at the heart of many of our dreams and fantasies and drives the narrative of fairy tales, which Carl Jung believed revealed something about the basis of human nature. It is for this reason that I have written this book in the form of a series of psychoanalytic allegories, with fairy tale-like titles, through which I try to shed light on some of the universal themes and eternal dilemmas we face in relationships, and which draw couples together and, all too often, tear them apart.

这种联结感是我们许多梦想和幻想的核心，也是童话故事的叙事驱动力。卡尔·荣格认为，童话揭示了人性的某些本质。正因如此，我以一系列精神分析寓言的形式，配上童话般的标题，创作了这本书。我试图借此阐明我们在人际关系中面临的一些普遍主题和永恒困境，这些主题和困境既能将伴侣联系在一起，也常常导致他们分崩离析。

The longing for transformation is at the heart of what often brings people to therapy, just as it is at the heart of the fairy tale, where a happy outcome is achieved only after the central character overcomes huge obstacles and adversity. Clearly, psychotherapy doesn’t transform the frog into a prince; however, it does attempt to take the patient on a journey where they come to understand that the frog and the prince are two halves of the same person and ‘transformation’ perhaps then comes from accepting this. Yet some patients seek a quick fix – a magic potion – and are disappointed when they find that there isn’t one.

渴望改变是人们寻求心理治疗的核心所在，正如童话故事的核心一样——主人公只有克服重重障碍和逆境才能获得幸福的结局。显然，心理治疗并不能把青蛙变成王子；但它确实试图引导患者踏上一段旅程，让他们逐渐明白青蛙和王子其实是同一个人的两面，而“改变”或许就源于接受这一点。然而，有些患者寻求的是速效药——一种灵丹妙药——当他们发现世上并无灵丹妙药时，便会感到失望。

The case histories in this book are inspired and informed by more than 35 years of practice and tens of thousands of sessions with many hundreds of living, breathing patients. The importance of any patient feeling safe in the knowledge that what they tell me is confidential means that I haven’t written about any specific individuals. Readers will ask, ‘But then are these stories true?’ The answer is that they are ‘true’ in the same way that fairy tales are ‘true’. They aim to tell a deeper truth about the human condition. Each chapter tells a story that represents problems and patterns of behaviour I have witnessed in different forms over and over again. Though they are not about any specific patient they offer truths about the human need for others and the reality of our vulnerability, about the inevitability of dependence and the fear of it.

本书中的案例取材于我三十五年以上的临床实践，以及与数百位鲜活患者进行的数万次咨询。我深知，让每一位患者都感到安心，并确信他们告诉我的内容将严格保密至关重要，因此我没有在书中提及任何具体的个人案例。读者可能会问：“那么，这些故事是真的吗？”答案是，它们如同童话故事一样“真实”。它们旨在揭示人类境况中更深层次的真相。每一章都讲述了一个故事，展现了我反复观察到的各种问题和行为模式。虽然这些故事并非针对任何特定的患者，但它们揭示了人类对他人的需求、我们脆弱的现实、依赖的必然性以及对依赖的恐惧等真相。

When exploring love relationships, it’s vital to question what is truth? Philosophers describe truth as that which accords with reality, but reality is subjective: my reality will be different from yours and yours from mine. I point this out because this question goes to the heart of couple therapy. In treatment, many discover that not only have they hidden the truth from others but that they have also been lying to themselves – because being honest with oneself usually means facing up to painful truths which we often avoid. Thus, there are two aspects to ‘truth’ between a couple: the first involves facing one’s own feelings and knowing about your own experiences; the second involves facing your partner’s feelings and understanding their experience. The challenge is whether these two truths can co-exist without one threatening to obliterate the other.

在探索恋爱关系时，至关重要的是要问：什么是真相？哲学家将真相定义为符合现实的事物，但现实是主观的：我的现实与你的不同，你的现实也与我的不同。我之所以指出这一点，是因为这个问题直指伴侣治疗的核心。在治疗过程中，许多人发现他们不仅对他人隐瞒了真相，而且也一直在欺骗自己——因为对自己诚实通常意味着要面对我们常常逃避的痛苦真相。因此，伴侣之间的“真相”包含两个方面：第一方面是正视自己的感受和经历；第二方面是正视伴侣的感受和经历。关键在于，这两种真相能否共存，而不至于一方威胁到另一方。

Most couples take a little time to become curious – to become interested in how their inner truth may not reflect some objective reality but is, at least in part, a reflection of their own family experience. But when partners do become curious, less defensive and open up about their feelings, they can rediscover each other and a different kind of truth emerges – one that is shared and which creates a new narrative. This is not simply an intellectual or cognitive knowing but rather an emotional process. As Jung said, ‘We should not pretend to understand the world only by intellect. We apprehend it just as much by feeling . The judgement of the intellect is only part of the truth.’ fn1

大多数伴侣需要一些时间才能产生好奇心——开始思考他们的内心真实感受或许并非反映某种客观现实，而至少在某种程度上反映了他们自身的家庭经历。但当伴侣们真正产生好奇心，放下防备，敞开心扉地表达感受时，他们就能重新发现彼此，一种不同的真相也会随之浮现——一种共享的真相，它创造了一种新的叙事。这并非仅仅是理性的认知，而是一个情感的过程。正如荣格所说：“我们不应妄称仅凭理智就能理解世界。我们同样也能通过感受来领悟世界。理智的判断只是真相的一部分。”<sup>1</sup>

Jung was wise – as a psychotherapist, I have learnt that all our experience is suffused with and shaped by our previous experiences. We approach every new event or relationship full of preconceptions – we are never free of these influences; though we may imagine ourselves to be impartial, objective witnesses to our lives, we are not. The past lives on in the present.

荣格的智慧不言而喻——作为一名心理治疗师，我逐渐认识到，我们所有的经历都深受过往经验的影响和塑造。我们带着先入为主的观念去面对每一件事或每一段新的关系——我们永远无法摆脱这些影响；即便我们自认为能够客观公正地见证自己的人生，事实并非如此。过去始终存在于当下。

In couple therapy, then, the aim is to seek truth – but not to possess it. Rather it is a process of unfolding something between a couple that leads to discoveries which in turn lead to understanding and, sometimes, to transformation. I hope that in writing this book I may help readers reach a deeper and richer insight into themselves and their own relationships. Couple therapy is largely about getting to know things about yourself and your partner that have been hidden from view behind our assumptions. It’s about letting go of one set of ‘truths’ and becoming open to a more shared understanding of each other – that is the truth about love.

因此，伴侣治疗的目标是寻求真相，而非占有真相。它是一个逐步揭示伴侣间某些东西的过程，由此带来新的发现，进而增进理解，有时甚至带来转变。我希望通过这本书，能够帮助读者更深刻、更丰富地了解自己和彼此的关系。伴侣治疗的核心在于发现那些被我们固有观念所掩盖的关于自己和伴侣的真相。它意味着放下既有的“真理”，敞开心扉去理解彼此——这才是爱的真谛。

Part One

第一部分

FRAGILE BONDS

脆弱的纽带

We are never so defenceless as when we love.

—Sigmund Freud, Civilization and Its Discontents

我们在恋爱时，往往是最无助的。——西格蒙德·弗洛伊德，《文明及其不满》

All humans are fragile, though we may spend a lifetime pretending we are not. We are born helpless and that experience of helplessness is not forgotten. It echoes through our lives and disturbs us in the dead of night when our grown-up selves are sleeping.

所有人类都是脆弱的，尽管我们可能终其一生都在假装自己并非如此。我们生来无助，而这种无助的体验永远不会被遗忘。它会在我们的一生中不断回响，并在我们成年后的夜晚，在我们熟睡之时，扰乱我们的心绪。

Our only real protection from human fragility is other humans. Humans with hands that lift us; humans with arms that hold us; humans with minds that understand us. Without that, we are alone – and no human is designed for that. But other humans also threaten us; they remind us of the times we were dropped, when the arms weren’t gently holding but roughly constraining and take us back to the times we were misunderstood. So, when it comes to love, we armour ourselves against this fragility because we are afraid.

我们唯一能真正抵御人性脆弱的屏障，便是其他人。是那些伸出援手扶起我们的人；是那些用臂膀拥抱我们的人；是那些用心灵理解我们的人。没有这些，我们将孤身一人——而没有人天生就该如此。但其他人也同样会给我们带来威胁；他们会让我们想起那些被抛弃的时刻，想起那些并非温柔拥抱而是粗暴束缚的岁月，想起那些不被理解的时光。所以，在爱情面前，我们筑起盔甲，抵御这种脆弱，因为我们害怕。

# ↩

Victoria and Rupert Refuse to Come out of the Doll’s House

维多利亚和鲁珀特拒绝离开玩偶之家

Some couples are shockingly childish. They bicker and fight, snap and wail, and like nothing better than having an audience to win over to their side. Once they’ve exhausted all their friends then a couple therapist often comes in handy!

有些夫妻幼稚得令人震惊。他们争吵不休，动不动就发脾气、嚎啕大哭，而且最喜欢的就是找人围观，好让别人站在他们这边。等他们把所有朋友都劝服了之后，婚姻咨询师往往就派上用场了！

I have colleagues who work only with individuals and insist they’d never want to work with a couple because they’d feel so irritated with the rowing. I remember many years ago teaching a seminar and a student therapist getting very cross with the case material I was presenting. Exasperated, they asked, ‘For goodness’ sake, why don’t they just call it a day if they can’t get on?’ It brought a brief round of applause and nodding of student heads.

我有些同事只接待个人咨询师，他们坚持说绝不想接待夫妻，因为他们会受不了夫妻间的争吵。我记得很多年前，我讲授一个案例时，一位学生治疗师非常生气。他恼火地问道：“天哪，如果他们合不来，为什么不干脆结束今天的咨询呢？” 这话引来一阵短暂的掌声和学生的点头。

We may disapprove of couples bickering or behaving like children, yet it seems to me that couples become couples partly because an intimate relationship is one of the only ways it’s acceptable for adults to regress. Where else can we talk in silly voices? Call and be called ‘pudding pie’ and suchlike? Who else can you throw water at or even ketchup in a play fight? Who else will read to you? Sing to you? Hold you and caress you? It is perhaps one of life’s paradoxes that it’s the norm for parents to share the warmth of a bed, whilst children, once past early infancy, are trained to sleep alone. Being a couple lets us return to this world of play and touch, which is generally barred to us in the rest of our adult lives.

我们或许不赞成伴侣争吵或像孩子一样玩耍，但在我看来，伴侣之所以成为伴侣，部分原因在于亲密关系是成年人回归童真、被社会接受的少数几种方式之一。还有什么地方能让我们用滑稽的声音说话？可以互相称呼对方“布丁派”之类的？还有谁能和我们一起玩水仗，甚至泼番茄酱？还有谁会给我们读书？唱歌？拥抱我们，抚摸我们？或许人生的一大悖论是：父母同床共枕是常态，而孩子一旦过了婴儿期，就被训练成独自睡觉。成为伴侣让我们得以重返这个充满游戏和触碰的世界，而这在成年生活中通常是被我们拒之门外的。

Nearly all intimate love relationships have childlike qualities: we use baby words of love with each other and snuggle, stroke and play. Love-making itself offers the opportunity to stroke and caress and suck and tickle and explore in a way that most of adult life doesn’t. Recently, on a beach in Greece I watched a couple sticking grass stalks up each other’s noses – testing how long they could each bear it. Rolling with laughter, I observed how completely in love they were and how much they were bonded by their childishness.

几乎所有亲密的爱情关系都带有孩童般的特质：我们用婴儿般的甜言蜜语彼此倾诉爱意，依偎、抚摸、玩耍。性爱本身就提供了抚摸、爱抚、吮吸、轻挠和探索的机会，而这在大多数成年生活中是无法实现的。最近，在希腊的海滩上，我看到一对情侣把草茎塞进对方的鼻孔里——测试彼此能忍受多久。我笑得前仰后合，注意到他们是多么相爱，以及这种孩子气是如何将他们紧紧联系在一起的。

But despite knowing this, I have to confess that there are some couples whose infantile behaviour is so regressive and destructive that it becomes hard to bear, even for an old hand like me.

但即便如此，我也不得不承认，有些夫妻幼稚的行为是如此倒退和具有破坏性，即使像我这样的老手也难以忍受。

Victoria and Rupert were extremely hard going. They were in their late thirties and beautiful, rich and clever but, I repeat, extremely hard going. Both could be disarmingly charming on their own but together they were a nightmare. So many dinner parties ruined, holidays disrupted and tearful phone conversations late at night had led to their friends drawing a line through their names and so they turned up in my consulting room, ready to put me through a similar experience.

维多利亚和鲁珀特真是难搞。他们都快四十岁了，漂亮、富有、聪明，但我再说一遍，他们真的很难搞。两人单独相处时都魅力十足，但在一起简直就是一场噩梦。无数次的晚宴被毁，假期被搅得天翻地覆，深夜里无数次泪流满面的电话争吵，以至于他们的朋友们都和他们断绝了关系。于是，他们竟然跑到我的诊室，准备让我也体验一把同样的痛苦。

I, however, having endured many hours listening to similarly warring couples, knew I had to take a different approach. There were tantrums and tears in the sessions and I received histrionic phone calls and emails between appointments, where each would forward me texts or emails that had passed between them. Sometimes I’d be copied into these exchanges and asked to adjudicate as if I was the giver of justice. Both convinced of their rightness, they would appeal to me with tear-filled eyes to validate their point of view. They’d come to each session having not spoken to each other for several days and then, each Thursday in my office, would eventually make up and leave my room together laughing and smiling like a pair of naughty children.

然而，在听过无数次类似的争吵之后，我知道我必须采取不同的方法。咨询过程中，他们经常大发脾气、泪流满面；在两次咨询之间，我还会接到他们情绪激动的电话和邮件，他们会把彼此之间的短信或邮件转发给我。有时，他们还会抄送我到这些邮件往来中，要求我像个正义的审判者一样做出裁决。双方都坚信自己是对的，他们会泪眼婆娑地恳求我认可他们的观点。每次咨询前，他们可能已经好几天没说过话了，但每个星期四，在我的办公室里，他们最终都会和好如初，然后像两个淘气的孩子一样，笑着一起离开。

There are some couples who, when in the middle of a row, voice their outrage at what they feel are unfair accusations and distortions of truth meted out by their partner. ‘If only I’d had a video running, it would prove me right. It just didn’t happen like that!’ they scream, each of them seeing everything through their own lens – a lens that is distorted and shaped by past experiences, which often include trauma, neglect and abuse. And this introduces confusion, making it hard to distinguish feeling from facts. The angrier and more upset partners get, the more assumptions are made about the motives and intentions of the other.

有些伴侣在争吵时，会义愤填膺地指责对方不公平的指责和歪曲事实。“要是我当时录下来就好了，就能证明我是对的。事情根本不是那样发生的！”他们大声嚷嚷，每个人都透过自己的视角看待一切——而这种视角往往被过往的经历所扭曲和塑造，这些经历通常包括创伤、忽视和虐待。这造成了混乱，使人难以区分感受和事实。伴侣越是愤怒和沮丧，就越容易对对方的动机和意图做出各种臆测。

I hoped, with careful work, Victoria and Rupert might break out of this cycle and begin to become curious. Curious about themselves and curious about each other. The assumptions they made about each other, together with the excitement they created to avoid feeling sad, left them repeating a cycle of anger, betrayal and passionate reconciliation over and over again. And whilst it sometimes seemed they were excited by it, I could see that, underneath the noise, they felt desperation and despair at never feeling understood or safe. I knew if anything was going to change, they needed to get depressed, they needed to recognise that their relationship wasn’t a doll’s house where the furniture could be thrown about and the figures tipped upside down with no consequences or damage. I wanted them to feel how serious and sad this was. I wanted them to talk about their fears. I wanted them, in short, to be different.

我希望，通过细致的努力，维多利亚和鲁珀特能够打破这个恶性循环，开始对彼此产生好奇心。他们对彼此的好奇，以及为了逃避悲伤而强加的兴奋，让他们一次又一次地重复着愤怒、背叛和激情和解的循环。虽然有时他们似乎乐在其中，但我能看出，在喧嚣之下，他们内心充满绝望，因为他们从未感到被理解或安全。我知道，如果想要改变现状，他们需要经历一段低谷期，他们需要意识到，他们的关系并非玩偶屋，不能随意摆弄家具、颠倒人偶而不会造成任何后果或伤害。我希望他们能感受到这件事的严重性和悲伤。我希望他们能倾诉自己的恐惧。简而言之，我希望他们能够有所改变。

Whether I was right to want all this is highly questionable. Should a psychotherapist have such clear goals for their patients? Isn’t it our job to facilitate what our patients want, not what we desire for them? I knew this, of course, so how was I to survive the frustrations of working with Victoria and Rupert? How was I to bear the endless sessions of petty fighting and rapturous reconciliation? And when, as my exasperated student rightly asked, is it time to call it a day?

我当初想要这一切是否正确，实在值得怀疑。心理治疗师是否应该为患者设定如此明确的目标？我们的职责难道不应该是帮助患者实现他们想要的，而不是强加给他们的吗？我当然明白这一点，那么，我该如何忍受与维多利亚和鲁珀特共事的种种挫折呢？我该如何承受没完没了的琐碎争吵和欣喜若狂的和解呢？正如我那位被我气得不行的学生所问的那样，究竟何时才是结束这一切的时候呢？

I found myself thinking back to another couple who I’d seen many years earlier. Roly and Clive were very young when they came, just 23 and 24. They too had passionate ups and downs, breaking up and reconciling repeatedly. The slightest thing would trigger mutual threats to end the relationship and I’d never know what to expect from week to week. I’d sternly encourage them to take the work with me seriously but it seemed impossible and after several weeks of no-shows, unpaid bills and frantic texts, I suggested in an email that perhaps they weren’t ready to settle down to therapy and that they should contact me when they felt they could commit.

我不禁回想起多年前遇到的另一对情侣。罗利和克莱夫来的时候很年轻，只有23岁和24岁。他们的感情也像他们一样，忽上忽下，分分合合。一点小事就能引发他们互相威胁要分手，我永远无法预料接下来会发生什么。我严厉地劝他们认真对待咨询，但这似乎是不可能的。几周过去了，他们屡次爽约，账单也拖欠，还不停地发短信催促。最后，我在邮件里建议他们，或许他们还没准备好接受咨询，等他们觉得可以认真对待的时候再联系我。

How ironic. Commitment was of course the very problem Roly and Clive were struggling with. Both felt too scared to really pledge themselves to the relationship and both found it impossible to commit to the therapy.

真是讽刺。罗利和克莱夫面临的问题恰恰就是难以做出承诺。他们都太害怕真正投入到这段感情中，也都觉得无法坚持接受治疗。

Was this, I wondered, Victoria and Rupert’s problem too? They were a fair bit older than Roly and Clive and the stakes were therefore considerably higher. On the other hand, they had the financial resources to play these games with each other, in ever more dramatic ways.

我心想，维多利亚和鲁珀特是不是也面临着同样的问题？他们比罗利和克莱夫年纪大得多，因此风险也更高。另一方面，他们也有足够的财力来玩弄这些游戏，而且手段越来越高明。

One grey Tuesday in February, I struggled into work with a streaming cold. Victoria and Rupert were the last appointment of the day and I, exhausted, secretly hoped they might cancel so I could go home and get into my PJs. Six o’clock came and went, and I was beginning to think about getting my coat when, fifteen minutes late, the buzzer went. They entered with a flurry, unzipping their matching Moncler down jackets and, without taking a breath, launched into their latest drama.

二月一个阴沉的星期二，我拖着感冒的疲惫艰难地去上班。维多利亚和鲁珀特是当天最后一个预约，我筋疲力尽，暗自希望他们能取消，这样我就可以回家换上睡衣了。六点钟到了，我正打算拿外套，这时，门铃响了，他们迟到了十五分钟。他们匆匆忙忙地走了进来，拉开同款蒙克莱羽绒服的拉链，还没来得及喘口气，就开始上演他们最新的闹剧。

It seemed they’d been skiing over a long weekend in Zermatt and on the second day Victoria had taken umbrage over Rupert’s provocative comment that her bum did indeed look big in her salopettes. She’d instantly hired a car and driven for five hours to meet friends skiing in St Moritz. Ordinary mortals would have had to stay put and work it out but, being impulse driven and rich, she didn’t need to. She could make her point in the most dramatic way, leaving Rupert alone on the side of the mountain.

他们似乎在采尔马特度过了一个漫长的滑雪周末，第二天，鲁珀特挑衅地评论维多利亚穿滑雪裤时屁股确实显得很大，维多利亚对此非常不满。她立刻租了一辆车，开了五个小时的车去圣莫里茨和朋友们滑雪。换作普通人，或许只能留在原地想办法解决，但她冲动又富有，根本不需要。她可以用最戏剧性的方式来表达自己的不满，把鲁珀特一个人留在山边。

This kind of ‘acting out’ is very anti-therapeutic. Therapy is about sitting with things, bearing feelings, tolerating discomfort, facing our fears. Victoria and Rupert seemed deeply committed to not committing to this process.

这种“反抗”行为非常不利于治疗。治疗的本质在于静下心来面对问题，承受情绪，忍受不适，直面恐惧。维多利亚和鲁珀特似乎铁了心要拒绝接受治疗。

There was, however, one thing they both wanted more than anything else and when I spoke about this in the sessions they’d go quiet and still as my words reverberated through them, echoing their oceanic desire to start a family. To be a family. Something neither of them had had when growing up. I won’t detail their individual backgrounds. You, the reader, can, I’m sure, imagine the circumstances of the neglect they’d suffered. Lots of money and very little care. Sent young to grand boarding schools. Many treats that hadn’t compensated for a lack of real attention and love. Lots of holidays and big gestures but no stability. It was very painful if you stopped for two minutes to think about it. Which is exactly what they didn’t or couldn’t do.

然而，他们俩都渴望一件事，胜过一切。每当我在咨询中谈及此事，他们都会安静下来，我的话语在他们心中回荡，仿佛在诉说着他们如海洋般深切的渴望——组建家庭，成为一个真正的家庭。这是他们成长过程中从未拥有过的。我不会赘述他们的个人经历。我相信，读者朋友们能够想象出他们所遭受的忽视。他们拥有大量的金钱，却缺乏关爱。年幼时就被送往豪华寄宿学校。许多优渥的待遇也无法弥补他们缺失的真正关注和爱。许多假期和盛大的仪式，却缺乏稳定的生活。只要稍加思考，便会感到无比痛苦。而这正是他们不愿或无法去思考的。

In the sessions, as the weeks went by, there were repeated damaging break-ups and make-ups. I’d be firm and stop them bickering and then I’d try to connect them to how sad this all was. How sad that they’d missed each other for three days when they’d planned to go to the theatre or to Paris, Rome or Zermatt. Every cancelled event or spoilt occasion. I’d speak to the waste of it all and the waste of their deepest hopes and gradually, very gradually, they began to thaw, to show genuine sadness and to turn back to each other sooner after each argument than had previously been the case.

在咨询过程中，随着几周时间的流逝，他们之间反复出现令人痛苦的分手和复合。我会态度坚决地制止他们的争吵，然后试图让他们意识到这一切有多么令人难过。他们原本计划一起去看戏，或者去巴黎、罗马或采尔马特，却因为种种原因错过了三天，这多么令人难过。每一次取消的活动，每一次被破坏的约会，都让他们感到遗憾。我会告诉他们这一切是多么的徒劳，他们最深切的希望是如何被辜负的。渐渐地，非常缓慢地，他们的关系开始缓和下来，开始流露出真切的悲伤，每次争吵后，他们都能比以前更快地和好。

Children love a doll’s house; it’s a place where fantasy can dominate and where the child can be all-powerful and in control. Victoria and Rupert, who were so fragile inside, liked to pretend they were unbreakable but of course they were not.

孩子们都喜欢娃娃屋；在娃娃屋里，想象力可以自由驰骋，孩子可以拥有至高无上的权力和控制权。维多利亚和鲁伯特内心脆弱，却喜欢假装自己坚不可摧，但实际上他们并非如此。

Rows between couples are inevitable. Differences are not only inevitable, but important. Perhaps more essential than agreement is the working through of our differences, so that we really find each other. You are not me. I am not you. And yes, that is difficult and disappointing but also interesting and sometimes exciting. And if we are just a ‘we’, then who am I?

情侣之间争吵在所难免。分歧不仅不可避免，而且至关重要。或许比达成共识更重要的是，我们能否克服分歧，真正找到彼此。你不是我，我不是你。没错，这很艰难，也很令人失望，但同时也很有趣，有时甚至令人兴奋。如果我们只是“我们”，那么我又是谁呢？

So, the trick of being a happy-enough couple isn’t to have no rows but to learn to make up well and to repair the relationship. Rupert and Victoria made up quickly enough in the early days of therapy but they never repaired anything, never learnt anything. It was manic repair to avoid feeling, to avoid thinking and to avoid knowing about their pain.

所以，维持一段足够幸福的夫妻关系的秘诀不在于不吵架，而在于学会好好和好，修复彼此的关系。鲁伯特和维多利亚在治疗初期很快就和好了，但他们从未真正修复过任何问题，也从未从中吸取任何教训。他们只是疯狂地试图修复关系，以此来逃避感受、逃避思考、逃避了解彼此的痛苦。

# ↩

Jack and Jill Tumble down the Hill

杰克和吉尔从山坡上滚下来

Jack Sprat could eat no fat,
His wife could eat no lean;
And so betwixt them both,
They lick’d the platter clean.

—Nursery rhyme

杰克·斯普拉特不吃肥肉，他的妻子不吃瘦肉；于是他们俩把盘子舔得干干净净。——童谣

Marriage and long-term partnerships can help us to develop and grow. The nurture and, indeed, the frustration that we encounter in our relationships help us mature. So when a couple comes to therapy, it’s often because this maturing process has got stuck or frozen and the couple, rather than finding their relationship helps them to flourish, instead find themselves trapped in patterns of destructive feelings and behaviour. Couple psychotherapy can unblock this, launching the couple back into a more creative journey through the life cycle of having children, raising and then launching them; developing careers; nurturing friendships; managing retirement and, of course, in time, facing old age and death. For some couples, whose relationship hasn’t matured, this frozen or stuck state has come about because of the avoidance of all conflict.

婚姻和长期伴侣关系能够帮助我们成长和发展。我们在关系中遇到的滋养，以及由此产生的挫折，都能帮助我们走向成熟。因此，当一对伴侣前来咨询时，往往是因为这种成熟的过程停滞不前，他们非但没有从关系中获得成长，反而深陷于破坏性的情绪和行为模式中无法自拔。伴侣心理治疗可以打破这种僵局，帮助伴侣重新开启一段更具创造性的人生旅程，包括生育子女、养育子女、送他们长大成人；发展事业；维系友谊；规划退休生活，当然，最终还要面对衰老和死亡。对于一些关系尚未成熟的伴侣来说，这种停滞不前的状态源于他们一直以来都在回避冲突。

I remember an early case, perhaps 30 years ago, which first brought this home to me. Both were artists and they lived in the countryside, in a quiet, isolated place, though it was not far from London. I shall call them Jack and Jill. They were an older couple with no children and no desire for children. As I got to know them, I concluded that the reason for this was that they still felt like children themselves; babes lost in the woods.

我记得大约三十年前的一个案例，它让我第一次真正理解了这一点。他们都是艺术家，住在乡下一个安静偏僻的地方，虽然离伦敦并不远。我姑且称他们为杰克和吉尔。他们是一对年纪较大的夫妇，没有孩子，也不想要孩子。随着我对他们的了解加深，我得出结论：原因在于他们觉得自己仍然像孩子一样，就像迷失在森林里的婴儿。

At that time, I was a fresh-faced trainee therapist working in the building of a large NHS clinic. It wasn’t a particularly friendly place but I was keen to follow the many rules about conducting appointments. In this clinic, the protocol was that when patients arrived, I had to phone down to an indifferent receptionist who would then send the couple up to my office, three floors above.

那时，我还是个初出茅庐的实习治疗师，在一家大型NHS诊所工作。那里的环境并不友好，但我还是努力遵守着各种预约流程的规定。这家诊所的流程是，病人到了之后，我必须先打电话给楼下那位冷漠的前台，由她把病人夫妇介绍到我位于楼上三层的办公室。

It was a Tuesday afternoon and I’d spent the morning in seminars and with my supervisor, preparing for a new couple. I closed the office window, looked at my watch and saw it was 2pm so I rang down to see if they’d arrived. The receptionist informed me the couple were here and were now on their way up. I knew nothing much about Jack and Jill but waited with anticipation by the lift to greet them and escort them to my room. The minutes ticked by and, as I watched the hands of the clock move gradually towards ten minutes past two, I began to wonder where they’d got to.

那是一个星期二的下午，我上午都在参加研讨会，还和我的主管一起准备迎接一对新人。我关上办公室的窗户，看了看表，发现已经下午两点了，于是打电话下去问他们到了没有。前台告诉我他们已经到了，正在上楼的路上。我对杰克和吉尔了解不多，但还是满怀期待地在电梯旁等着迎接他们，并带他们去我的房间。时间一分一秒地过去，看着时钟的指针缓缓指向两点十分，我开始纳闷他们到底去了哪里。

Then, turning to the adjacent stairs, I could see an older couple slowly hauling their way up to where I was waiting. I wasn’t sure if this was Jack and Jill, so we stood there slightly awkwardly until I said, ‘Hello, I’m Susanna Abse. Are you here to see me?’ They nodded and silently followed me down the corridor towards my sparsely furnished office with its clinical linoleum floor and metal windows.

然后，我转身看向旁边的楼梯，看到一对老夫妇正缓缓地朝我走来。我不确定他们是不是杰克和吉尔，所以我们略显尴尬地站在那里，直到我开口说道：“您好，我是苏珊娜·阿布斯。请问您是来见我的吗？”他们点点头，默默地跟着我沿着走廊走向我那间陈设简陋的办公室，办公室里铺着普通的油毡地板，装着金属窗户。

By the time I reached the door, the couple were lagging some 20 feet behind me. Admittedly, I’d walked briskly but their pace was snail-like and once inside, it seemed to take an age for them to dispense with their bags and coats and settle themselves.

等我走到门口时，那对夫妇已经落后我大约20英尺了。诚然，我走得很快，但他们的步伐却像蜗牛一样慢，进了屋之后，他们似乎过了很久才放下包和外套，安顿下来。

I introduced myself properly and told them we had until 3.15pm and that this was a consultation to explore whether couple psychotherapy might be helpful for them. And then I asked them to tell me a little about why they’d come.

我正式地做了自我介绍，告诉他们我们下午3点15分之前可以见面，这次咨询是为了探讨伴侣心理治疗是否对他们有帮助。然后我请他们简单说说来访的原因。

There was a long pause and I took this opportunity to study them closely. Jack was tall and very thin, and I thought that once he would have been very handsome. His hair was splattered with grey and looked like it hadn’t seen a comb for some months.

一阵漫长的沉默后，我趁机仔细打量起他们来。杰克身材高瘦，我想他以前一定很英俊。他的头发已经夹杂着不少灰白，看起来好几个月没梳过了。

Jill also looked a bit uncared for in a baggy tweed skirt and thick, dark tights that had seen better days. She wore an impressive orange bead necklace and her hair, which was pinned in a loose bun, was dyed scarlet red. I could see her white roots as she bent to place her bag on the blue lino beside her and as she straightened up, she looked at me and gave a small, warm smile.

吉尔穿着宽松的粗花呢裙子和厚厚的深色丝袜，看起来有些邋遢，丝袜也已经穿旧了。她戴着一条醒目的橙色珠串项链，头发染成了鲜红色，随意地挽成一个发髻。她弯腰把包放在身旁的蓝色油毡地板上时，我能看到她白色的发根。她直起身子，看着我，给了我一个温暖的微笑。

The silence continued but eventually, Jack, looking anxiously at Jill, broke the silence.

沉默持续了一段时间，但最终，杰克焦急地看着吉尔，打破了沉默。

‘We’ve been having trouble with our neighbours.’ He stopped and I nodded encouragingly for him to continue.

“我们和邻居之间一直有些矛盾。”他停顿了一下，我鼓励他继续说下去。

Again, he glanced at Jill before slowly explaining that their neighbours were objecting to a new studio they’d built on their land. I felt perplexed but curious – this was certainly an unusual subject to open with. Jack described how the studio, though far from their nearest neighbours, was on the side of a hill and therefore very visible. Their neighbours were complaining that the building spoiled the view and had now written to the local planning authorities, who’d informed them that they should have got permission before building. They were very worried, Jack continued, as they feared they were going to have to tear it down. I could sense the anxiety emanating off him.

他又看了吉尔一眼，然后缓缓解释说，他们的邻居反对他们在自家土地上新建的工作室。我感到困惑又好奇——这的确是一个不同寻常的开场白。杰克解释说，工作室虽然离最近的邻居很远，但建在山坡上，因此非常显眼。邻居们抱怨说，这栋建筑破坏了景观，现在已经写信给当地规划部门，而规划部门告知他们，他们应该在建造之前获得许可。杰克继续说道，邻居们非常担心，因为他们害怕不得不拆掉这栋建筑。我能感受到他身上散发出的焦虑。

Jill frowned but said nothing, so I prodded a little and asked if this concern was causing difficulties between them. Again, there was a long silence before, once again, Jack took the lead. ‘Maybe,’ he said.

吉尔皱了皱眉，但什么也没说，于是我稍作追问，问这件事是否给他们之间造成了困扰。又是一阵长时间的沉默，然后杰克再次开口。“也许吧，”他说。

I turned to Jill. ‘I wonder if you wanted to say anything further, Jill. Perhaps you see things differently?’ Little did I know then that this question went to the heart of their problem. Could she see things differently? Apparently not.

我转向吉尔。“吉尔，你还有什么想说的吗？或许你的看法和我不同？”当时的我并不知道，这个问题直击他们问题的核心。她的看法真的和我不同吗？显然不是。

Although Jack and Jill seemed hesitant to discuss any problems between them, they did tell me a little more about their lives. They’d met on their first day at art school, both new to London and quite overwhelmed by it all. Jack said he was attracted to Jill’s serenity; she seemed so calm and composed – ‘Zen-like’. Jill said that she’d been struck by how tall Jack was; he seemed like the strong and silent type, which reminded her of her brother. They talked animatedly about how they’d developed a way of working together that had been central to the making of their art. Inseparable since they were 18, they were now in their late fifties. They made me think of the artists Gilbert and George – a heterosexual version of that couple, two peas in a creative pod. Their work had clearly been the driving force of their existence and Jill spoke at some length about what a wonderful sculptor Jack was and how much she tried to emulate his work ethic, though sometimes she found that quite challenging. She smiled broadly and laughed as she said this and he laughed expansively too, though I couldn’t really make out what was funny. As the session went on, I noticed that both of them laughed and smiled a great deal. Was this a way of covering up more uncomfortable feelings?

尽管杰克和吉尔似乎不愿谈及彼此之间的任何问题，但他们还是向我讲述了一些他们的生活。他们在艺术学校的第一天相遇，当时两人都初来乍到伦敦，对一切都感到有些不知所措。杰克说他被吉尔的宁静所吸引；她看起来如此沉着冷静——“像禅宗一样”。吉尔说她当时就被杰克的身高所震撼；他看起来像是那种沉默寡言、意志坚定的人，这让她想起了自己的哥哥。他们兴致勃勃地谈论着他们如何发展出一种独特的合作方式，这种方式对他们的艺术创作至关重要。从18岁起就形影不离的他们，如今都已年近六十。他们让我想起了艺术家吉尔伯特和乔治——这对异性恋夫妇，就像一对创作上的知己。他们的创作显然是他们生活的动力，吉尔滔滔不绝地讲述了杰克是一位多么杰出的雕塑家，以及她如何努力效仿他的职业道德，尽管有时她觉得这相当具有挑战性。她说这话时笑容灿烂，还大笑起来，他也跟着哈哈大笑，但我实在听不出哪里好笑。随着咨询的进行，我注意到他们俩笑得很频繁。这难道是在掩饰内心深处的不安吗？

After they left, I wrote ‘Babes in the wood?’ on my notepad, which was my shorthand for a particular kind of couple who find any conflict or differences particularly challenging and will do anything to keep things smooth and harmonious between them. As a result, all the conflict and difficulties happen with people outside the little couple world, with in-laws or siblings or, perhaps, neighbours. I had the sense that Jack and Jill were trying to live in a kind of childlike refuge, buried in the countryside away from the intrusions and demands of the outside world. The only blot on the horizon seemed to be their neighbours, who they feared were out to get them.

他们走后，我在笔记本上写下了“林中孩童？”，这是我用来形容那种特别的夫妻的简写：任何冲突或分歧都让他们感到格外棘手，他们会不惜一切代价维持彼此间的和谐与平静。结果，所有的冲突和困难都发生在他们小世界之外的人身上，比如姻亲、兄弟姐妹，或者邻居。我感觉杰克和吉尔仿佛生活在一个孩童般的世外桃源，隐匿在乡间，远离外界的侵扰和压力。地平线上唯一的阴影似乎就是他们的邻居，他们害怕邻居会找他们的麻烦。

‘Babes in the wood’ couples try to create a relationship where partners, like good mothers, apprehend and meet each other’s needs in a complete, almost unspoken way. Each partner adapts to the other so that there is an illusion of oneness which can feel like a blissful experience of being held and secure.

懵懂的情侣试图建立一种关系，在这种关系中，伴侣如同慈母一般，能够完全理解并满足彼此的需求，几乎无需言语。双方互相适应，从而营造出一种浑然一体的错觉，这种错觉会带来被拥抱和安全感的幸福体验。

You and I

Have so much love

That it

Burns like fire,

In which we bake a lump of clay

Moulded into a figure of you.

And a figure of me.

Then we take both of them,

And break them into pieces,

And mix the pieces with water,

And mould again a figure of you,

And a figure of me.

I am in your clay

You are in my clay

In life we share a single quilt.

In death we will share one coffin

—Kuan Tao-Sheng, ‘Married Love’

你我之间，爱意浓烈如火，我们用这爱，将一团泥土，塑造成你的模样，也塑造成我的模样。然后，我们将它们一一取出，掰成碎片，与水混合，再次塑造成你的模样，也塑造成我的模样。我在你的泥土里，你在我的泥土里。生前，我们共用一床被子；死后，我们共用一口棺材。——关涛生，《夫妻之爱》

This poem speaks to that wonderful feeling of oneness that most love affairs begin with. When we fall in love and place our heart in someone’s hands – which is, after all, quite a risky thing to do with a stranger – feeling completely fused together gives an illusion of security. Unconsciously, we believe, ‘If we are one – you can’t hurt me. If we are the same, locked forever in a loving embrace, you’ll never leave me.’

这首诗描绘了大多数爱情故事开始时那种美妙的合二为一的感觉。当我们坠入爱河，将自己的心托付给某人——毕竟，对一个陌生人这样做是相当冒险的——那种完全融合的感觉会给人一种安全感。我们会不自觉地相信：“如果我们合二为一，你就伤害不了我。如果我们永远在一起，永远紧紧相拥，你就永远不会离开我。”

In most relationships, adult partners go through a gradual disillusionment and separation process. Life happens and the honeymoon ends. Suddenly you’re living not with this ideal person but with someone more real, with their own point of view and their own separate needs. This disillusionment can herald the end of a relationship or it can be the start of a new phase. Usually, it feels like a painful loss and couples can spend years and years working through this disappointment towards a more realistic view of what their relationship can offer. It will certainly be less romantic but for many couples this phase also heralds a greater intimacy because it’s more truthful, and intimacy and closeness are always enhanced by feeling understood.

在大多数恋爱关系中，成年伴侣都会经历一个逐渐消退和疏离的过程。生活总会发生各种变故，蜜月期终会结束。突然间，你不再与那个理想中的伴侣生活在一起，而是与一个更加真实的人相处，这个人有自己的观点和需求。这种消退可能预示着一段关系的结束，也可能预示着新阶段的开始。通常，这会让人感到痛苦的失去，伴侣们可能需要花费数年时间才能走出失望，对彼此关系的真正价值形成更现实的认识。这段关系无疑会少一些浪漫，但对许多伴侣来说，这个阶段也预示着更深层次的亲密，因为彼此更加坦诚，而理解总是能增进亲密感和亲近感。

I wasn’t sure whether Jack and Jill would take up the offer of couple psychotherapy, I thought that it might be too much for them – it seemed that they had built a life to protect them from disagreement and the rough and tumble of relationships. But, to my surprise, after some days of consideration, they wrote to say they’d like to come on a weekly basis to see me. They made it clear that this would be a big commitment; the journey would take them nearly two hours each way and so I, still in post-graduate training, felt some trepidation about whether their commitment would be matched by my capacity to help. It felt unnerving to work with a couple who were old enough to be my parents.

我一开始并不确定杰克和吉尔是否会接受伴侣心理治疗，我觉得这对他们来说可能负担太重——他们似乎已经建立起一套保护自己免受争吵和情感冲突的生活方式。但令我惊讶的是，经过几天的考虑，他们写信告诉我，他们想每周来见我。他们明确表示这将是一项很大的投入；单程就要将近两个小时，因此，我这个还在接受研究生培训的人，不禁有些忐忑，不知道自己是否能够胜任他们的工作。毕竟，要和一对年纪足以当我父母的夫妇一起工作，这让我感到有些不安。

The next session didn’t bring any further clarification of the problems between them, rather, they spoke obsessively about their neighbours and their fears about the council. They talked at length about their worry that they’d have to knock down the studio and how this would interfere with Jack’s preparation for the prestigious solo show he was going to have the following year. I heard endlessly about how important this was: his first solo exhibition and an honour. Something no gallery had ever offered him before.

下一次会面并没有进一步澄清他们之间的问题，反而让他们喋喋不休地谈论邻居以及对市政厅的担忧。他们详细地讨论了工作室可能被拆除的顾虑，以及这将如何影响杰克为明年即将举办的盛大个展所做的准备。我听他们反复强调这次展览的重要性：这是他的首次个展，也是一项莫大的荣誉。此前没有任何一家画廊向他提供过这样的机会。

‘And how’s that for you, Jill?’ I asked. ‘Perhaps it’s quite a challenge for Jack to be doing this solo, without you?’

“吉尔，你感觉如何？”我问。“对杰克来说，没有你，独自完成这件事或许是个不小的挑战吧？”

‘The issue is the kiln,’ she said, ignoring my question. ‘It cost thousands and took weeks to put in and we simply can’t afford to do that again. It took up the last of the money. If they say we have to demolish the studio, well, it’s going to be …’ she trailed off, her forehead furrowed like the twisted paper tissue in her hand. I began to feel that they were both terrified of talking about anything intimate. Was their fear of the studio being demolished also a metaphor for what they feared therapy might do to their relationship? But it was much too early to say this; they wouldn’t hear it and wouldn’t understand.

“问题出在窑炉上，”她说道，完全无视我的问题。“它花了数千块钱，安装也花了几个星期，我们实在负担不起再花一次了。这花光了我们最后的积蓄。如果他们说我们必须拆掉工作室，那可就……”她声音越来越小，额头皱得像她手里那团揉皱的纸巾。我开始觉得他们俩都害怕谈论任何私密的事情。他们害怕工作室被拆掉，是不是也隐喻着他们害怕心理治疗会破坏他们的关系？但现在说这些还为时过早；他们听不进去，也不会理解。

When they finally left, I made straight for my desk drawer and the packet of Silk Cut I kept there. Hauling myself onto the window ledge and cracking open the window, I perched on the stone windowsill and lit up. This was going to be a slow burn, I thought to myself.

他们终于离开后，我径直走向办公桌抽屉，拿出我放在里面的那包Silk Cut香烟。我爬上窗台，把窗户打开一条缝，坐在石窗台上，点燃了一支。我心想，这将会是一场慢火煎熬。

Every one of us has a kind of internal template that shapes how we respond to others. As infants and children, we observe and absorb the relationships around us and these observations form interior images that shape our expectations and fears about intimacy. The impressions aren’t fixed; I imagine them like a veil falling gently over our eyes, distorting reality, softening edges and giving us glimpses beyond. I think this is true for all of us but if our childhood experiences of family life have been fragile, destructive and frightening then the internal images we’ve formed of relationships can be very alarming, leaving us fearful and distrusting. Humans are vulnerable and fragile, easily wounded and easily hurt. More vulnerable than the animals closest to us, dogs, who seem to heal much more quickly than humans.

我们每个人都有一种内在的模板，它塑造了我们如何回应他人。婴儿和孩童时期，我们观察并吸收周围的人际关系，这些观察会在内心形成图像，进而影响我们对亲密关系的期待和恐惧。这些印象并非一成不变；我将其比作一层面纱，轻轻地蒙住我们的双眼，扭曲现实，柔化棱角，让我们得以窥见表象之外的世界。我认为这适用于我们所有人，但如果我们童年时期的家庭生活经历脆弱、充满破坏性且令人恐惧，那么我们形成的关于人际关系的内在图像可能会非常令人担忧，使我们充满恐惧和不信任。人类是脆弱的，容易受伤。我们比身边最亲近的动物——狗——更加脆弱，而狗似乎比人类愈合得更快。

I was reminded of this when Mazy arrived during lockdown. A chunky mutt around a year old, she’d been patiently waiting in kennels in Bosnia, a street dog looking for a home. After three days’ travelling in a lorry, locked in a crate, she was friendly but smelly when she met us. Mazy would take whatever was going, would wag her tail, but she wouldn’t look you in the eye and would just as happily head off with the nearest stranger who looked like they had better treats. If we accidentally dropped the lead, she would run, oblivious to us, looking for her next meal ticket. Next came a period of rebellion and refusal to co-operate – a kind of selfish entitlement that meant treats were snatched and toys were guarded. Then, three months after her arrival, in early August, she seemed to relax and became more biddable. And then we fell in love. She’d look me deep in the eyes and I’d look back and that intense sense of connection was suddenly there. I trusted her and she trusted me. It amazed me. Mazy amazed me. I thought of all the years I’d worked with some of my patients and how slowly and painfully their trust had emerged. Dogs, it seems to me, are less fragile than humans. When hurt they can mend, and they can mend faster.

疫情封锁期间，Mazy的到来让我再次想起了这件事。她是一只大约一岁的胖乎乎的杂种狗，之前一直在波斯尼亚的犬舍里耐心等待，是一只渴望找到新家的流浪狗。在卡车里被关在笼子里颠簸了三天后，她见到我们时虽然很友好，但身上却散发着一股难闻的气味。Mazy会接受任何食物，摇着尾巴，但她不会直视你的眼睛，而且会毫不犹豫地跟最近的陌生人跑开，只要对方看起来有更好的零食。如果我们不小心把牵引绳掉了，她就会毫不在意地跑开，寻找她的下一顿“饭票”。接下来是一段叛逆期，她拒绝合作——一种自私的优越感，意味着她会抢走零食，守护玩具。然后，在她来到我们家三个月后的八月初，她似乎放松了下来，变得更加听话。然后，我们爱上了她。她会深深地看着我的眼睛，我也回望她，那种强烈的联结感突然涌上心头。我信任她，她也信任我。这让我感到惊讶。梅齐让我感到惊讶。我想起了我多年来与一些病人相处的经历，以及他们建立信任的过程是多么缓慢而痛苦。在我看来，狗比人类更坚强。受伤后，它们可以愈合，而且愈合得更快。

Jack and Jill hadn’t mended. Whatever had troubled them in their childhood was now steering their current relationship. Something had scared them when they were little and their strategy to deal with the fear that they might get hurt again was to create a kind of shared idealised retreat, away from the world and from the ghosts that lived in the nursery.

杰克和吉尔的关系并没有和好。童年时期困扰他们的那些事，如今依然影响着他们的关系。小时候，他们曾被某些东西吓到，为了克服再次受伤的恐惧，他们创造了一个共同的理想避难所，远离尘世，也远离那些萦绕在育儿室里的幽灵。

The following week, I waited for Jack and Jill in my office. I had rung down to reception ten minutes earlier and been told they were on their way up. But where were they? My mind drifted back to the first session and how they’d ‘disappeared’ then too. I picked up the phone and rang down again, asking the receptionist to double-check they weren’t still waiting to be invited up. But no, she told me, they’d already headed up.

接下来的一周，我在办公室等杰克和吉尔。十分钟前我打电话给前台，他们说他们正在来的路上。可是他们去哪儿了？我的思绪回到了第一次见面时，他们也是“消失”的。我拿起电话又打了一遍，请前台再次确认他们是不是还在等着被邀请上来。但前台告诉我，他们已经上去了。

Finally, I heard a quiet rustling outside my open door and, holding it wide, I could see Jack and Jill standing, as if in a queue, along the wall of the corridor. I gestured them in and slowly they made their way to the two chairs, which they perched gingerly on the edge of.

最后，我听到敞开的门外传来轻微的窸窣声，我把门打开，看到杰克和吉尔沿着走廊的墙站着，好像在排队。我示意他们进来，他们慢慢地走到两把椅子旁，小心翼翼地坐在椅子边缘。

‘Seems like you’re feeling a bit hesitant about being here today,’ I said, smiling warmly.

“看来你今天来这里有点犹豫啊，”我笑着说。

Jill stared at me and in her stare, I felt a huge yearning. But she said nothing and neither did Jack.

吉尔凝视着我，从她的目光中，我感受到了一种强烈的渴望。但她什么也没说，杰克也没说话。

‘I think you’d probably both like me to understand everything about you and your troubles without having to explain anything.’

“我想你们俩大概都希望我能完全了解你们的一切，包括你们遇到的困难，而无需我做任何解释。”

Jack nodded and smiled.

杰克点点头，笑了。

‘Perhaps that’s what it’s like between the two of you too? A feeling of needing to be understood without having to speak?’

“或许你们俩之间也是这样？一种无需开口就能被理解的感觉？”

Jack nodded again and Jill said, ‘Yes, but …’ She paused. ‘But Jack doesn’t seem to understand me now.’

杰克再次点了点头，吉尔说：“是的，但是……”她停顿了一下。“但是杰克现在似乎不理解我的意思。”

I waited, hoping she would say more but she didn’t.

我等着，希望她能再说些什么，但她没有。

‘What is it, Jill, that he doesn’t understand?’ I asked. I knew this was a risky strategy, that asking a question might lead to me asking another, until I was essentially cross-examining her. But I felt I had to help her along a bit if we were to make any progress.

“吉尔，他到底哪里不明白？”我问。我知道这是个冒险的策略，问一个问题很可能会引出更多的问题，最终我几乎是在盘问她。但我觉得，如果我们想要取得任何进展，就必须帮她一把。

‘I have no more income; we have no more money.’

“我没有收入了；我们没有钱了。”

I looked at Jack but his face was blank.

我看向杰克，但他面无表情。

‘That must be really quite frightening.’

“那一定很可怕。”

Jill then began to speak, telling me she’d inherited money, a great deal of money. They’d lived off her inheritance since they left art school but the last of it had gone on building the studio. Jack needed it and so they built it but now they had nothing left. She shrugged her shoulders helplessly and again I looked at Jack who was staring out of the window.

吉尔接着开口，告诉我她继承了一笔钱，一大笔钱。自从他们离开艺术学校后，就一直靠这笔遗产生活，但最后一点钱都用来盖工作室了。杰克需要这笔钱，所以他们才盖了工作室，但现在他们什么都没剩下。她无奈地耸了耸肩，我又看向杰克，他正望着窗外。

I confess a wave of rage came over me. For God’s sake Jack, I thought, get a grip. Then I wondered if this feeling in me was possibly linked to Jill’s suppressed anger?

我承认，一股怒火涌上心头。看在上帝的份上，杰克，我想，冷静点。然后我开始怀疑，我内心的这种感觉是否与吉尔压抑的愤怒有关？

‘Would you like Jack to be more engaged with this, Jill? Perhaps it feels like you’re alone with the worry about money?’

“吉尔，你希望杰克能更多地参与到这件事中来吗？也许你觉得只有你一个人在为钱发愁？”

She looked thoughtful and said, with an air of finality, ‘I don’t want to worry Jack.’

她若有所思地看了看，语气坚定地说：“我不想让杰克担心。”

A sense of hopelessness came over me. Then I rallied and said, ‘Do you feel concerned, Jack? About the financial situation?’

我顿时感到一阵绝望。然后我振作起来，问道：“杰克，你担心吗？担心财务状况？”

He shook his head and pursed his lips but didn’t speak. I decided to be blunter.

他摇了摇头，抿了抿嘴，但没有说话。我决定直截了当地说。

‘What would it mean for you, Jack, if the money runs out?’

“杰克，如果钱用完了，对你来说意味着什么？”

He looked taken aback, as though this was a question he’d never considered. I could see that Jill was watching him intently. ‘I don’t really know. I think we’d be fine.’

他看起来很吃惊，好像这个问题他从未想过。我看到吉尔正专注地看着他。“我也不知道。我想我们应该没问题。”

The three of us sat in silence for some time. I felt hopeless and began to worry that they wouldn’t come back and my training supervisor, whom I had to present the case to, would see me as a failure. I had to do something. But what?

我们三人沉默地坐了一会儿。我感到绝望，开始担心他们不会回来，而我的培训主管——我必须向他汇报情况——会认为我失败了。我必须做点什么。可是，我该做什么呢？

The silence seemed interminable. Eventually, I said, ‘I think in different ways you’re both telling me how challenging it is to be here and how scary it is to discuss anything difficult between you. I noticed today that it took you a long time to come upstairs, as if you’re both very reluctant in some way to start this process, and I notice that both of you seem very committed to keeping things smooth between you.’

沉默似乎永无止境。最终，我开口说道：“我觉得你们俩都在用不同的方式告诉我，待在这里有多么艰难，以及你们之间讨论任何棘手的问题有多么可怕。我注意到今天你们花了很长时间才上楼，好像你们都有些不情愿开始这个过程，而且我也注意到你们俩似乎都非常想维持彼此之间的和平。”

Relief washed over me as Jack began to speak. ‘Jill doesn’t seem to want to be … close. I don’t know why and it’s a bit of a shame …’

杰克开口说话时，我如释重负。“吉尔似乎不想……亲近我。我不知道为什么，这有点可惜……”

‘Close?’ I repeated.

“快到了吗？”我重复道。

‘Yep. That’s right. Close,’ Jack said, looking down at his feet.

“嗯，没错，差不多了。”杰克说着，低头看着自己的脚。

‘Do you perhaps mean that you don’t have any sexual intimacy anymore?’

“你是不是指你们之间已经没有任何性生活了？”

They both nodded.

他们俩都点了点头。

‘Can you tell me a little about how that part of your life has been over the years?’ I suggested.

“您能跟我说说这些年来您生活中的那部分经历吗？”我建议道。

Jack then spoke at some length about how they’d had a good sex life. How they were both virgins when they met and how, in those days, people didn’t have sex before marriage. But they had and it was part of breaking free from their families. But then it stopped. They didn’t seem to know why it had stopped and when I asked how long it was since they’d last had sex, I was shocked to hear that it was 25 years.

杰克随后滔滔不绝地讲述了他们曾经多么美好的性生活。他们相遇时都是处男处女，在那个年代，人们婚前守贞。但他们婚前有过性行为，这算是他们摆脱家庭束缚的一种方式。然而后来，性生活戛然而止。他们似乎也不知道原因，当我问起他们上次性生活是什么时候时，我震惊地得知已经过去了25年。

‘I think it’s less than that, Jack. Much less,’ Jill said. Jack didn’t look at her nor demur but simply sat stony-faced, looking at me.

“我觉得比那少得多，杰克。”吉尔说。杰克既没看她，也没反驳，只是面无表情地坐在那里，看着我。

I felt ill-equipped to respond. What could I usefully say to this couple who were nearly 30 years older than me?

我感到自己不知所措。对于这对比我年长近30岁的夫妇，我能说些什么有用的话呢？

The sessions continued like this for many weeks. Neither of them would speak without being prompted and my attempts to open up any exploration between them was met with silence, laughter or they changed the subject. It was my first salutary lesson in seeing how rigid and complete a couple’s defences could be. They worked together seamlessly to keep me out. And yet, and yet, they kept coming, so I felt somewhere there was a part of them that hoped for change.

这样的会面持续了好几个星期。他们俩都不主动开口，我试图打开他们之间的心扉，但得到的要么是沉默，要么是笑声，要么就是他们转移话题。这是我第一次深刻地体会到，夫妻之间的防御机制可以多么严密和完整。他们配合默契，把我拒之门外。然而，即便如此，他们还是坚持来，所以我感觉他们内心深处还是渴望改变的。

In the weekly case discussion group I attended as part of my training, Jack and Jill became a regular feature. I’d talk about them often, seeking help. My young colleagues would look sympathetically at me as I began to speak about the frustration I felt with the couple. My supervisor encouraged me to keep going, saying that by bearing the frustration and interpreting their fear of change, he believed that, sooner or later, like warm water on a lump of ice, they’d begin to melt and open things up.

在我每周参加的案例讨论小组里，杰克和吉尔的案例成了常客。我经常谈论他们，寻求帮助。当我开始倾诉我对这对夫妇的沮丧时，年轻的同事们会同情地看着我。我的主管鼓励我坚持下去，他说，只要我忍受这种沮丧，并理解他们对改变的恐惧，他相信，迟早有一天，就像温水融化冰块一样，他们会开始融化，敞开心扉。

Whilst the physical vista of my consulting room is simply its four white walls, each patient brings in, along with their problems, the richness of their internal and, indeed, their external life. They talk about their homes, their new sofa and the friends they’ve invited for lunch. They discuss holidays and argue over school choices, evoking in my mind’s eye a home, a restaurant, a friend or even a meal. I follow my patients through their lives and on that journey, I try to help them make sense of all the feelings and conflicts that life provokes. However, just occasionally a patient brings nothing. No images. No events. No friends. The world they evoke inside me is empty, devoid of life. These are the most worrying cases and the hardest to bear.

我的诊室虽然只有四面白墙，但每位病人带来的，不仅是他们的问题，还有他们丰富多彩的内心世界，乃至他们丰富多彩的外部生活。他们谈论自己的家，新买的沙发，以及邀请来吃午饭的朋友。他们讨论假期，争论择校，这些都让我的脑海中浮现出一个个家、一家餐厅、一位朋友，甚至一顿饭的画面。我陪伴着我的病人走过他们的人生旅程，在这个过程中，我努力帮助他们理解生活中所有的感受和冲突。然而，偶尔也会有病人什么也带来。没有画面，没有事件，没有朋友。他们在我心中唤起的世界是空荡荡的，毫无生气。这些是最令人担忧、最难承受的案例。

Jack and Jill were like this. I had no images, no scenes or interactions inside my mind to help me understand their lives. All I had was their blankness, which seemed, despite their profession, to lack any colour or creativity. Issues they touched on, such as the lack of sex or money, though obviously important, somehow got dropped. Nothing seemed to get developed or resolved and I felt dull and frustrated, disappointed that nothing seemed to change or move. I was stuck. They were stuck.

杰克和吉尔就是这样。我的脑海中没有任何画面、场景或互动来帮助我理解他们的生活。我能感受到的只有他们的空白，尽管他们从事着某种职业，但这种空白似乎缺乏任何色彩或创造力。他们谈到的一些问题，比如性生活或金钱的匮乏，虽然显然很重要，却不知为何总是被搁置。似乎没有什么问题得到发展或解决，我感到麻木和沮丧，失望于一切都停滞不前。我被困住了。他们也被困住了。

Though I had enquired on several occasions, they’d told me very little about their early family lives and strangely, what they’d told me was so bland it seemed to slip from my mind as soon as they spoke. So I felt excited and alert when, during one session six months after they’d started therapy, Jill began to speak about her sister.

虽然我曾多次询问，但他们很少提及早年的家庭生活，而且奇怪的是，他们说的那些事儿都平淡无奇，我一听就忘得一干二净。所以，在他们开始接受治疗六个月后的一次咨询中，吉尔突然谈起她的妹妹时，我感到既兴奋又警觉。

‘She’s coming to stay with us next week,’ Jill said brightly. ‘My younger sister, Joan. She’s coming out of hospital.’

“她下周要来和我们一起住，”吉尔兴高采烈地说。“我妹妹琼，她刚出院。”

I waited and hoped my face showed that I was interested to hear more. I was now wary of becoming like a cross-examiner, asking question after question.

我静静地等待着，希望我的表情能表现出我很乐意继续听下去。我小心翼翼地避免自己变成一个盘问者，一个接一个地问问题。

‘She’s schizophrenic. I think I told you.’ I was sure she hadn’t. ‘She’s coming to stay so I’ve been sorting out a room.’ She paused. ‘Which is difficult because it means moving so much stuff. I asked Jack to help but you’re too busy, aren’t you, Jack?’

“她有精神分裂症。我想我跟你说过。” 我确信她没说过。“她要来住一段时间，所以我一直在收拾房间。” 她停顿了一下。“这很困难，因为这意味着要搬很多东西。我让杰克帮忙，但你太忙了，对吧，杰克？”

Jack nodded. ‘I’m not looking forward to this.’

杰克点了点头。“我可不想面对这件事。”

‘Her coming?’ I queried. As usual, it was like getting blood out of a stone but gradually Jack admitted he was worried about Jill getting too tired, which would disrupt their work.

“她要来吗？”我问道。和往常一样，这简直难如登天，但杰克最终还是承认，他担心吉尔会太累，影响他们的工作。

‘Joan can be quite demanding, particularly of Jill. How are you going to get it all done if you’ve got to look after her all the time? We really need to focus on the show,’ Jack said, his tone now slightly querulous.

“琼对吉尔的要求很高，尤其是对她。你要是得一直照顾她，怎么可能把所有事情都做完呢？我们真的需要把精力集中在节目上，”杰克说着，语气中带着一丝抱怨。

‘She’s had it awfully hard, Jack. We’ve been lucky. She’s been in and out of hospital all her life. I think she was very affected by what happened with my parents,’ Jill said, addressing me.

“杰克，她过得太艰难了。我们很幸运。她一生都在医院里进进出出。我想她深受我父母遭遇的影响，”吉尔对我说。

‘What happened with your parents?’ I asked, suddenly curious and hoping that something important might now be shared. But I tried to hold my curiosity in check, if Jill could see how interested I was, she would shut down and disappear. It was like tempting a nervous wild animal to come and eat from your hand.

“你父母怎么了？”我突然好奇地问道，希望能听到什么重要的消息。但我努力克制住自己的好奇心，如果吉尔看出我这么感兴趣，她肯定会立刻闭嘴消失。这就像引诱一只紧张的野生动物过来吃你手里的东西一样。

‘Well. Long story,’ she giggled awkwardly. And then she told me that her mother had often been ill with ‘nervous complaints’, which her father had found infuriating. There would be horrible fights where he would become violent, telling the children he was teaching their mother to behave.

“嗯，说来话长，”她尴尬地笑了笑。然后她告诉我，她母亲经常因为“神经衰弱”而生病，这让她父亲非常恼火。他们之间会发生可怕的争吵，父亲会变得暴力，并告诉孩子们他是在教训他们的母亲要懂事。

It was painful to listen to and I began to feel sad for her.

听起来很让人难过，我开始为她感到难过。

‘It must have been very frightening for you and your sister,’ I said. But she didn’t reply and, as Jill spoke more about her mother’s illness, I began to wonder how much she’d had to disconnect from these traumatic events, losing the capacity to be in touch with many kinds of feelings.

“这对你和你妹妹来说一定很可怕，”我说。但她没有回答，随着吉尔继续讲述她母亲的病情，我开始怀疑她究竟在多大程度上与这些创伤性事件脱节，以至于失去了感知各种情感的能力。

‘The problem was that even though my father would try quite patiently to explain to her that she couldn’t spend all night locking and unlocking the doors, she just couldn’t help herself. And then he’d explode and hit her.’ Jill looked stricken and almost puzzled as she spoke.

“问题是，尽管我父亲很有耐心地向她解释，她不能整晚不停地锁门开门，但她就是控制不住自己。然后他就会勃然大怒，打她。”吉尔说着，神情痛苦，几乎有些困惑。

As she continued, it began to be clear that her mother had suffered from obsessional compulsions. Jill described how she’d clean manically, even though they had maids. Her mother was terrified that she and her sister had lice in their hair and would insist on washing and combing their hair four or five times a day. When things were bad, her mother would lock herself in her bedroom and refuse to come out and sometimes that went on for days, perhaps weeks. Jill couldn’t remember which.

随着讲述的深入，吉尔渐渐明白母亲患有强迫症。她描述说，即使家里有女佣，母亲也会疯狂地打扫卫生。母亲害怕她和妹妹头发里有虱子，坚持每天给她们洗头梳头四五次。情况糟糕的时候，母亲会把自己锁在卧室里，拒绝出来，有时甚至持续几天，几周。吉尔记不清具体是几天还是几周了。

‘I think it was hard on Joan, she was so little. And in a different way for my elder brother, Ted.’

“我觉得这对琼来说很艰难，她当时还那么小。而对我的哥哥泰德来说，情况则有所不同。”

‘Why for Ted?’ I asked.

“为什么是泰德？”我问。

‘He’d get involved. I’d run away and hide in the summer house, but Ted …’ She paused and looked at Jack. ‘Ted would try to protect Mother. He’d always try to protect her and then my father would hit him too.’

“他会插手。我会逃走躲到避暑别墅里，但是泰德……”她停顿了一下，看向杰克。“泰德会想方设法保护妈妈。他总是想保护她，然后我爸爸也会打他。”

She stopped and looked at me, then sighed but she didn’t cry.

她停下来看着我，然后叹了口气，但她没有哭。

‘He killed himself, you know. When he was 21. Just before I met you, wasn’t it?’ she said, turning to Jack.

“你知道吗，他自杀了。他才21岁。就在我认识你之前，对吧？”她说着，转向杰克。

He nodded but said nothing.

他点了点头，但什么也没说。

‘Have you heard Jill talk about all this before, Jack?’ I asked.

“杰克，你以前听吉尔说过这些事吗？”我问。

He shook his head, looking suddenly overwhelmed. ‘I knew about Ted but not about the other stuff, no. I knew Jill’s father was cranky and I knew your mother wasn’t always well. But you never told me about this.’ I thought how sad it was that Jill had never shared this with Jack, but I was beginning to understand how little they really talked about anything painful or difficult.

他摇了摇头，突然显得有些不知所措。“我知道泰德的事，但其他的事我一概不知。我知道吉尔的父亲脾气暴躁，也知道你母亲身体不太好。但你从来没跟我说过这些。”我想，吉尔从未跟杰克提起过这些，真是令人难过。但我开始明白，他们之间很少谈及任何痛苦或困难的事情。

‘Jack never met my mother; she died just before we graduated. Had a heart attack,’ Jill said baldly.

“杰克从未见过我母亲；她就在我们毕业前去世了。死于心脏病，”吉尔直截了当地说。

‘She was very thin,’ Jack added.

“她很瘦，”杰克补充道。

‘She didn’t eat. She never ate. Neither did Ted.’ And suddenly I noticed how thin Jack was. He looked half-starved.

“她不吃东西。她从来不吃东西。泰德也不吃。”我突然注意到杰克有多瘦。他看起来像是饿坏了。

After they left, I thought about what I’d been missing; everything seemed much more serious. I was suddenly aware of how vulnerable they were and that if Jack and Jill began to open things up, their stuck sameness might become something quite unstable and even, perhaps, perilous.

他们走后，我开始反思自己错过了什么；一切似乎都变得更加严肃了。我突然意识到他们有多么脆弱，如果杰克和吉尔开始敞开心扉，他们僵化的现状可能会变得非常不稳定，甚至可能很危险。

Something shifted in me after that. I stopped feeling frustrated and began to feel deep concern and, perhaps because they sensed my concern, they began to talk more freely in their sessions. I learnt that Joan had also tried to kill herself on several occasions. I learnt that before he died, Jill’s father had developed Lewy Body Dementia, with the result he’d begun to have vivid, psychotic hallucinations. The doctors missed the dementia and he’d been committed to a psychiatric hospital; the same hospital that her mother had been in and out of. The more I learnt about her family, the more I began to understand just why she’d retreated ‘into the woods’ with Jack.

那之后，我的内心发生了某种转变。我不再感到沮丧，而是开始深感担忧。或许是因为他们察觉到了我的担忧，他们在咨询中也开始更加坦诚地交流。我了解到琼也曾多次试图自杀。我还了解到，吉尔的父亲在去世前患上了路易体痴呆症，导致他开始出现生动而精神错乱的幻觉。医生们未能诊断出他的痴呆症，他被送进了精神病院；而吉尔的母亲也曾多次出入那家医院。我对她的家庭了解得越多，就越能理解她为什么会和杰克一起“隐居”到森林深处。

As the weeks passed, it became clear that Joan was causing problems between them. She demanded lots of care and attention, which disrupted the seemingly smooth, unruffled surface of their life. Where once they talked haltingly about the neighbours and the planning department, they now talked incessantly about Joan. I heard about the mess she’d left in the kitchen, about her wandering about at night, leaving on all the lights, and I had the sense, and said so, that whilst this was a nuisance, it was also a way for them to bond with each other. The problems, once again, were outside of their relationship – they could cosily join up against a common enemy, such as the planners or now, it seemed, Joan.

随着时间推移，琼给他们之间带来的问题越来越明显。她需要大量的照顾和关注，这打破了他们看似平静祥和的生活。以前他们只是断断续续地谈论邻居和规划部门，现在却不停地谈论琼。我听说她把厨房弄得一团糟，晚上到处闲逛，还总是开着灯。我感觉，也确实说过，虽然这很烦人，但这也是他们增进感情的一种方式。再一次，问题出在了他们关系之外——他们可以心照不宣地联合起来对抗共同的敌人，比如规划部门，或者现在看来，就是琼。

However, one small but significant difference between them began to be tentatively expressed. For some time, they’d been talking about how much time it was taking for Jack to make this one piece. The sculpture seemed to involve a complex mosaic of thousands of glass shards and Jack was increasingly stressed that it would never be completed on time. After hearing about this problem for the fifth time, I found myself asking if they’d ever thought about getting any help? I knew many artists had studio assistants.

然而，他们之间一个虽小却意义重大的分歧开始显露出来。一段时间以来，他们一直在讨论杰克制作这件作品所花费的时间。这件雕塑似乎由成千上万块玻璃碎片组成，结构复杂，杰克越来越担心它永远无法按时完成。在第五次听到这个问题后，我不禁问他们是否考虑过寻求帮助？我知道很多艺术家都有工作室助理。

‘We never allow anyone but us into the studio,’ Jack insisted.

“我们绝不允许除我们以外的任何人进入录音室，”杰克坚持道。

I thought about how the studio seemed like a kind of microcosm of their relationship, something that shut out the world – a kind of retreat.

我想，工作室就像是他们关系的缩影，一个与世隔绝的地方——一种避世之所。

‘Why not?’ I asked. I was feeling that they needed a challenge. Their complete agreement over Joan’s misdeeds had left me wanting to disrupt their accord.

“为什么不呢？”我问。我觉得他们需要一些挑战。他们对琼的恶行竟然完全达成一致，这让我很想打破他们的默契。

‘Well, we just never do. No one would be able to help; it’s not like that, Susanna,’ Jack blustered.

“唉，我们从来不这么做。没人能帮上忙；事情不是你想的那样，苏珊娜，”杰克气急败坏地说。

‘Maybe Joan could help. She could polish the glass. She could even stick the glass,’ Jill said tentatively.

“或许琼能帮上忙。她可以把玻璃擦亮，甚至可以把玻璃粘起来。”吉尔试探性地说。

‘I don’t think so. She wouldn’t anyway,’ Jack said, dismissing her. Turning to me, he added, ‘She’s very lazy. She doesn’t get out of bed till midday.’ He laughed.

“我不这么认为。反正她也不会，”杰克不以为然地说。他转向我，补充道：“她很懒。不到中午都不起床。”说完，他笑了。

‘I don’t know. It could be good for her. And it’d really help me,’ Jill uncharacteristically persisted.

“我不知道。这对她来说可能是件好事。而且对我来说也很有帮助。”吉尔一反常态地坚持道。

Jack shrugged and then they began to talk about Joan’s slovenly ways again, smoothing down the little ripple that had emerged between them.

杰克耸了耸肩，然后他们又开始谈论琼邋遢的生活方式，平息了两人之间出现的一丝小摩擦。

But these differences began to emerge more frequently. I could see that Jill was beginning to find her own voice, challenging Jack just a little. Had it helped her to watch me gently challenge him? Was she beginning to feel less frightened of taking her own view?

但这些分歧开始越来越频繁地出现。我看得出来，吉尔开始有了自己的想法，也开始稍微挑战杰克。看着我温和地挑战他，对她有帮助吗？她是不是开始不再那么害怕表达自己的观点了？

It was September and I’d been working with Jack and Jill for nearly a year. I’d just returned from my summer break and it was the first session back. As usual, I phoned down to reception to tell them to come up and, once again, the minutes ticked past the hour and they didn’t appear. I stood in the doorway looking down the long corridor towards the lifts expecting them at any minute to emerge. The lift doors opened and a group of people tumbled out but Jack and Jill were not amongst them. I went back into my office and dialled down to reception but, though I tried several times, the phone was engaged and I couldn’t get through. I looked anxiously down the corridor again – still no sign. Where were they?

那是九月，我和杰克、吉尔一起工作快一年了。我刚结束暑假回来，这是开学后的第一节课。像往常一样，我打电话到前台让他们上来，时间一分一秒地过去，他们却迟迟没有出现。我站在门口，望着长长的走廊尽头的电梯，盼着他们随时都能出来。电梯门开了，一群人涌了出来，但杰克和吉尔不在其中。我回到办公室，再次拨打前台电话，但尽管我打了好几次，电话始终占线，无法接通。我焦急地再次望向走廊——仍然不见踪影。他们到底去哪儿了？

It was nearly twenty past the hour when I heard their footsteps outside my door, I jumped up from my chair and held the door wide as they shuffled in. I waited patiently, though I didn’t feel patient, as they arranged their bags and then we sat down, looking at each other intently.

快到二十分的时候，我听到门外传来他们的脚步声。我立刻从椅子上跳起来，把门大开，让他们拖着脚步走了进来。我耐心地等着，虽然心里并不耐烦。他们整理好行李后，我们坐了下来，彼此凝视着。

‘Was there a problem downstairs?’ I asked. ‘I wondered where you’d got to.’

“楼下出什么事了吗？”我问。“我想知道你去了哪里。”

They looked embarrassed; Jill had her head lowered and Jack avoided my eye. A kind of awkwardness descended on the room and I felt myself grow hot with discomfort, though I didn’t understand why. Had I asked something I shouldn’t?

他们看起来很尴尬；吉尔低着头，杰克则避开了我的目光。房间里弥漫着一种尴尬的气氛，我感到一阵燥热，浑身不自在，却又不明白为什么。难道我问了什么不该问的问题吗？

Jill raised her head. ‘I’m sorry we kept you waiting. Sometimes, we go in the toilets … together … for a cuddle. Sometimes, and I think it’s when we’re stressed out, we have a cuddle in the toilets before coming in.’ And then she looked at Jack and they both laughed and so did I as I remembered all the other times they’d seemed to take forever coming up from the waiting room. ‘Maybe some of the stress today is coming back after the long break?’ I said.

吉尔抬起头。“抱歉让你们久等了。有时候，我们会一起去洗手间……抱抱。有时候，我觉得是因为我们压力比较大，所以会在进来之前先在洗手间抱抱。”说完，她看了看杰克，他们俩都笑了，我也跟着笑了，因为我想起了之前几次他们从候诊室出来好像过了好久好久。“也许今天因为休息时间太长，压力又回来了？”我说。

It was quiet then for a while and then Jill spoke again. ‘Joan’s back in hospital. I took her back last weekend.’ She looked glum. ‘She smashed up one of Jack’s pieces in the studio.’

一阵沉默后，吉尔又开口了。“琼又住院了。上周末我把她送回去的。”她看起来很沮丧。“她在工作室里砸坏了杰克的一件作品。”

I drew a sharp, shocked intake of breath and looked at Jack who sighed mightily as he slowly began to speak. ‘Yup, completely destroyed it. With a hammer.’

我倒吸一口凉气，震惊不已，看向杰克，他重重地叹了口气，缓缓开口道：“没错，彻底毁了。用锤子砸的。”

There was something shocking about this destruction, such a counterpoint to Jack and Jill’s impassive calm. ‘Mad’ Joan, amok with a hammer, whilst they sat there and calmly explained that the piece wasn’t in fact one that Jack planned to show and what a relief it had been that she hadn’t smashed ‘Cave’.

这种破坏令人震惊，与杰克和吉尔的冷静沉着形成了鲜明的对比。“疯子”琼挥舞着锤子横冲直撞，而他们却坐在那里，平静地解释说，这件作品其实并非杰克计划展出的，幸好她没有砸碎《洞穴》。

‘Cave?’ I questioned.

“山洞？”我问道。

‘Oh, that’s the piece Joan was helping with and it’s really large and an important piece. That would’ve been a complete disaster if she’d taken a hammer to that!’

“哦，那是琼帮忙做的那件作品，它真的很大，而且很重要。如果她拿锤子砸它，那就彻底完蛋了！”

They began to talk about the piece – how intricate it was and how they hoped it would sell. The piece appeared to be a kind of inverted mosaic, most of which was hidden from view. They talked on and on about the number of glass pieces that were involved and how much Jack’s dealer thought it might sell for. At first, I felt quite engaged with their chatter but then I remembered Joan and this shocking act of violence.

他们开始谈论那件作品——它多么精巧复杂，以及他们希望它能卖个好价钱。这件作品看起来像是一种倒置的马赛克，大部分都被遮挡住了。他们滔滔不绝地谈论着作品中用了多少玻璃碎片，以及杰克的经销商估计它能卖多少钱。起初，我被他们的谈话吸引住了，但随后我想起了琼和那起令人震惊的暴力事件。

‘As you talk about this piece of sculpture, it makes me think how much you both hide from view; how much you both retreat into a kind of cave, away from painful things. You’ve told me that something terrible and violent has happened, yet it’s very difficult for you to really stay with that. Perhaps, also, the thought of talking to me about this made you retreat together into a kind of “toilet cave” before the session?’

“你谈到这件雕塑作品时，让我想到你们俩都隐藏了多少东西；你们都躲进某种洞穴，逃避痛苦的事情。你告诉我发生了可怕的暴力事件，但你很难真正面对它。或许，想到要和我谈论这件事，你们在咨询前也一起躲进了某种‘厕所洞穴’里？”

Jack looked at me glaringly, clearly annoyed.

杰克恶狠狠地瞪了我一眼，显然很生气。

‘I don’t know why we come to see you, Susanna. I really didn’t want to come today. I don’t see the point and if Jill wasn’t so into it, I’m afraid I’d never come again. I really don’t think it’s useful to dig all of this up; we need to look forward, not back. I’ve got to focus on the exhibition now, not Joan or this … stuff.’

“苏珊娜，我不知道我们为什么要来看你。我今天真的不想来。我觉得没意义，要不是吉尔那么热衷，恐怕我以后都不会来了。我觉得把这些事翻出来真的没用；我们应该向前看，而不是向后看。我现在得专注于展览，而不是琼或者这些……破事。”

I’d never heard Jack be so tetchy or so forthcoming and it felt like a huge relief that here he was, for the first time, speaking his mind.

我从未听过杰克如此暴躁或如此坦率，他第一次说出自己的想法，这让我如释重负。

‘Don’t be so rude, Jack!’ Jill interjected. ‘Susanna’s just trying to help us. I’m sick of you being so negative about our sessions.’

“杰克，别这么没礼貌！”吉尔插嘴道，“苏珊娜只是想帮我们。我受够了你对我们的治疗总是这么消极。”

‘I don’t think it is helpful. If Susanna hadn’t suggested it, Joan wouldn’t have come into the studio at all. And the whole thing’s really upset everything and put it all back. And you’ve been in a complete state since. How is that helpful?’ Jack concluded, his face reddened and his voice shaky with rage.

“我觉得这没用。如果不是苏珊娜提议，琼根本不会来录音棚。这件事把一切都搞砸了，让之前的努力都白费了。而且你从那以后一直心神不宁。这有什么用呢？”杰克总结道，他脸涨得通红，声音因愤怒而颤抖。

It was as though some dam had broken and something raw and violent was now exposed in him. The anger so long suppressed now sat in the room. I tried to speak about how frightening these feelings were and how much they’d tried to avoid them but I didn’t get very far. The session ended badly, with neither of them looking me in the eye as they left.

仿佛一道堤坝决堤，他内心深处某种原始而狂暴的东西瞬间爆发。长久以来被压抑的愤怒此刻弥漫在房间里。我试图和他们谈谈这些感受有多么可怕，以及他们如何努力逃避，但收效甚微。咨询以糟糕的方式结束，他们离开时甚至都没正眼看我。

I was concerned but unsurprised when the following week I got a message from them saying they were sorry but they couldn’t come today. They’d never cancelled a session before and I felt worried that they’d been so frightened by the conflict that they’d now terminate the therapy. I sat in the consulting room alone, chewing on my biro as I drafted a letter to say that I looked forward to seeing them next week. But the following week, I waited for the hour and, again, they didn’t come. I checked with the office. Had they called? No, they hadn’t. I drafted another letter acknowledging how difficult the last session had been and reminding them that I’d be waiting for them the following week. I knew if they didn’t arrive again, I’d probably have to close the case and that would cause problems with my training and leave me feeling I’d failed and let Jack and Jill down. My group of fellow trainees consoled me and my supervisor talked about how couples could powerfully avoid change if it threatened their relationship.

一周后，我收到他们的信息，说很抱歉今天来不了，我虽然担心，但并不意外。他们以前从未取消过咨询，我担心他们是不是因为冲突而感到害怕，所以决定终止治疗。我独自坐在咨询室里，一边嚼着圆珠笔，一边起草一封信，告诉他们我期待下周见到他们。但下周，我等了一个小时，他们还是没来。我问了办公室，他们打电话了吗？没有。我又起草了一封信，承认上次咨询很艰难，并提醒他们我下周会等他们。我知道如果他们再次爽约，我可能不得不结案，这会影响我的培训，也会让我觉得自己失败了，辜负了杰克和吉尔。我的同事们安慰我，我的督导也谈到，如果改变会威胁到他们的关系，夫妻双方可能会极力回避。

By the following week, I expected nothing; they hadn’t been in touch, and I was sure they weren’t going to come. So it was much to my surprise when at 3pm on the dot the phone rang and the receptionist informed me that Jack and Jill were on their way up. Seconds later, I heard them coming along the corridor and I opened the door to let them in.

到了下周，我什么也没期待；他们一直没联系我，我确信他们不会来了。所以，下午三点整，电话铃声响起，前台告诉我杰克和吉尔正在来的路上，这让我非常惊讶。几秒钟后，我听到他们沿着走廊走来，便打开门让他们进来。

‘We’re really sorry about last week, Susanna,’ Jill said hurriedly as she sat down. ‘We should have been in touch but we’ve had such a difficult time.’ She nodded her head at Jack and I followed her gaze to Jack’s hand, which was hidden under a substantial bandage.

“苏珊娜，我们对上周的事真的很抱歉，”吉尔一边坐下一边匆匆说道，“我们本应该联系你的，但我们最近实在太难了。”她朝杰克点了点头，我顺着她的目光看向杰克的手，他的手被厚厚的绷带包扎着。

Jack looked at me and there was something shamefaced and awkward in his gaze.

杰克看了我一眼，眼神中带着一丝羞愧和尴尬。

‘What happened?’ I asked gently.

“发生了什么事？”我轻声问道。

‘You say,’ Jack appealed to Jill. I looked at Jill, who looked shrunken and old, as though all the life had been sucked out of her.

“你说，”杰克对吉尔说道。我看着吉尔，她看起来憔悴苍老，仿佛所有的生命力都被抽走了。

‘He stabbed himself with a point chisel. He had an … an … upset and afterwards he went into the studio and, well, er … hurt himself.’

“他用尖凿刺伤了自己。他当时情绪很低落，之后他去了录音室，然后，呃……伤到了自己。”

There was a silence.

一片寂静。

‘He was in hospital. Just got out yesterday …’ she said, trailing off, her voice barely audible.

“他之前在医院，昨天刚出院……”她说着，声音渐渐低了下去，几乎听不见了。

It took some time but gradually I heard how they had had to call an ambulance and how, in casualty, Jack had become so distressed that they’d admitted him to the psychiatric ward. I said how frightening this must have been, for Jack himself and for Jill to see Jack like this, when he was always so quiet and controlled.

过了一会儿，我才慢慢了解到他们是如何叫了救护车，以及杰克在急诊室里情绪崩溃，被送进了精神科病房的。我说，这对杰克本人来说一定很可怕，对吉尔来说也是如此，看到杰克这样，他平时总是那么安静沉稳。

They reacted to my comments with silence. Jack, head bowed, stared at his hand and Jill looked at him expectantly.

他们沉默不语，没有回应我的话。杰克低着头，盯着自己的手，吉尔则满怀期待地看着他。

‘It’s not the first time, Susanna. I’ve seen him like this before. He’s done it before,’ Jill said awkwardly, as though confessing something to me that was secret.

“这已经不是第一次了，苏珊娜。我以前见过他这样。他以前就这么做过。”吉尔尴尬地说，仿佛在向我坦白什么秘密。

I turned to Jack. Would he say more?

我转向杰克。他还会再说些什么吗？

‘When we were students. I got in a state just before our finals, our graduation show.’

“我们还是学生的时候，在期末考试和毕业演出前夕，我情绪非常低落。”

‘You cut your wrists,’ Jill interjected, challenging Jack to be more specific.

“你割腕了，”吉尔插话道，质问杰克要不要说得更具体些。

‘Yep,’ Jack nodded reluctantly. ‘Yes, I did. I thought I was going to fail.’

“嗯，”杰克不情愿地点了点头。“是的，我当时以为自己要失败了。”

The atmosphere in the room felt electric, as though Jill was humiliating him and stripping Jack of every ounce of his pride. I could feel the sense of shame and sadness that sat between them and I felt I had to find a way to help Jack speak about himself.

房间里的气氛令人窒息，仿佛吉尔正在羞辱他，剥夺杰克所有的尊严。我能感受到他们之间弥漫的羞耻和悲伤，我觉得我必须想办法帮助杰克敞开心扉，谈谈自己。

But it wasn’t Jack who spoke then; it was Jill who told me about the psychiatrist they’d talked to and the discussion of medication and the follow-up appointment they had to attend next week. And, as she talked, I felt her soothing Jack. She talked almost as if it was she who had stabbed herself, as though it was both of them who were due to see the doctor next Tuesday. I felt wrapped up in this comforting chatter whilst Jack stayed silent, imprisoned in his feelings. The moment of raw honesty had evaporated and we were back to everything being shut down between them. Every feeling was to be calmed and everything I said or tried to explore as the session went on was met with resistance and smiles.

但当时开口说话的不是杰克，而是吉尔。她告诉我他们之前咨询过的精神科医生，讨论过药物治疗，以及下周的复诊预约。吉尔说话的时候，我感觉她在安抚杰克。她说话的语气仿佛是她自己刺伤了自己，仿佛下周二要去看医生的是他们俩。我沉浸在这令人安心的谈话中，而杰克却沉默不语，被困在自己的情绪里。刚才那坦诚的时刻已经消散，他们之间又回到了封闭的状态。所有的情绪都需要被安抚，而随着咨询的进行，我说的每一句话，我试图探索的每一个细节，都换来的是他们的抵触和微笑。

My mind drifted; I felt powerless to help them be more real. Perhaps I was even wrong to try to open this up – after all, stirring things up seemed to have made things worse. Maybe they just needed to settle things down and go back to what they felt safe with. Who was I to know?

我思绪飘忽，感觉无力帮助他们更坦诚。或许我当初就不该试图打开这扇门——毕竟，搅浑水似乎让事情变得更糟。也许他们只是需要平静下来，回到让他们感到安全的地方。我又能知道什么呢？

I sat there, gloomy and uncertain how to help, so I said nothing and we sat in silence as Jill’s mollifying chatter trailed off.

我坐在那里，心情沮丧，不知道该如何帮忙，所以什么也没说，我们静静地坐着，吉尔的安慰性絮语渐渐消失。

‘Maybe, we’ve been wondering, should we perhaps take a bit of a break from seeing you?’ Jill began again. ‘I think we’ll be seeing the psychiatrist for a while … maybe it would be better if we just did that?’

“或许，我们一直在想，是不是应该暂时停止见你？”吉尔再次开口。“我想我们会去看一段时间的精神科医生……也许我们这样做会更好？”

‘Perhaps you’re worried it’ll be too much for Jack? You want to protect him and think maybe it’d be easier for him to stop coming here?’

“或许你担心杰克承受不住？你想保护他，觉得他最好别再来这里？”

‘Yes, I think so.’

“是的，我也这么认为。”

We both looked at Jack, waiting for his input.

我们俩都看着杰克，等着他发表意见。

‘We’ll keep coming. You want to come, Jill, so we’ll keep coming,’ Jack said.

“我们会继续来的。吉尔，你想来，所以我们就会继续来。”杰克说。

‘It’s fine, Jack. We can come back when you’re feeling better,’ Jill responded. ‘We could come back, couldn’t we?’ Jill asked, looking anxiously at me.

“没关系，杰克。等你感觉好些了我们再来。”吉尔回答道。“我们可以再来，对吧？”吉尔焦急地看着我问道。

Jill’s anxious fussing felt stultifying and I had a sense this over-protectiveness would force Jack into further silence. And then suddenly I thought about Jill’s brother and his suicide. Was this what made Jill so careful not to upset Jack? Was she like this because she was always terrified that he’d kill himself?

吉尔焦虑不安的唠叨让我感到窒息，我感觉这种过度保护会让杰克更加沉默。突然，我想到了吉尔的哥哥和他的自杀。是不是因为这个，吉尔才如此小心翼翼地不让杰克难过？她是不是因为一直害怕他会自杀才这样？

‘I was thinking, Jill, about your brother and how you said how much Jack, when you first met, had reminded you of him.’

“吉尔，我一直在想你的哥哥，还有你说过你第一次见到杰克时，觉得他很像你哥哥。”

She nodded and I went on.

她点点头，我继续说道。

‘And I was noticing right now how much you seem to want to protect Jack, even when I can see you’ve got quite a lot of your own feelings about what’s happened.’

“我刚才注意到，你似乎非常想保护杰克，即使我看得出来，你对发生的事情也有很多自己的感受。”

She nodded again, though less emphatically.

她再次点头，但这次的力度不如上次那么大了。

‘I suppose I was thinking that this wish to protect Jack might be so strong because you’re very worried that history might repeat itself and you might lose Jack the same way you lost your brother.’

“我想，你如此强烈地想要保护杰克，可能是因为你非常担心历史会重演，你会像失去哥哥一样失去杰克。”

‘Is that right?’ Jack asked, looking intently at Jill. ‘Is that what you’re worried about?’

“真是这样吗？”杰克问道，目光紧紧地盯着吉尔。“你担心的就是这个吗？”

Jill gave a little shrug. ‘Maybe … maybe.’ She mused. And then she talked more about Ted and how much she missed him. His death had come completely out of the blue and to this day she didn’t understand why he’d killed himself. She described how he took his life by driving his van off the cliffs near where they’d grown up. They’d all had lunch together the day before and he’d seemed fine, his usual self. Then we all sat in silence, thinking about Ted as Jill quietly wept.

吉尔耸了耸肩。“也许……也许吧。”她沉思着。然后她又开始谈起泰德，谈起她有多么想念他。他的死完全是晴天霹雳，直到今天她仍然不明白他为什么要自杀。她描述了他是如何开着面包车冲下他们长大地附近的悬崖结束自己生命的。就在前一天，他们还一起吃了午饭，他看起来一切正常，就像往常一样。然后我们都沉默地坐着，想着泰德，吉尔则默默地流下了眼泪。

‘It seems you’ve never really been able to make sense of your brother’s death. Do you feel you can understand why Jack tried to hurt himself?’ I asked.

“看来你一直没能真正理解你哥哥的死。你觉得你能理解杰克为什么会试图伤害自己吗？”我问道。

‘Not really, no. I know I should but I don’t. I don’t.’

“不，真的没有。我知道我应该这样做，但我做不到。我做不到。”

‘Perhaps it feels very dangerous to ask him, Jill?’

“吉尔，你觉得问他这个问题很危险吗？”

She nodded and looked at Jack expectantly but he was silent, wrapped in his own terror.

她点点头，满怀期待地看着杰克，但他却沉默不语，被自己的恐惧所笼罩。

‘I don’t know what he’s thinking, Susanna. I used to. But now, I don’t think I do.’

“我不知道他在想什么，苏珊娜。我以前知道。但现在，我想我不知道了。”

‘Maybe that sense that you really knew each other’s thoughts, felt so close and sure of each other has changed?’

“或许那种彼此了解对方想法、感觉如此亲密、如此信任对方的感觉已经改变了？”

‘Jill’s changed,’ Jack said baldly.

“吉尔变了，”杰克直截了当地说。

‘Have I? I haven’t! I don’t think I have. Have I?’

“我有吗？我没有！我想我没有。我有吗？”

‘In what way has Jill changed, Jack?’ I asked.

我问：“吉尔有哪些变化，杰克？”

‘Do you still love me?’ Jack said, ignoring me now as he turned to Jill.

“你还爱我吗？”杰克说着，不再理会我，转身走向吉尔。

‘Of course I do. I do! Is that why you stabbed yourself? Is it? I do love you Jack, I do. Oh, I do.’

“当然，我爱你。我爱你！这就是你刺伤自己的原因吗？是吗？杰克，我爱你，真的爱你。哦，我爱你。”

Back then, I felt disappointed that I didn’t help Jack and Jill more. I had the zeal and idealism of a young therapist and didn’t understand that a couple only need change a very little bit to make life more rewarding and hopeful. They had been a ‘babes in the wood’ couple and their whole relationship was structured to keep out the dark and scary uncertainties that had threatened them in their childhoods. Gradually they’d come a little way out of this retreat and faced the things in themselves and each other that had haunted them for years. They’d become more open and authentic with each other, and even with me, and, like with all relationships, this openness brought a greater resilience to themselves and their marriage.

那时，我感到很失望，觉得自己没能帮到杰克和吉尔更多。我当时满怀年轻治疗师的热情和理想，却不明白夫妻只需要做出一点点改变，就能让生活更加充实和充满希望。他们就像一对懵懂的“森林里的婴儿”，他们的整个关系结构都是为了抵御童年时期那些黑暗而可怕的不确定因素。渐渐地，他们走出了这种封闭的状态，开始正视那些多年来一直困扰着他们自己和彼此的伤痛。他们变得更加坦诚，对彼此，甚至对我也是如此。就像所有关系一样，这种坦诚为他们自身和他们的婚姻带来了更大的韧性。

Jack began to see a psychoanalyst on his own, which not only helped him with his fears but made Jill feel a bit less responsible for him and for always making sure he was OK. Eventually, after four years, I was leaving the clinic and we agreed that this seemed like it was the right time to stop the couple therapy. I think we could have gone on forever. There was something timeless about the way they lived their lives and that timelessness got into the work with me. We’d become comfortable together and, though from time to time they’d show me that they could be different people with different minds, their longing to be as one was deep inside them. I think they just felt safest there.

杰克开始独自接受心理分析，这不仅帮助他克服了恐惧，也让吉尔感到自己不再那么需要承担照顾他、确保他一切安好的责任。最终，四年后，我离开了诊所，我们都认为现在是时候结束伴侣治疗了。我想我们本可以一直治疗下去。他们的生活方式有一种永恒的特质，这种特质也融入了我的治疗工作中。我们相处得很自在，虽然他们偶尔会展现出不同的性格和想法，但他们内心深处渴望合二为一。我想，他们只是觉得合二为一最安全。

# ↩

Kristof Keeps Kissing the Frog

克里斯托夫不停地亲吻青蛙

I sometimes wonder if humans are up to managing all the feelings that our biology seems to have endowed us with. Years ago, I used to have a recurring dream that I was driving a car but I was too small to reach the pedals with my feet. The car careered towards disaster as I strained to touch the brake. Did the dream represent my anxiety that I wouldn’t be able to manage my own feelings? A childhood hangover, perhaps, of those early experiences of being a toddler, overwhelmed by emotions and unable to contain them? As we grow older, most of us learn not to stamp our feet and roll about on the floor wailing but love affairs can still evoke emotions that spin our heads.

我有时会想，人类是否能够驾驭我们与生俱来的所有情感。多年前，我经常做同一个梦：我开着车，但个子太小，够不到踏板。我拼命想踩刹车，车子却失控冲向了危险的深渊。这个梦是不是象征着我害怕自己无法控制情绪？或许是童年时期那些难以抑制的情绪，让我对幼年时期的情感体验产生了某种预感？随着年龄的增长，我们大多数人学会了不再跺脚哭闹，但爱情仍然会激起我们难以承受的情感。

For some patients, it can come as a shock to discover that they have feelings and wishes they have no conscious awareness of. Because feelings can be so powerful, humans find all sorts of ways of repressing them. Some people sublimate their desires in physical activity. Others use an intense focus on work, a video game or a gripping novel. Sometimes we can somatise repressed emotions, so they get expressed by our body in the form of a headache, a backache or a mysterious stomach upset. And there are, of course, less healthy avenues we adopt to repress and manage emotions, where we numb ourselves with alcohol or drugs.

对一些患者来说，发现自己拥有意识层面无法察觉的情感和愿望，可能会感到震惊。由于情感的力量如此强大，人们会找到各种各样的方式来压抑它们。有些人会通过体育锻炼来释放欲望。有些人则会全身心投入工作、电子游戏或引人入胜的小说。有时，我们会将压抑的情绪躯体化，使其以头痛、背痛或不明原因的胃部不适等形式在身体上表现出来。当然，我们也会采取一些不太健康的途径来压抑和控制情绪，比如用酒精或药物麻痹自己。

But there is one form of managing feelings that is far less known and generally understood, which in psychoanalytic theory is known as ‘projection’. Projection is a mental process whereby we attribute to someone else something we reject or disown in ourselves.
