A typical and common example, which most of us will have employed at some time or another, is when we feel ashamed about a feeling, such as being greedy or aggressive, and shed that shame by identifying that trait in others.

但还有一种情绪管理方式鲜为人知，也鲜为人理解，在精神分析理论中被称为“投射”。投射是一种心理过程，我们会将自己拒绝或否认的某些特质归因于他人。一个典型且常见的例子，我们大多数人或多或少都曾使用过，就是当我们对某种感觉感到羞耻，例如贪婪或好斗时，我们会通过在他人身上找到同样的特质来摆脱这种羞耻感。

Projection can also help explain the inexplicable, such as how and why humans can descend into mass hatred of others and genocide. We have unfortunately seen many situations where one group demonises another group as having ugly traits, such as dishonesty or greed, and then attacks them in a hateful and sometimes murderous way for these traits. One group is then ‘pure’ whilst the other is filled up with all these reviled qualities.

投射也能帮助我们解释一些难以解释的现象，例如人类为何会陷入对他人普遍的仇恨和种族灭绝。不幸的是，我们已经目睹了许多这样的例子：一个群体妖魔化另一个群体，将他们描绘成具有丑陋的特质，例如不诚实或贪婪，然后以充满仇恨甚至杀戮的方式攻击他们。于是，一个群体就成了“纯洁无瑕”的，而另一个群体则被贴上了所有这些令人憎恶的标签。

In a less dramatic way, projection is something I frequently see in the consultancy room. One patient, who came to see me because he was struggling with lethargy and depression, began a session by telling me that over the weekend he’d taken his teenage son to task for spending all weekend playing video games and staring into his phone. The patient complained that he’d bought his son a guitar and paid for lessons, but he never practised or buckled down to learning or doing anything useful. It didn’t take long for us to understand that he was shouting at his son for exactly the things he felt most anxious about in himself, which was his own difficulty with being productive and proactive. He’d started therapy because he felt a failure and had, over his lifetime, been unable to fulfil his promise. Together, we came to understand that he’d been distancing himself from these feelings by accusing his boy of being lazy and aimless. As this realisation dawned on him, his frustration with his son lessened and their relationship improved.

不那么戏剧化地说，我在咨询室里经常看到投射现象。一位来找我的病人，因为他感到精神萎靡和抑郁，在咨询开始时就告诉我，周末他责备了十几岁的儿子，因为他整个周末都在玩电子游戏和盯着手机。这位病人抱怨说，他给儿子买了吉他，还付了学费让他上课，但他儿子从来不练习，也不认真学习，更不会做任何有用的事情。我们很快意识到，他之所以对儿子大吼大叫，恰恰是因为他自己最焦虑的事情——缺乏效率和积极性。他开始接受治疗是因为他觉得自己很失败，一生中都没能兑现自己的承诺。我们一起意识到，他之所以指责儿子懒惰、漫无目的，其实是在逃避这些感受。当他意识到这一点后，他对儿子的不满减少了，父子关系也改善了。

There is also a more specific kind of projection that commonly occurs between intimate partners called ‘projective identification’. This process occurs when we project a trait we don’t like in ourselves onto our partner and they, often wordlessly and without even realising it, take it off us. If, for example, we’ve grown up in a family where vulnerability is perceived as shameful and ‘weak’, we may shed that shame by projecting our vulnerability into our partner and then we treat them as if they are very fragile. The wonderful thing is that if our partner isn’t too bothered or ashamed of their vulnerability (maybe they grew up in a family where it was OK to feel a bit needy at times) we can find ourselves, gradually over time, less worried about being ‘weak’. We’ve learnt something emotionally from our partner – that the trait we felt ashamed about isn’t actually as bad as we thought. In this way, we can begin to know and like parts of ourselves that we’ve previously denied. And of course, this spurs psychological growth and development. This is the wonderfully creative part of relationships, where we learn and mature emotionally within a loving partnership.

还有一种更特殊的投射方式，常见于亲密伴侣之间，称为“投射性认同”。当我们把自己不喜欢的某种特质投射到伴侣身上时，这个过程就发生了。而伴侣往往会在不知不觉中，甚至无意识地，就接受了这种特质。例如，如果我们成长在一个将脆弱视为羞耻和“软弱”的家庭，我们可能会通过将自己的脆弱投射到伴侣身上来摆脱这种羞耻感，然后我们会像对待非常脆弱的人一样对待他们。奇妙的是，如果我们的伴侣并不太在意或羞于承认自己的脆弱（也许他们成长在一个允许偶尔感到需要关爱的家庭），我们会发现自己会逐渐不再那么担心自己“软弱”。我们从伴侣身上学到了一些东西——我们曾经感到羞耻的特质实际上并没有我们想象的那么糟糕。这样，我们就能开始了解并喜欢上自己以前否认的那些部分。当然，这也会促进心理的成长和发展。这是人际关系中充满奇妙创造力的部分，我们可以在充满爱的伴侣关系中学习和成长。

Sometimes the projected trait is ‘held’ by one partner for years and years. An example is where one person (often the woman) feels anxiety, whilst the other (often the man) simply doesn’t. Perhaps women are more comfortable with the feeling of being anxious whereas men prefer a self-image that’s unruffled, stoic and calm? The woman frets about the children, the damp patch in the bedroom and her mother’s health, whilst the man remains apparently unbothered. Partners often divide up feelings in this way so that one person holds a difficult feeling on behalf of the couple. However, my years as a couple therapist have taught me that often, despite appearances to the contrary, the biggest anxieties, which appear to be felt by only one partner, are actually shared.

有时，伴侣中的一方会“持有”这种投射特质长达数年之久。例如，一方（通常是女性）感到焦虑，而另一方（通常是男性）却毫无感觉。或许女性更能坦然面对焦虑的感受，而男性则更倾向于展现一种沉着冷静、坚忍克己的形象？女性会为孩子、卧室里的潮湿痕迹以及母亲的健康而忧心忡忡，而男性则似乎毫不在意。伴侣之间常常以这种方式分担彼此的感受，让一方代表双方承受难以承受的情绪。然而，我多年作为伴侣治疗师的经验告诉我，很多时候，尽管表面看来并非如此，但那些看似只有一方感受到的最大焦虑，实际上是双方共同承担的。

Julian and Kristof had been together more than ten years. They seemed charming on first meeting and told me they needed help because they couldn’t agree whether they should become parents.

朱利安和克里斯托夫在一起已经超过十年了。他们初次见面时就给人感觉很迷人，并告诉我他们需要帮助，因为他们无法就是否要孩子达成一致。

Kristof dressed beautifully in clothes that were just on the edge of looking too young for him. He was in his forties and looked very fit but he had a worn look and his skin was lined as though he’d had too much sun. Every so often, he’d smile or laugh, his face would light up and he’d suddenly look like a little boy. This boyish quality created a maternal feeling in me that suggested he needed a lot of love and care.

克里斯托夫穿着考究，但衣服却显得有些稚气未脱。他四十多岁，身材健硕，但略显沧桑，皮肤上布满了皱纹，像是晒伤了。他时不时会露出笑容，脸上绽放出光彩，仿佛瞬间变成了一个小男孩。这种孩子气让我产生了一种母性的怜惜，觉得他需要很多爱和关怀。

Julian, despite being eight years younger than Kristof, was much more sober and restrained, his face unlined and unmoving. He always wore a navy suit and polished brogues to the sessions and rarely spoke without being asked a question.

朱利安虽然比克里斯托夫小八岁，却更加沉稳内敛，脸上几乎没有皱纹，表情也十分平静。他每次来参加会议都穿着海军蓝西装和锃亮的布洛克鞋，除非有人问他问题，否则他很少主动开口。

In early sessions, they established what appeared to be the nub of their problem, which was that all the feelings and longing belonged to Kristof. He was the one who wanted them to have children; the one who wanted more sex; the one who wanted a holiday and the one who wanted a new sofa. Whatever they discussed, whether it was becoming parents or moving to a new house, Kristof took the lead and Julian either complied or passively resisted. It was as if Julian had no wishes and no desires of his own and was working as hard as he could to be invisible.

在最初的几次咨询中，他们似乎找到了问题的症结所在：所有的情感和渴望都源于克里斯托夫。是他想要孩子；是他想要更多性生活；是他想要度假；是他想要新沙发。无论他们讨论什么，无论是为人父母还是搬家，克里斯托夫都占据主导地位，而朱利安要么顺从，要么消极抵抗。仿佛朱利安没有任何自己的愿望和欲望，他竭尽全力地让自己隐形。

This was very frustrating to work with. When I offered Kristof my thoughts and understanding about what was happening between them, he’d listen eagerly, seeming to absorb it. Or, at other times, he’d reshape my thought and make it his own, and though this could be because he’d initially disagreed with my idea, it was quite often to begin a playful and creative exchange. In short, he appeared to be letting me help him.

和他共事非常令人沮丧。当我向克里斯托夫表达我对他们之间发生的事情的想法和理解时，他会认真倾听，似乎能完全理解。但有时，他也会改写我的想法，将其变成他自己的。虽然这可能是因为他最初并不认同我的观点，但更多时候，这是为了开启一段轻松而富有创意的交流。总之，他看起来好像在让我帮他。

Julian responded quite differently. When I offered him some understanding that I hoped would reach his heart, he seemed to let it roll down from his chest and off his body. He didn’t so much reject my thoughts – he simply didn’t engage with them. It was exasperating. I tried and tried to get closer to Julian but it felt as though he was impervious. Although he was always polite and listened earnestly, it seemed as though he simply didn’t have any emotional insight or opinions about their issues. Kristof owned them all. Julian would say he was fine, everything was fine, and it seemed this couple mutually accepted that Kristof was the one who was upset, anxious and needy. Often, I’d spend an entire session listening to Kristof complaining and appealing to Julian in a rather desperate way, whilst Julian, though not overtly aggressive, sat silent, pretty much unmoved.

朱利安的反应截然不同。当我试图用一些理解打动他时，他似乎毫不在意，任由这些话从胸口滑落，最终消失。他并非拒绝我的想法，而是根本不予理会。这令人恼火。我一次又一次地尝试拉近与朱利安的距离，但他却像个无动于衷的人。尽管他总是彬彬有礼，认真倾听，但他似乎对他们之间的问题没有任何情感上的洞察或看法。克里斯托夫似乎完全掌控着一切。朱利安总是说他没事，一切都很好，这对夫妻似乎都默认了克里斯托夫才是那个感到沮丧、焦虑和需要帮助的人。很多时候，我得花一整节课的时间听克里斯托夫近乎绝望地抱怨和恳求朱利安，而朱利安虽然没有表现出明显的攻击性，却只是默默地坐着，几乎无动于衷。

Experience had taught me that this situation, which seemed so polarised, was almost certainly a shared problem. What could be the underlying reason why they’d shaped their relationship in this way? For a long time, I simply couldn’t understand what was holding them together so powerfully. I was, however, interested in the fact that Julian, who was seemingly so compliant and yet so empty in the sessions, was by far the most successful at work. He had set up a tech business in his twenties and now employed close to 100 people. It was challenging to imagine how this man, who sat so colourlessly on my grey couch, had the gumption and drive to create such a successful business. I began to notice that whenever (though it was very occasionally) we talked about his work, he’d become much more animated. I commented on more than one occasion that all Julian’s passion and ambition seemed to be lodged in his work, whilst Kristof held the passion and ambition for the relationship.

经验告诉我，这种看似两极分化的局面，几乎可以肯定是一个共同的问题。他们为何会以这种方式维系彼此的关系？很长一段时间，我都无法理解是什么让他们如此紧密地联系在一起。然而，我注意到朱利安在咨询中看似顺从却又空洞无物，但他在工作中却是最成功的。他二十多岁时就创办了一家科技公司，如今员工近百人。很难想象，这个在我灰色沙发上面无表情的男人，究竟是如何拥有如此雄心壮志和干劲，打造出如此成功的企业。我开始注意到，每当我们谈到他的工作时（虽然很少），他就会变得兴致勃勃。我不止一次地指出，朱利安所有的热情和抱负似乎都倾注在了工作上，而克里斯托夫则把热情和抱负寄托在了这段关系上。

Interestingly, when Julian talked about his work, Kristof would grow sulkily silent. But then the conversation would take its usual turn and flow back to Kristof’s sense of deprivation and longing. Nothing seemed to be changing, which, of course, started to leave me as frustrated as Kristof.

有趣的是，每当朱利安谈起他的工作，克里斯托夫就会闷闷不乐地沉默不语。但随后，话题又会像往常一样回到克里斯托夫的失落感和渴望上来。一切似乎都没有改变，这当然也让我和克里斯托夫一样感到沮丧。

The question of ‘progress’ in treatment is a complicated one in psychoanalytic therapy. In cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT), the aim is usually what we would call ‘symptom reduction’. For instance, if a patient comes with depression, once that depression has lifted, the treatment is complete. In other therapies, ‘goals’ for treatment are discussed and agreed between patient and therapist and a set number of sessions are arranged to try to meet them. Psychoanalytic treatment isn’t like that at all, which is why some people are critical of it. But the exciting thing about working in this way is the experience of something unfolding, of great new connections being made, of the yawning canyon between feeling and understanding being occasionally bridged. And when feeling and thinking come together, it can really help us stand in our own shoes and have the sensation of being whole. Many people who come to see me are really quite frightened, though they won’t necessarily consciously know it. Understanding what frightens them, looking it in the eye and recognising the origins of that fear, is life affirming and life expanding. It brings us closer to our own emotional truth and this promotes mental growth.

在精神分析疗法中，“进展”的概念十分复杂。认知行为疗法（CBT）的目标通常是我们所说的“减轻症状”。例如，如果患者患有抑郁症，一旦抑郁症状消失，治疗就结束了。在其他疗法中，治疗的“目标”由患者和治疗师共同讨论并达成一致，然后安排一定次数的疗程来努力实现这些目标。精神分析疗法完全不同，这也是为什么有些人对它持批评态度的原因。但这种治疗方式令人兴奋之处在于，它能让我们体验到某种事物的展开，建立起全新的联系，偶尔还能弥合感受与理解之间巨大的鸿沟。当感受与思考融为一体时，它能真正帮助我们正视自己的处境，并感受到自身的完整。许多来找我的人其实都很害怕，尽管他们未必能意识到这一点。理解他们的恐惧所在，直面恐惧，并认清恐惧的根源，这本身就是一种肯定生命、拓展生命的方式。它使我们更接近自己的情感真相，从而促进心理成长。

But couple therapy is somewhat different to individual psychoanalytic treatment because couples often come with a more specific agenda. They want to stop arguing; they want to have sex; they want to agree on where to live or how to discipline their children. They come because they hope by coming, they’ll feel happier or more content. Or they come because they’re in two minds as to whether to stay together or separate. They may learn a huge amount about themselves (sometimes a great deal more than in an individual therapy) but they usually still want to resolve something and then end their therapy, shutting their bedroom door behind them.

但伴侣治疗与个体心理分析治疗有所不同，因为伴侣通常带着更具体的目的前来。他们想要停止争吵；他们想要恢复性生活；他们想要就居住地或如何管教孩子达成一致。他们前来是希望通过治疗感到更快乐或更满足。或者，他们前来是因为他们还在犹豫是否要继续在一起。他们可能会对自身有更深入的了解（有时甚至比个体治疗了解得更多），但他们通常仍然希望解决某些问题，然后结束治疗，关上卧室的门。

And what do I want as a therapist? I’ve been trained not to want very much at all. The influential British psychoanalyst Wilfred Bion cautioned the psychoanalyst against ‘desire’. The job of the analyst is not to want a particular outcome for a patient or even for a session. The job of the analyst, he said, was simply to be truly present with the patient without a whole set of pre-conceived thoughts or expectations. To uncover the truth of a person, the psychoanalyst must be wholly available, without all the baggage of previous experience or knowledge. ‘The psychoanalyst should aim at achieving a state of mind so that at every session he feels he has not seen the patient before.’ fn1

作为一名治疗师，我想要什么呢？我接受的训练是不要抱有太多的欲望。颇具影响力的英国精神分析学家威尔弗雷德·比昂告诫精神分析师要警惕“欲望”。分析师的工作并非为患者，甚至为每次治疗，设定特定的结果。他说，分析师的工作仅仅是真正地与患者同在，不带任何先入为主的观念或期望。为了揭示一个人的真相，精神分析师必须完全敞开自己，抛开所有过往经验或知识的包袱。“精神分析师应该努力达到一种心境，在每一次治疗中，他都感觉自己从未见过这位患者。”<sup>1</sup>

This way of thinking has helped me (an impatient person) to be more patient. I’m also quite clear that my patient’s development will take its own time and, though I foster this emotional growth by my presence, interest and curiosity, I can’t force it to happen.

这种思考方式帮助我（一个急性子）变得更有耐心。我也很清楚，病人的成长需要时间，虽然我会通过陪伴、关心和好奇心来促进他们的情感发展，但我无法强迫他们成长。

Nevertheless, despite this training, I confess I was very exasperated by this case. I found Kristof easier than Julian but as the months went on and his continual complaints didn’t change, I found myself becoming frustrated with him too.

然而，尽管接受过这样的培训，我还是得承认，这个案子让我非常恼火。我觉得克里斯托夫比朱利安好对付，但随着几个月过去，他不断抱怨，我发现自己也开始对他感到沮丧了。

We were 14 months into their therapy when something happened. Julian and Kristof’s regular weekly session time was late on a Thursday evening. They were usually my last patients of the week, which of course didn’t make my frustration any easier to bear. But one Tuesday evening at 6.30, I was just packing up for the day when my buzzer went, which was curious as I wasn’t expecting anyone.

在他们的治疗进行了14个月之后，发生了一件事。朱利安和克里斯托夫每周的例行治疗时间是周四晚上。他们通常是我一周中最后接待的病人，这当然让我更加感到沮丧。但在一个周二晚上6点半，我正准备收拾东西下班，这时门铃响了，这很奇怪，因为我并没有预料到会有人来。

I lifted the receiver to hear the cheery voice of Kristof saying, as he usually did, ‘Hi, it’s Kristof, we’re heeere!’

我拿起听筒，听到克里斯托夫像往常一样用欢快的声音说：“嗨，我是克里斯托夫，我们到了！”

For a moment, I felt utterly confused. What day was it? What time? And, indeed, I said this aloud down the receiver. I could hear an intake of breath at the end of the line and then Kristof’s voice saying to Julian, ‘We’ve got the wrong day.’

那一刻，我彻底懵了。今天是星期几？几点？说真的，我对着话筒把这些问题都问了出来。我听到电话那头传来一声倒吸冷气的声音，然后是克里斯托夫对朱利安说：“我们搞错日期了。”

‘Oh dear. Yes, I think you have,’ I replied.

“哦，天哪。是的，我想你已经有了。”我回答道。

We quickly ended this strange conversation over the intercom, with them laughing nervously and saying they’d see me on Thursday. I paused a little while in my consulting room to give them time to get on their way, then left for home, pondering on this turn of events.

我们很快通过对讲机结束了这段奇怪的对话，他们尴尬地笑着说周四见。我在诊室里稍作停留，让他们有时间离开，然后回家了，心里一直在琢磨刚才发生的一切。

Two days later, on Thursday, I waited with some anticipation for Julian and Kristof to arrive. I imagined that Julian would be ashamed of the mistake but I doubted he would show it, whilst Kristof would extravagantly express his ‘mortification’ at the incident.

两天后的星期四，我满怀期待地等待着朱利安和克里斯托夫的到来。我想朱利安会为自己的错误感到羞愧，但我怀疑他是否会表现出来，而克里斯托夫则会极尽夸张地表达他对这件事的“羞愧”。

They kept me waiting quite a while and it occurred to me that perhaps they weren’t going to come. But then, 12 minutes late, the buzzer went and they entered my room in a rush.

他们让我等了很久，我都开始怀疑他们是不是不来了。但过了12分钟，门铃响了，他们匆匆忙忙地进了我的房间。

‘Oh, my goodness,’ Kristof said breathlessly, ‘what idiots were we!’ And he proceeded to explain that Julian had texted him that afternoon to meet outside John Lewis, which was the usual place they met before walking together to my office. Kristof, who hadn’t been working that day, left home, got on the Tube and met Julian without any thought that they’d got the wrong day. All of this was delivered with great hilarity and extravagant gestures. Gradually, however, as he continued to grandstand, he began to blame and shame Julian.

“我的天哪，”克里斯托夫气喘吁吁地说，“我们真是太蠢了！”他接着解释说，那天下午朱利安发短信约他到约翰·刘易斯百货公司外面见面，那是他们通常见面的地方，之后他们会一起走到我的办公室。克里斯托夫那天不用上班，他出门坐地铁去见朱利安，完全没意识到他们搞错了日子。他一边说着这些，一边夸张地比划着，场面十分滑稽。然而，随着他继续卖弄，渐渐地，他开始责怪和羞辱朱利安。

‘Thing is … Julian can’t wait to see you, Susanna. Every week, he asks me if we’re seeing you on Thursday when he’s already got it in his diary! I don’t know why but he talks about you all the time! Don’t you, dearest?’ he said, smirking.

“是这样的……朱利安迫不及待地想见到你，苏珊娜。他每周都问我周四是不是能见到你，明明他已经把那天记在日历上了！我不知道为什么，但他总是提起你！是不是，亲爱的？”他笑着说。

As you can imagine, I felt most surprised by this information. Julian, who sat so impassively every week, had given absolutely no indication at all of any devotion to the therapy and certainly not to me. Everything about him made me feel as though he came dutifully, not enthusiastically. I also wondered about Kristof exposing Julian in this way. It was rather cruel and made me wonder what feeling, at that moment, he was trying to get ‘out’ of him and ‘into’ Julian. Shame? Neediness? A feeling of humiliation?

可想而知，我听到这个消息时感到非常震惊。朱利安每周都面无表情地坐在那里，丝毫没有流露出对治疗的任何投入，更别提对我了。他的一举一动都让我觉得他只是出于义务而非热情而来。我也在想，克里斯托夫这样揭露朱利安的真面目究竟有何用意。这相当残酷，让我不禁思考，在那一刻，他究竟想从自己身上“释放”出什么情绪，又想让朱利安感受到什么？是羞耻？是渴求？还是某种屈辱感？

I said, ‘Perhaps you both feel a little ashamed about turning up two days early? Maybe it feels humiliating to make that kind of mistake? Maybe it makes you both feel it reveals your attachment to me and to coming here, leaving you rather vulnerable?’

我说：“也许你们俩都对提前两天到达感到有些羞愧？也许犯这种错误让你们觉得很丢脸？也许这让你们觉得这暴露了你们对我和来这里的依恋，让你们显得很脆弱？”

They both looked serious and nodded and slowly they began to talk about how important the sessions were and how they looked forward to them.

他们俩神情严肃地点了点头，然后慢慢地开始谈论这些会议的重要性以及他们对这些会议的期待。

‘We wouldn’t still be together if we weren’t seeing you,’ said Julian, before uncharacteristically adding, ‘Kristof would have left me by now.’

“如果我们没见到你，我们就不会在一起了，”朱利安说道，然后又一反常态地补充道，“克里斯托夫现在早就离开我了。”

There was a silence that yawned between them and Kristof, who looked confused and querulous, responded, ‘I don’t know why you think I would have left … much, much more likely that you would have.’

他们之间陷入了漫长的沉默，克里斯托夫一脸困惑和抱怨地回答说：“我不知道你为什么认为我会离开……更有可能是你离开。”

I was interested in this new development and how it now seemed clearer that they shared a fear that the other would end the relationship. Kristof had certainly expressed this concern before but not Julian. Was something shifting?

我对这一新进展很感兴趣，现在看来，他们似乎都害怕对方会结束这段关系。克里斯托夫之前确实表达过这种担忧，但朱利安没有。是不是有什么变化？

Some weeks went by and at each session they seemed to be becoming more open. Whereas before we seemed to go around the same issues over and over, new avenues of discussion were beginning to open up. Just before the Easter break, I started the session by reminding them I was going to be away for two weeks. They both looked subdued and nodded and Julian, in a businesslike manner, patted his phone and said, ‘Yes, in the diary.’ Then neither of them spoke for quite some time.

几周过去了，每次会面他们似乎都变得更加坦诚。以前我们总是反复讨论同样的问题，现在新的讨论方向开始出现了。复活节假期前，我在会面开始时提醒他们我将外出两周。他们俩看起来都很沮丧，点了点头。朱利安公事公办地拍了拍手机，说：“好的，记在日程表上了。”然后他们俩沉默了很久。

I said, ‘Perhaps it feels quite upsetting to have a break from sessions at this time?’

我说：“在这个时候暂停训练可能会让人感到非常沮丧吧？”

Kristof ignored my comment and, addressing Julian, said, ‘I think we need to talk to Susanna about what you said on Saturday.’

克里斯托夫无视了我的评论，转而对朱利安说：“我认为我们需要和苏珊娜谈谈你星期六说的话。”

Julian squirmed uncomfortably and glared at Kristof. ‘Be my guest,’ he answered.

朱利安不安地扭动着身子，怒视着克里斯托夫。“请便，”他回答道。

At this, Kristof began to recount their conversation. They’d talked seriously at the weekend about splitting up because Julian had decided he didn’t want to progress any plans about having children. Ever. He didn’t want things to change between them; he thought Kristof wouldn’t be able to cope with a child’s demands and he couldn’t bear to go through the whole process of trying to find a surrogate or trying to adopt. He wasn’t going to do it. Not now. Not ever. After a pause, Kristof concluded by saying, ‘If children are off the table, then I told him we couldn’t really go on. We just don’t want the same things and don’t have a future.’

这时，克里斯托夫开始讲述他们的对话。周末他们认真地谈过分手的事，因为朱利安决定不再考虑要孩子。他不想改变他们之间的关系；他觉得克里斯托夫无法应对孩子的需求，也无法承受寻找代孕或领养的整个过程。他不想这么做。现在不想。以后也不会。停顿片刻后，克里斯托夫总结道：“既然孩子不在考虑范围内，那我就告诉他，我们真的没法继续下去了。我们想要的东西不一样，也没有未来。”

A gloomy sense of doom settled into the room. Julian sat upright, staring into the distance, avoiding my eye and Kristof, his arms crossed, shoulders slumped, glanced back and forth between me and his partner.

房间里弥漫着一种阴郁的厄运感。朱利安笔直地坐着，目光投向远方，避开我的视线；克里斯托夫双臂交叉抱在胸前，肩膀耷拉着，目光在我和他的同伴之间来回游移。

For the rest of the session, I tried to get them to be more in touch with their sadness. I spoke about how desperate this situation felt to them and tried to explore their feelings about their seemingly unbridgeable differences but they didn’t really respond and stayed in their angry bubbles. I felt alarmed. Were they going to split in this precipitous way? Suddenly their relationship, which had up till now felt so solidly stuck, seemed very precarious.

在接下来的咨询中，我试图引导他们更深入地感受自己的悲伤。我谈到他们感到多么绝望，并试图探究他们对看似无法弥合的分歧的感受，但他们并没有真正回应，仍然沉浸在愤怒的情绪中。我感到担忧。他们会就此决裂吗？他们之前看似牢不可破的关系，突然间变得岌岌可危。

This uncertainty often goes along with change. Whilst some couples make steady progress and some couples make no progress at all, there is often a kind of jeopardy in the process of lasting change. This jeopardy can lead to a break-up or it can even lead to a breakdown; opening things up and getting in touch with feelings that have been long repressed can be perilous, requiring the therapist to ‘hold’ the patient carefully through this period of instability and transformation. Were Kristof and Julian about to break up or about to break through?

这种不确定性往往伴随着改变。有些伴侣稳步前进，有些伴侣则毫无进展，但持久改变的过程中常常伴随着某种风险。这种风险可能导致分手，甚至导致关系崩溃；敞开心扉，触及那些长期压抑的情感可能充满危险，需要治疗师小心翼翼地陪伴患者度过这段不稳定和转变的时期。克里斯托夫和朱利安是即将分手，还是即将突破重围？

I said some general words about how one of the most corrosive things couples can do is make threats to end the relationship, how these threats heighten anxieties about abandonment and undermine basic security and trust. I wondered if they were really in touch with what a big step this was and suggested that we could talk more about this next week before they decided. They both agreed.

我简单地说了几句，指出情侣间最具破坏性的行为之一就是以分手相威胁，这种威胁会加剧被抛弃的焦虑，破坏基本的安全感和信任。我怀疑他们是否真正意识到这是一个多么重大的决定，并建议我们下周再详细讨论，然后再做决定。他们都同意了。

Three days later I got a text from Julian informing me Kristof had moved out and asking for a session as soon as possible. It seemed such a breakthrough for Julian to make this kind of request that I agreed to see him the following day. As he entered my room, I thought how shell-shocked he looked. He sat on the sofa, stiffly upright, his eyes wide and glassy, and robotically recounted the events leading up to Kristof leaving.

三天后，我收到朱利安的短信，他告诉我克里斯托夫已经搬走了，并希望尽快安排一次咨询。朱利安提出这样的请求，在我看来意义非凡，所以我同意第二天就去见他。他走进我的房间时，我感觉他像是受到了极大的惊吓。他僵硬地坐在沙发上，双眼圆睁，目光呆滞，机械地讲述着克里斯托夫离开前发生的事情。

‘Kristof’s at Francine’s, you know his sister …’ he trailed off and we sat in silence. Eventually, I asked him to tell me more about what had happened after the last session and he painstakingly explained that Kristof had become angry with him and said that he now realised he’d been wasting his time. Julian shrugged at this and waited for me to ask more; he seemed unmoved, as usual, even though it seemed he’d just lost his partner.

“克里斯托夫在弗朗辛家，你知道他妹妹……”他声音渐渐低了下去，我们沉默不语。最后，我问他上次咨询之后发生了什么，他才费力地解释说克里斯托夫生他的气了，说他现在意识到自己一直在浪费时间。朱利安耸了耸肩，等着我继续追问；他一如既往地无动于衷，尽管他似乎刚刚失去了伴侣。

‘You’re very certain about not wanting children?’ I asked.

“你非常确定不想生孩子吗？”我问。

As usual, a question from me, made him squirm. ‘I don’t know. Not really, I just kinda feel it’s not really going to happen. I think it’s just too much of a long shot, really. I can’t see us being able to go through with the whole thing. And, to be honest, I don’t think Kristof could cope with it. I just don’t think we’re in a good enough place to do something like that. How can we be talking about splitting up and having children at the same time? It seems ridiculous to me.’

像往常一样，我的问题让他有些局促不安。“我不知道。真的不知道，我总觉得这事儿不太可能发生。我觉得这希望渺茫，真的。我看不出我们能坚持下去。而且说实话，我觉得克里斯托夫也承受不了。我觉得我们现在的情况还不够好，做不了这种事。我们怎么能一边谈分手一边生孩子呢？这在我看来太荒谬了。”

It occurred to me, as he fumbled for words, that these muddled feelings might be linked to them being a gay couple and I wondered if I could find a way to explore that with him.

当他语无伦次地寻找合适的词语时，我突然想到，这些混乱的情绪可能与他们作为一对同性恋伴侣有关，我想知道我是否可以找到一种方法与他探讨这个问题。

‘I wonder, Julian, whether you think that you and Kristof would make good parents?’ I asked tentatively.

“朱利安，我想知道，你觉得你和克里斯托夫会是好父母吗？”我试探性地问道。

‘Not sure we would, to be honest,’ Julian replied.

“说实话，我不确定我们会不会这么做，”朱利安回答道。

‘Why not?’

为什么不呢？

‘Lots of things. Not sure either of us are … cut out for it.’

“很多事情。我不确定我们俩是否……适合做这件事。”

‘Cut out for it? Because you’re gay?’

“因为你是同性恋，所以就适合这份工作？”

Julian shrugged, looking uncertain how to respond. ‘Maybe.’

朱利安耸了耸肩，似乎不知该如何回应。“也许吧。”

‘Perhaps a part of you doesn’t think a gay couple could make a family? Be good parents?’

“或许你内心深处并不认为同性伴侣能够组建家庭？能够成为好父母？”

‘My parents certainly wouldn’t,’ Julian responded, suddenly animated. ‘They’d be … horrified.’

“我父母肯定不会，”朱利安突然激动起来，回答道，“他们会……吓坏的。”

Julian then began to talk about his family and how much they’d disapprove. They could barely look him and Kristof in the eye and he couldn’t imagine what they’d do if he had a kid.

朱利安接着开始谈起他的家人，以及他们会有多么反对。他们几乎不敢正眼看他和克里斯托夫，他无法想象如果他有了孩子，他们会作何反应。

‘Kristof simply doesn’t seem to understand my family. His sisters and his mother are just so different to mine, not …’

“克里斯托夫似乎根本不了解我的家庭。他的姐妹和母亲跟我的家人截然不同，一点也不……”

‘Homophobic?’ I supplied.

“恐同？”我反问道。

‘Yes, I guess so,’ Julian said in a flat voice. ‘Kristof just doesn’t get that things are complicated; he just wants what he wants and gets so upset when I can’t always give it to him.’

“是啊，我想也是，”朱利安语气平淡地说。“克里斯托夫根本不明白事情很复杂；他只想要他想要的，当我不能总是满足他时，他就会非常生气。”

‘You’re describing how angry and upset Kristof is but I’m noticing that you seem almost unmoved?’ I commented. He looked at me long and hard, as though, like a child, he was trying to win a staring competition. ‘I wonder what happens to your feelings, Julian? You seem not to feel any anger or sadness, despite Kristof leaving.’

“你一直在描述克里斯托夫有多生气多难过，但我注意到你似乎几乎无动于衷？”我说道。他盯着我看了很久，就像个孩子一样，想赢一场瞪眼比赛。“朱利安，我很好奇你的感受怎么了？克里斯托夫离开后，你似乎一点也不生气，也不难过。”

At that point, he seemed to give up. He dropped his head and began to cry. I felt a surge of compassion – a feeling that Julian rarely generated in me – and I spoke to him about how hard he found it to let himself grieve. Abruptly, he stopped crying and said with bitterness and anger, ‘What’s the fucking point of crying? It won’t bring him back.’

那一刻，他似乎放弃了。他低下头，开始哭泣。我心中涌起一股强烈的同情——这种感觉朱利安很少让我产生——于是我和他谈起他如何难以让自己沉浸在悲伤之中。他突然停止了哭泣，带着苦涩和愤怒说道：“哭有什么用？哭也让他复活不了。”

‘It might,’ I said. ‘I think Kristof would be shocked to see you so distressed; I don’t think you’ve ever shown these kinds of feelings to him, or me, before?’

“也许吧，”我说。“我想克里斯托夫看到你这么难过会很震惊；我想你以前从未在他面前，或者在我面前，流露出过这种情绪吧？”

He nodded and he began to talk tentatively about how he really did care hugely for Kristof but that he really hated feeling this way. He felt as though Kristof had trapped him into something and was always trying to trap him further.

他点点头，开始试探性地诉说自己其实非常在乎克里斯托夫，但他真的很讨厌这种感觉。他觉得克里斯托夫把他困在了某种陷阱里，而且总是想方设法让他陷得更深。

‘I wonder what you feel the trap is?’ I said. ‘Perhaps if you acknowledge that you want him and a life with him, you fear he’ll drop you? If you can tell yourself that you don’t really care about him, you can maintain an illusion you won’t be hurt? I do wonder, Julian, what happened to you in childhood that has made it so hard for you to show you need people?’

“我想知道你觉得陷阱是什么？”我说。“也许如果你承认你想要他，想要和他共度一生，你就会害怕他会抛弃你？如果你告诉自己你其实不在乎他，你就能维持一种不会受伤的假象？朱利安，我很好奇，你童年时究竟经历了什么，让你如此难以向人表达你的需要？”

I waited and watched Julian, hoping that now he’d open up more about his childhood. He’d told me so little and in such a factual way that I still had little real picture of his family. If things were to shift between him and Kristof, something needed to be unlocked. We would have to get closer to understanding why he feared showing his feelings and why connecting to his needs was so hard for him.

我静静地观察着朱利安，希望他能敞开心扉，多谈谈他的童年。他之前跟我说过的很少，而且都只是陈述事实，所以我对他的家庭仍然知之甚少。如果他和克里斯托夫之间的关系想要有所进展，就必须解开一些谜团。我们需要更深入地了解他为什么害怕表露自己的感情，以及为什么他难以理解自己的需求。

Julian looked thoughtful. ‘You know I went to boarding school at seven?’

朱利安若有所思地说：“你知道我七岁就上寄宿学校了吗？”

‘At seven? No, I didn’t know you went so young. I thought you went when you were older. Do you know why they sent you at such a young age?’

“七岁？不，我不知道你这么小就去了。我以为你年纪更大一些才去。你知道他们为什么让你这么小就去吗？”

He shook his head. ‘I don’t remember but my mother, you know, wasn’t very loving. She always says I was very clingy. I don’t think she could stand it.’

他摇了摇头。“我不记得了，但我母亲，你知道，不太爱我。她总是说我特别黏人。我想她受不了这一点。”

I noticed he used the word ‘it’ but I wondered if he meant ‘me’.

我注意到他用了“它”这个词，但我不知道他是不是想说“我”。

Julian told me he remembered his mother always promising to come up and kiss him goodnight if he put himself to bed. He’d sit on the landing waiting and waiting and then sometimes, when he couldn’t wait any longer, he’d go downstairs to see her and then his father would laugh at him and take him back upstairs and spank him for getting out of bed.

朱利安告诉我，他记得妈妈总是答应他，如果他自己上床睡觉，妈妈就会上来亲吻他道晚安。他会坐在楼梯平台上等啊等，有时等得实在等不及，就会下楼去看妈妈，然后爸爸就会嘲笑他，把他拉回楼上，因为他擅自下床而打他屁股。

I imagined him as a little boy, wanting his mother so badly. I felt my eyes welling up. How could his parents have neglected him so cruelly? How could his father have mocked him for wanting attention? But whilst I was full of feeling, Julian had recounted the story coldly, as if it concerned someone else.

我仿佛看到他还是个小男孩，多么渴望母亲的陪伴。我的眼眶不禁湿润了。他的父母怎么能如此残忍地忽视他？他的父亲怎么能嘲笑他渴望关注？然而，就在我百感交集之时，朱利安却冷漠地讲述着这个故事，仿佛它与自己无关。

‘Julian, it seems you can’t connect to that little boy you’re describing. It’s as though you’ve lost touch with some part of yourself, as though you’re frozen. I think you avoid feeling things – to want, to desire, to need Kristof is just too dangerous. To have passionate, loving feelings for him is somehow … shameful.’

“朱利安，你似乎无法与你描述的那个小男孩建立联系。就好像你与自己的一部分失去了联系，仿佛你被冻结了一样。我认为你在逃避感受——想要、渴望、需要克里斯托夫都太危险了。对他产生热烈的爱意，不知为何……是件羞耻的事。”

He then spoke of several humiliations during his childhood but perhaps the most telling was that whenever his father spanked him – which happened often – he would wet himself and his father would become even more furious, telling him he was pathetic and disgusting.

然后他谈到了童年时期遭受的种种羞辱，但最能说明问题的是，每当他父亲打他屁股时——这种情况经常发生——他都会尿裤子，而他父亲会更加愤怒，说他很可怜，很恶心。

As the session went on, Julian began to connect his inability to declare his feelings for Kristof with these childhood experiences. He said one thing he knew was that he never wanted to depend on anyone.

随着谈话的进行，朱利安开始将自己无法向克里斯托夫表达感情的原因与这些童年经历联系起来。他说，他唯一清楚的事情就是，他永远不想依赖任何人。

Once Julian left, I composed an email to them both, saying that I was sorry things had become so difficult, letting Kristof know I’d seen Julian separately and encouraging them to come on Thursday. I felt bad that I’d failed to help them manage this crisis but it was possible that Julian and Kristof, who’d been stuck in the same gear for so long, were now beginning a process of great change. Whether this change would make or break their relationship, we just had to wait and see.

朱利安离开后，我给他们俩都写了封邮件，表示很抱歉事情变得如此艰难，并告诉克里斯托夫我单独见过朱利安，鼓励他们周四过来。我为自己没能帮他们渡过难关而感到愧疚，但朱利安和克里斯托夫或许正经历着一段漫长的停滞期，如今可能正开启一段巨大的变革。至于这段变革会让他们的关系走向何方，我们只能拭目以待。

The rest of my week was busy. I was writing a book review and had a string of meetings on top of my usual practice. I thought about Julian and Kristof from time to time but when Thursday evening came around, it still wasn’t certain they were coming. At 6.30pm I suddenly felt a wave of huge disappointment. Was the work going to end like this? I felt dumped and confused. Surely, this couple who’d seemed so attached to each other would try to work things out?

这周剩下的时间都很忙。除了日常工作，我还得写一篇书评，还要参加一连串的会议。我不时会想起朱利安和克里斯托夫，但到了周四晚上，他们是否会来仍然不确定。下午六点半，我突然感到一阵巨大的失望。难道工作就这样结束了吗？我感觉被抛弃了，也很困惑。这对看起来如此亲密的夫妇，难道不应该努力解决问题吗？

As the minutes dragged on, I began to lose hope. I looked at my phone – no message. I contemplated drafting an email and had just written ‘ Dear Julian and Kristof ,’ when the buzzer went.

随着时间一分一秒地过去，我开始感到绝望。我看了看手机——没有消息。我考虑要不要写封邮件，刚写完“亲爱的朱利安和克里斯托夫”，门铃就响了。

For the first time in their treatment, Julian, ashen but alert, entered the room first. Kristof, behind him, lacked his usual bounce, shuffling in rather reluctantly, eyes down as if he was entering the headteacher’s office. Julian uncharacteristically started, apologising for being late and then launching into documenting recent developments.

这是他们接受治疗以来第一次，朱利安脸色苍白但精神矍铄，率先走进房间。跟在他身后的克里斯托夫一反常态，慢吞吞地拖着脚步走了进来，低着头，仿佛要走进校长办公室。朱利安一反常态地开口，先是为迟到道歉，然后开始记录最近的情况。

‘Well, I did what you told me. We saw each other last night and I told Kristof how much I cared about him and how I wanted it to work, just like you said.’

“嗯，我照你说的做了。我们昨晚见面了，我告诉克里斯托夫我有多在乎他，以及我多么希望我们能成功，就像你说的一样。”

It was impossible not to notice how Julian had failed to take ownership of his own desire to woo Kristof back but instead couched it in a way that suggested that, like a good little boy, he was simply following my orders. Having delivered his crisp report, Julian went silent, waiting, as usual, for someone else to take up the reins.

朱利安并没有坦然承认自己想要挽回克里斯托夫的愿望，而是像个乖孩子一样，把这想法包装得好像只是在执行我的命令。他简洁明了地汇报完后便沉默不语，像往常一样等待其他人接手。

Kristof was unmoved and something in his presence seemed grumpy, so I commented on how he appeared reluctant to be here. He responded by admitting the only reason he’d come was because he knew how much I’d been trying to help them and didn’t want to let me down.

克里斯托夫面无表情，他身上似乎透着一股不悦，于是我指出他看起来不太情愿来这里。他回应说，他来这里的唯一原因是因为他知道我一直在尽力帮助他们，不想让我失望。

The atmosphere felt hopeless and I felt myself sinking into my own thoughts as we all sat in a gloomy silence. After a while, I looked up and saw the stricken look on Julian’s face; there were beads of sweat on his forehead and he was glancing anxiously at Kristof, who stared at the floor, his expression closed. I caught his eye but instead of responding to my look, he turned to Kristof.

气氛令人绝望，我们沉默地坐着，我也不禁陷入沉思。过了一会儿，我抬起头，看到朱利安一脸痛苦，额头上渗出汗珠，他焦急地看着克里斯托夫，克里斯托夫则低着头，面无表情。我与他对视，但他没有回应，而是转向了克里斯托夫。

‘Please come home, Kristof. Why do you have to leave? Susanna doesn’t think you have to.’

“克里斯托夫，求你回家吧。你为什么要离开？苏珊娜觉得你没必要走。”

Kristof remained impassive and spoke with heavy sarcasm. ‘Well let me list it for you. We’re going to split up because you don’t want children. You don’t want sex. You don’t want to move. You don’t want to go on holiday and you never want to talk about anything!’

克里斯托夫面无表情，语气充满讽刺。“好吧，我来给你列举一下。我们要分手是因为你不想生孩子，你不想有性生活，你不想搬家，你不想去度假，而且你从来不想谈任何事情！”

Julian started to well up. ‘You seem so certain of that, Kristof,’ I observed. ‘And yet I think Julian was trying to tell you something different.’

朱利安的眼眶开始泛红。“克里斯托夫，你似乎对此深信不疑，”我说道，“但我认为朱利安想告诉你的其实是另一回事。”

Julian interrupted. ‘It’s not that I don’t want those things. It’s not that I don’t love you. I do. It’s just that I don’t know whether we can manage the whole process … see it through … and that you won’t end up leaving me anyway.’

朱利安打断道：“不是我不想要那些东西，也不是我不爱你，我爱你。只是我不知道我们能不能顺利完成整个过程……坚持到底……也不知道你最终会不会还是离开我。”

Kristof shook his shoulders dismissively.

克里斯托夫不屑地耸了耸肩。

‘I’m just not sure you won’t leave,’ Julian repeated. ‘What if it doesn’t go right? A baby is so demanding. I don’t know that we’ve got that much, you know … energy.’

“我只是不确定你是否会离开，”朱利安重复道。“万一情况不顺利怎么办？照顾婴儿太费劲了。我不知道我们是否有足够的精力。”

‘What? What? I’ve got the energy. I’m always giving and look how patient I’ve been with you. Look how long I’ve coped with you and all your faffing about.’

“什么？什么？我精力充沛。我一直都在付出，看看我对你多有耐心。看看我忍受了你多久，忍受了你所有的胡闹。”

‘But I’ve just said how much I love you.’

“但我刚才已经说过我有多爱你了。”

‘Because Susanna told you to.’

“因为苏珊娜让你这么做的。”

‘No. I mean it. I’m just frightened whether we’d be able to see it through with a child. It’s a huge responsibility. And financially that’ll all be on me. And I’m frightened that I mightn’t be able to look after a child like you want me to.’ He paused. ‘And that you might not be able to cope with the child’s needs.’

“不，我是认真的。我只是害怕我们能不能撑到孩子出生。这是一份巨大的责任。而且经济上的所有费用都将由我承担。我害怕我可能无法像你希望的那样照顾好孩子。”他停顿了一下。“也害怕你可能无法应对孩子的需求。”

I asked Julian whether this lack of confidence could be linked to the feelings he’d had as a small boy, when his mother couldn’t bear his neediness. Could this, perhaps, be informing his worry that Kristof might not be able to bear a child’s neediness?

我问朱利安，这种缺乏自信是否与他小时候的经历有关，那时他的母亲无法忍受他的依赖。这是否可能影响了他的担忧，让他觉得克里斯托夫可能无法忍受孩子的依赖？

There was silence. I didn’t think Julian had taken in what I said but I thought Kristof had heard it. Julian put out his hand to Kristof in a simple gesture of hope. I looked at it suspended in mid-air, with its unspoken request that Kristof take it. He didn’t. Julian withdrew his hand slowly and began to cry but still Kristof didn’t move.

一片寂静。我以为朱利安没听进去我说的话，但克里斯托夫听到了。朱利安向克里斯托夫伸出手，一个简单的希望的手势。我看着他的手悬在半空中，无声地请求克里斯托夫握住它。他没有。朱利安慢慢地缩回手，开始哭泣，但克里斯托夫仍然一动不动。

‘This is quite a turnaround Kristof, isn’t it?’ I observed. ‘All the needy longings that were in you are now in Julian and yet somehow you can’t respond. I wonder why you’re finding it so difficult to do so? This is what you’ve been asking for – for Julian to show you how much he loves you and wants you.’

“克里斯托夫，这转变可真不小，不是吗？”我说道，“你以前那些渴望和需要，现在都转移到了朱利安身上，可你却怎么也回应不了。我真不明白你为什么这么难做到？你一直想要的就是这个——让朱利安向你证明他有多爱你，多需要你。”

I waited for Kristof to say something but he still sat there silent, so I continued.

我等着克里斯托夫开口说话，但他仍然沉默不语，所以我继续说道。

‘It makes me think back to when you talked about your father leaving. You said your mother turned to you for comfort and that it felt like her needs squeezed out all of yours. Maybe it’s hard to imagine a relationship where two people can respond to each other, where both of you could, at times, be needy and vulnerable?’

“这让我想起你之前谈到父亲离开时的情景。你说母亲向你寻求安慰，感觉她的需求完全压倒了你的需求。也许很难想象两个人能够彼此回应，都能在某些时候感到需要帮助和脆弱，这样的关系是很难建立的吧？”

Kristof looked interested and nodded.

克里斯托夫看起来很感兴趣，点了点头。

‘So perhaps whilst there’s been something terrible about Julian having been previously so withdrawn, at the same time it’s protected you from feeling the burden of his need. Like you felt burdened by your mother?’

“所以，或许朱利安之前那种孤僻的性格虽然很糟糕，但同时也保护了你，让你免受他需要你的负担。就像你曾被母亲的重担压得喘不过气来一样？”

To my surprise, Kristof didn’t respond but Julian said, ‘I’ve always known that Kristof finds it hard to take on things I want.’

令我惊讶的是，克里斯托夫没有回应，但朱利安说：“我一直都知道克里斯托夫很难接受我想要的东西。”

‘That’s rubbish!’ Kristof exploded. ‘I’ve always been there for you.’

“胡说八道！”克里斯托夫怒吼道，“我一直都在你身边。”

Julian looked at him but Kristof turned away. ‘Do you remember when I got made redundant and I was in such a mess?’

朱利安看了他一眼，但克里斯托夫转过身去。“你还记得我被裁员的时候吗？当时我有多狼狈？”

‘Yes. Of course. I was the one supporting you.’

“是的，当然。是我在支持你。”

‘Actually, Kristof, you were so tough. Really tough. Telling me to get a grip and “man up”. That’s probably when I gave up the idea that you could ever really care for me.’

“克里斯托夫，说真的，你当时太严厉了。真的非常严厉。你叫我振作起来，像个男人一样。大概就是从那时起，我彻底放弃了你会真正关心我的想法。”

‘Such rubbish. So you’re saying it’s my fault you don’t want a child or any commitments?’

“真是胡说八道。所以你的意思是，你不想生孩子或者不想承担任何责任都是我的错？”

‘I don’t think that’s what Julian is saying, Kristof. I think he’s been trying to explore and acknowledge the source of his own issues but he’s also saying that you have your own part to play. It’s difficult for both of you to really recognise that this is a shared problem. That moment of disappointment when you were made redundant, Julian, and you felt Kristof couldn’t respond, was that, perhaps, when you finally shut down what was already just a sliver of hope inside you that someone would come if you called?’

“克里斯托夫，我不认为朱利安是这个意思。我认为他一直在试图探究并承认自己问题的根源，但他同时也在说，你也有责任。你们俩都很难真正意识到这是一个共同的问题。朱利安，你被裁员时感到失望，觉得克里斯托夫无法回应你，那是不是你彻底扼杀了心中仅存的一点希望——你以为只要呼唤就会有人回应？”

‘Yes,’ Julian agreed, ‘I stopped having expectations so I wouldn’t be disappointed again and then I felt, “Why should I say yes when you wanted things?”’

“是的，”朱利安同意道，“我不再抱有任何期望，这样我就不会再次失望了，然后我想，‘既然你想要什么，我为什么要答应呢？’”

Kristof looked up and over at Julian and I felt something more hopeful was happening. I knew it was the end of the session but I felt an urgency to say something that would hold them until the following week.

克里斯托夫抬起头，看向朱利安，我感到一丝希望正在酝酿。我知道这次谈话即将结束，但我迫切地想说些什么，好让他们能坚持到下周。

‘Neither of you are going to be able to meet each other’s desires completely but the relationship exists in the trying. Some of these attempts to connect and respond to each other will work and some won’t but it’s the persistence to keep going, to keep asking and relating, that makes a relationship grow and not wither and die.’

“你们俩都不可能完全满足对方的愿望，但关系就存在于这种尝试之中。有些尝试会成功，有些则不会，但正是这种坚持不懈、不断询问和交流的精神，才能让关系成长，而不是枯萎消亡。”

I didn’t know what would happen next, I never do. Will a couple find a way through or will they cross that mysterious line that beyond which lies separation? However long I’ve worked, however many hours I’ve spent in the consulting room, it is always impossible to know whether a couple, when they hit the crux of their conflicts, will travel on together or part.

我不知道接下来会发生什么，我从来都不知道。一对伴侣能否找到解决之道，还是会跨越那条神秘的界线，走向分离？无论我工作了多久，无论我在咨询室里待了多少个小时，我始终无法预知，当一对伴侣遇到冲突的关键时刻，他们是会携手前行，还是就此分道扬镳。

But though it was touch and go for many weeks, Julian and Kristof seemed to hang in there. Slowly, a profound shift developed in the balance of the give and take. Julian began to recognise his own needs and desires; it seemed he stopped projecting them all into Kristof who, though it was a struggle, was also becoming less and less fearful of Julian collapsing onto him as his mother had when he was young. This was a huge change in their dynamic, a move away from projective identification to each being more fully themselves in the relationship. We call this kind of development ‘taking back projections’ where partners reintegrate and ‘own’ feelings which have previously been denied and then pushed into their partner. Once couples begin to make this kind of change, they can find a new way of being together and for Julian and Kristof this allowed them to be more vulnerable, leading to a closeness that had hitherto been avoided.

尽管接下来的几周情况都十分危急，朱利安和克里斯托夫似乎还是坚持了下来。慢慢地，他们之间的付出与索取之间的平衡发生了深刻的转变。朱利安开始正视自己的需求和渴望；他似乎不再把所有需求和渴望都投射到克里斯托夫身上。虽然这很艰难，但克里斯托夫也越来越不害怕朱利安会像他小时候母亲那样突然崩溃，依赖他。这对他们的关系模式来说是一个巨大的改变，他们从投射式的认同转向在关系中更加完整地展现自我。我们称这种发展为“收回投射”，即伴侣重新整合并“拥有”那些之前被否认并强加给对方的感受。一旦伴侣开始做出这种改变，他们就能找到一种新的相处方式。对朱利安和克里斯托夫来说，这让他们能够更加坦诚，从而建立起一种此前一直回避的亲密关系。

But this change brought out into the open another whole area of difficulty, which, up until now, had been running like an underground river in spate – hidden but extremely powerful. Painfully, but together, we came to understand that neither of them had any real conviction they could make things work between them. They believed that being gay precluded them from having a loving, long-term relationship. It was as though the homophobia and stereotyping they’d experienced all around them was also inside them, poisoning and undermining their belief they could make something good and lasting together. Bringing this out into the light made this fear less powerful and, although they decided not to discuss the thorny issue of children for 12 months, by the time I last saw them, they’d already begun the process of adoption.

但这一变化也暴露了另一个棘手的问题，这个问题此前一直像暗流涌动的地下河一样暗流涌动——隐秘却威力无穷。我们痛苦地、但共同地意识到，他们俩其实都没有真正相信彼此能够维系这段关系。他们认为，身为同性恋就注定无法拥有充满爱意的长久关系。仿佛他们从小到大所经历的恐同症和刻板印象也渗透到了他们的内心，毒害并动摇着他们共同创造美好长久关系的信念。将这一切公之于众后，这种恐惧有所减弱。虽然他们决定在12个月内不去讨论孩子这个棘手的问题，但当我最后一次见到他们时，他们已经开始办理领养手续了。

# ↩

The Fates Conspire, and Rapunzel Lets down Her Hair

命运女神密谋，长发公主放下了她的头发

It was January and approaching my husband’s birthday. I had no idea what to get him and he was providing me with no suggestions. I noticed he’d propped on his desk a postcard that he’d bought of a linocut he’d seen at a small exhibition near King’s Cross. As he clearly admired it, I decided to see if I could buy the original. The etching was of a woman bent and laden, leading a horse along the canal towpath on a winter’s day. It was particularly evocative because my husband had previously written a book, The Water Road , about a journey through England’s inland waterways. Coincidentally, he’d also recently been teaching himself how to make lino prints and this black-and-white picture echoed some of his own work.

当时是1月，我丈夫的生日快到了。我不知道该送他什么礼物，他也没给我任何建议。我注意到他桌上放着一张明信片，是他之前在国王十字车站附近的一个小型展览上看到的一幅版画。他显然很喜欢这幅画，于是我决定看看能不能买到原作。这幅版画描绘的是一位佝偻着身子、肩扛重物的女子，在冬日里牵着一匹马沿着运河的纤道前行。这幅画格外触动我，因为我丈夫之前写过一本书，叫《水路》，讲述的是他穿越英格兰内陆水道的旅程。巧合的是，他最近也在自学版画，这幅黑白版画的风格与他的一些作品颇为相似。

It took some time to find the contact details of the artist, Chris Slaney, but when I did, I began an email correspondence regarding a possible purchase. I told Chris why I thought my husband would like the print and he asked for his name. When I gave it he immediately wrote back, excitedly informing me that he’d read The Water Road the previous year and the book had inspired him to make the print. I was astonished and excited as I knew my husband would enjoy this story and it would make the present even more meaningful. It set me to pondering that grey area between mere coincidence and deeper unconscious connections.

我花了些时间才找到艺术家克里斯·斯莱尼的联系方式，找到之后，我便开始和他邮件沟通，商讨购买事宜。我告诉克里斯为什么我觉得我丈夫会喜欢这幅版画，他问我丈夫的名字。我告诉了他之后，他立刻回复，兴奋地告诉我他去年读过《水路》，这本书启发他创作了这幅版画。我既惊讶又激动，因为我知道我丈夫会喜欢这个故事，这会让这份礼物更有意义。这件事让我开始思考，究竟是巧合还是更深层次的潜意识联系，究竟是巧合还是联系？

The following day, I had an enquiry from a prospective patient called Jackson. Could I see him quite urgently? He was in despair as his wife had left him and life felt very dark. His email said he’d got my name from Mr X, who had recommended me. I immediately recognised the name as Mr X was a well-known TV personality. Strangely, I’d never met him and nor did I remember knowing anyone who had.

第二天，我收到一位名叫杰克逊的潜在病人的咨询。他问我能否尽快给他看诊。他非常绝望，因为妻子离开了他，生活一片黑暗。他在邮件里说，他是从X先生那里得知我的，X先生推荐了我。我立刻认出了这个名字，因为X先生是一位知名的电视名人。奇怪的是，我从未见过他，也不记得认识任何认识他的人。

Jackson was very tall – so tall, in fact, that he had to bend his head as he came through the door into my office in Queen Anne Street. He was rake thin with a bony, aristocratic face that was open and engaging. I warmed to him immediately and his story quickly elicited my sympathies. He told me that he’d known his wife, Carla, for nearly 20 years. They’d met at university and married soon after graduation. He had felt they were well suited and had made each other very happy, though they hadn’t had children – Carla, he told me, had felt their lives together were already richly fulfilling and rewarding. Jackson had respected her preference to remain childless but now, at 41, she had suddenly become pregnant by another man and left him. Understandably, he felt shell-shocked and mystified by these events.

杰克逊个子很高——事实上，高到他走进我位于安妮女王街的办公室时不得不低下头。他身材瘦削，骨瘦如柴，长着一张高贵的脸，却又不失亲切和蔼。我立刻对他产生了好感，他的故事也很快打动了我。他告诉我，他和妻子卡拉相识近20年了。他们在大学相识，毕业后不久便结了婚。他觉得他们很般配，彼此都很幸福，虽然他们没有孩子——他告诉我，卡拉觉得他们的生活已经非常充实而有意义。杰克逊一直尊重她不要孩子的意愿，但现在，41岁的她突然怀了另一个男人的孩子，离开了他。可想而知，他对此感到震惊和困惑。

Jackson’s story wasn’t entirely unfamiliar. Over the years, I’ve seen several patients who have been devastated by revelations and events that seem to come out of the blue. There was the woman whose husband suddenly vanished, abandoning her and his two teenage children (he was found much later, living with his young lover in Thailand) and the deeply sad case of the woman whose husband had, without any warning, drowned himself. Jackson, like both of these patients, had no prior inkling to what was going on and I could see he was utterly confused and desperately reliving the past to try to find the clues he felt he’d missed with Carla.

杰克逊的故事并非完全陌生。这些年来，我见过不少病人，他们都因突如其来的变故和打击而深受打击。比如，一位女士的丈夫突然失踪，抛弃了她和两个十几岁的孩子（后来人们发现他与年轻情人住在泰国）；还有一位女士的丈夫毫无预兆地溺水身亡，这令人无比悲痛。杰克逊和这两位病人一样，事先对发生的一切毫不知情。我能看出他完全懵了，拼命地回忆过去，试图找到他觉得当初和卡拉在一起时错过的线索。

Soon after Jackson came to see me, a colleague asked if I might take a referral. He had seen a couple who’d now broken up and he wanted to refer the woman, who was very distressed about the ending of the relationship. Her name was Grace and I arranged to meet her the following week.

杰克逊来找我之后不久，一位同事问我是否可以接受转介。他之前见过一对分手的情侣，想把那位因为分手而非常痛苦的女士转介给我。她叫格蕾丝，我安排下周和她见面。

When Grace arrived, I was immediately struck by her ethereal beauty. She appeared at my door like an illustration from a fairy tale. Her hair was honey blonde and pinned up carelessly so that luxurious ringlets framed her face and tumbled down onto her shoulders like Rapunzel. She’d only been married eight months and yet her dreams were already dashed. Her husband Dylan had left her, saying he’d made a terrible mistake in marrying her.

格蕾丝一到，我就被她超凡脱俗的美貌深深吸引。她出现在我家门口，宛如童话故事里的人物。她一头蜜金色的秀发随意地挽起，几缕卷曲的秀发垂落在她脸颊两侧，宛如长发公主般倾泻而下。她结婚才八个月，梦想却已破碎。她的丈夫迪伦离开了她，说娶她是个天大的错误。

‘He claims he still loves me but he wants to be with a man. He says he’s sorry but apparently he’s now gay. Nine months ago, he didn’t know? And now he does? And he’s “sorry”?!’

“他说他仍然爱我，但他想和男人在一起。他说他很抱歉，但显然他现在是同性恋了。九个月前他不知道？现在知道了？还说‘抱歉’？！”

She berated herself bitterly in the session, just as Jackson had done. ‘How could I not have known? No one else is surprised. My friends say they always knew – it was so obvious he was gay. Did I have my eyes closed? Why couldn’t I see what everyone else did?’

在谈话中，她像杰克逊一样，对自己进行了深深的自责。“我怎么会不知道呢？其他人都不觉得奇怪。我的朋友们说他们一直都知道——他是同性恋这件事太明显了。难道我一直闭着眼睛吗？为什么我看不出来其他人都能看出来？”

I felt very warm towards Grace; she seemed so sad and lost. She was 34 years old and feared she’d never meet anyone else or have children now. She felt Dylan had almost certainly robbed her of having babies. We talked for an hour and then Grace left, agreeing to come and see me the following week at the same time. Then the buzzer for my next session went.

我对格蕾丝感到非常温暖；她看起来那么悲伤和迷茫。她34岁，害怕自己再也遇不到其他人，也无法生育孩子。她觉得迪伦几乎肯定剥夺了她拥有孩子的权利。我们聊了一个小时，然后格蕾丝离开了，并同意下周同一时间来见我。这时，我下一次咨询的铃声响了。

Bounding up the stairs came Jackson and, as he entered, I was struck by the similarity of their stories. Both had been left and neither saw it coming. Both were not only grieving their marriage but also felt humiliated and preoccupied with the consequent loss of the chance to become parents. It felt very strange. Another coincidence.

杰克逊蹦蹦跳跳地跑上楼来，他一进门，我就被他们俩的经历的相似之处震惊了。他们俩都被抛弃了，而且谁也没料到会发生这种事。他们不仅为婚姻的破裂而悲痛，也为失去为人父母的机会而感到羞辱和痛苦。这感觉很奇怪。又是一个巧合。

Jackson and Grace settled down to their respective therapies. Every week, Grace would leave my office and Jackson would enter ten minutes later. For nearly two hours I listened to their experiences and their feelings and was consistently struck at how profoundly their stories echoed across the two sessions. I began to wonder if they’d like each other and whether they’d find solace in each other’s company. I idly fantasised that they might bump into each other on the stairs one day and somehow, as in a movie, connect. Perhaps they could give each other the children they both longed for?

杰克逊和格蕾丝各自开始了他们的治疗。每周，格蕾丝离开我的办公室，十分钟后杰克逊就会进来。将近两个小时里，我倾听着他们的经历和感受，不由自主地被他们的故事在两次治疗中如此深刻的共鸣所震撼。我开始思考他们是否会喜欢彼此，是否会在彼此的陪伴中找到慰藉。我甚至幻想，也许有一天他们会在楼梯上偶遇，像电影里那样，彼此产生某种联系。或许他们还能为彼此生下他们都渴望的孩子？

A few months later, spring had drifted back into London. The trees had that particularly pleasing lime-green leaf and, as I walked towards Queen Anne Street, the air smelled of the new season. Mid-morning came, the buzzer went and Grace arrived with her hair down around her face. Her skin looked warmer somehow and something spring-like also seemed to be inhabiting her.

几个月后，春天再次降临伦敦。树木换上了令人赏心悦目的淡绿色叶子，我走向安妮女王街，空气中弥漫着春天的气息。上午十点左右，门铃响了，格蕾丝走了进来，头发披散在脸庞周围。她的皮肤看起来更暖和了，仿佛也散发着春天的气息。

‘I’ve been wanting to tell you something.’ She paused. ‘I’ve met someone. It happened in February. I don’t know why I didn’t tell you sooner. To be truthful, I think I felt a bit awkward.’ She paused again. ‘I haven’t told anyone, actually.’

“我一直想告诉你一件事。”她顿了顿。“我遇到了一个人。那是二月份的事。我不知道为什么没早点告诉你。说实话，我觉得有点尴尬。”她又顿了顿。“其实，我还没告诉任何人。”

My mind raced. Was it Jackson? Could it be Jackson she was seeing? I was so caught up in the chain of coincidences that for a moment my imagination ran riot. But then reality intruded into my musings and I remembered that only last week, Jackson had been bemoaning his difficulty in meeting someone new, saying that he still didn’t feel attracted to anyone and couldn’t stop fantasising that Carla would come back to him.

我脑子里一片混乱。是杰克逊吗？她是不是在和杰克逊约会？我完全沉浸在这一连串的巧合中，一时间我的想象力彻底失控。但现实很快打断了我的思绪，我记起就在上周，杰克逊还在抱怨自己很难找到新对象，说他仍然对任何人都没有感觉，而且总是忍不住幻想卡拉会回到他身边。

‘I wonder why it feels awkward, Grace?’ I asked.

“格蕾丝，我不知道为什么你会觉得尴尬？”我问道。

‘Well, he’s a bit famous; you’ll probably have heard of him. And he’s married. So …’ and she trailed off.

“嗯，他有点名气，你可能听说过他。而且他已婚。所以……”她的话渐渐低了下去。

I waited, saying nothing.

我静静地等待着，一言不发。

After a while, she began to talk, explaining that her new lover had two young children. I listened rather sceptically as she told me how sorry he professed to be for dragging her into this tricky situation. He was apparently very aware that she was still getting over her marriage to Dylan.

过了一会儿，她开始说话，解释说她的新情人有两个年幼的孩子。我半信半疑地听着，她告诉我他多么抱歉把她拖进这棘手的境地。他显然很清楚她还没从和迪伦的婚姻中走出来。

‘To be really truthful, I’m not sure how I feel about it all. I’m not even sure I really like him. Of course, I’m flattered by the attention but I feel a bit bad about his wife … and his kids.’

“说实话，我对这一切感觉很复杂。我甚至不确定自己是否真的喜欢他。当然，我对大家的关注感到荣幸，但我有点儿替他的妻子……和孩子们感到难过。”

‘But maybe a bit excited too?’ I asked and she nodded.

“但也许也有点兴奋吧？”我问，她点了点头。

Her face slightly flushed and her tone slightly giggly, she talked about how he seemed totally paranoid. He was very fearful they’d be seen and that the tabloids would find out he was having an affair. The previous week, he had come to see her in her third-floor flat and had insisted, even though it was broad daylight, that she pull down the blinds, just in case someone with a long lens was peeping in. I wondered aloud if the fact that it was so cloak and dagger quite suited her right now but she protested that it wasn’t what she wanted and she knew it was wrong.

她脸颊微微泛红，语气带着一丝笑意，说他看起来疑神疑鬼的。他非常害怕被人看到，害怕小报发现他有外遇。上周，他来她三楼的公寓找她，即便当时是光天化日之下，他也坚持要她拉下窗帘，以防有人用长焦镜头偷窥。我忍不住问她，这种偷偷摸摸的做法是不是正合她意，但她却抗议说这不是她想要的，她也知道这样做不对。

I was beginning to think how interesting it was that she seemed, once again, to have found a man who couldn’t really commit to her and who wasn’t being honest. And there was also something about secrets that seemed to link her experiences. Firstly, there was Dylan, who’d not disclosed the confusion he felt about his sexuality, and now here was someone who was married and who therefore very clearly needed to keep their relationship private. I was chewing over how to begin to explore this with her when she giggled.

我开始琢磨，她似乎又一次找到了一个无法真正对她负责、也不诚实的男人，这真是耐人寻味。而且，她的经历似乎都和秘密有关。先是迪伦，他没有坦白自己对性取向的困惑；现在又是一个已婚人士，显然需要对他们的关系保密。我正琢磨着该如何跟她探讨这个问题，她却咯咯地笑了起来。

‘Do you want to know who it is? Shall I tell you?’

“你想知道他是谁吗？要我告诉你吗？”

I sat silently, I was curious but why was she tantalising me in this way? I wondered.

我静静地坐着，心中充满好奇，她为什么要这样挑逗我呢？我纳闷道。

‘It’s Mr X,’ she said.

“是X先生，”她说。

After that revelation, I didn’t really speak for what remained of the session. Mr X! The same Mr X who’d recommended Jackson to me. I felt confused and a bit alarmed. In my work, confidentiality and clear boundaries are absolutely essential to protect my patients and now it felt as if something was breaching those boundaries. It was as if Mr X had somehow got right inside my consulting room. Suddenly, it felt as if I was the one with a secret. I pondered this after Grace left. I was shaken by the enormous coincidence that Grace and Jackson, whose sessions with me were separated by a mere ten minutes, were also suddenly connected through him. And as this was another coincidence in a series of them, I felt a little spooked.

在那之后，剩下的咨询时间里我几乎没怎么说话。X先生！就是那个向我推荐杰克逊的X先生。我感到困惑，也有些惊恐。在我的工作中，保密和明确的界限对于保护我的病人至关重要，而现在感觉好像有人突破了这些界限。就好像X先生不知怎么地闯进了我的咨询室。突然间，我觉得自己好像也藏着秘密。格蕾丝离开后，我一直在思考这件事。格蕾丝和杰克逊的咨询时间只相隔十分钟，却都通过他联系在一起，这让我感到震惊。而且，这已经是一系列巧合中的又一个了，这让我感到有些毛骨悚然。

Both Freud and Jung, those great fathers of psychoanalysis, were very curious about coincidences and speculated about their links to the paranormal. Freud, despite his deeply religious upbringing, never came to a settled conclusion about whether there was a spiritual world and, fearing he’d undermine the scientific basis of psychoanalysis, he largely avoided the whole topic. Jung, on the other hand, developed a theoretical framework that incorporated mystical elements, which went beyond the known and provable. He called the phenomenon of coincidence, synchronicity and described it as an essentially mysterious connection between the personal psyche and the material world, based on the fact both of these are forms of energy.

弗洛伊德和荣格，这两位精神分析的奠基人，都对巧合现象充满好奇，并推测它们与超自然现象的联系。弗洛伊德虽然成长于宗教氛围浓厚的家庭，但他始终未能就是否存在精神世界得出确切结论。由于担心这会动摇精神分析的科学基础，他基本上回避了这一话题。而荣格则发展出一套融合了神秘元素的理论框架，超越了已知和可证明的范畴。他将巧合现象称为“共时性”，并将其描述为个人心灵与物质世界之间一种本质上神秘的联系，其基础是两者都是能量的形式。

Personally, I lean towards Freud’s more rationalist approach and consider the words of Helene Deutsch – one of the first female psychoanalysts – to be very apposite: ‘Occult powers are to be sought in the depth of the psychic life, and psychoanalysis is destined to clarify this problem in the same manner in which it has previously clarified other “mysterious” happenings in the human psyche.’ fn1

就我个人而言，我更倾向于弗洛伊德更为理性主义的进路，并且认为海伦·德意志（Helene Deutsch，最早的女性精神分析学家之一）的话非常贴切：“神秘的力量需要在心灵深处去探寻，而精神分析注定要以同样的方式阐明这个问题，正如它之前阐明了人类心灵中其他‘神秘’的现象一样。”<sup>1</sup>

For instance, one patient came to me saying that she feared from her dreams that she was demonic. She dreamt of buried bodies, of her teeth turning to fangs and of alien monsters erupting from her chest. It was alarming for her and sometimes the dreams were so graphic it was alarming for me. But careful analysis of these dreams revealed themselves to be infantile imaginings that came from her deeply repressed childhood rage. Eventually we understood that it wasn’t the rage that was the issue for her but rather the way her family situation had required her, as a very young child, to repress it, leaving her feeling guilty and unnatural for feeling so angry. Now the only way these emotions could be expressed was through her dreams.

例如，一位病人来找我，说她做梦时害怕自己变成了恶魔。她梦见被埋葬的尸体，梦见自己的牙齿变成獠牙，梦见外星怪物从胸口破体而出。这些梦让她感到恐惧，有时梦境的画面如此逼真，也让我感到不安。但仔细分析这些梦境后，我们发现它们其实是她童年时期被深深压抑的愤怒所产生的幼年想象。最终我们明白，问题不在于愤怒本身，而在于她幼年时的家庭环境迫使她压抑这种愤怒，让她因为如此强烈的愤怒而感到内疚和不自然。如今，这些情绪只能通过梦境来表达。

By the time Grace arrived the following week, I felt much less alarmed. Yes, here was a series of strange coincidences but although London is a big city, I knew from experience that it could also be a small world, so I focused my attention on what meaning this affair with a married man had for Grace and why she was excited by it. In the session, she talked to me about the deep connection she felt to Mr X and how, although their relationship seemed fated, she felt that she’d known him forever. She chattered on about their plans for a night away and as I listened silently her mood began to shift from excited to reflective.

格蕾丝一周后到达时，我感觉安心多了。没错，这的确是一连串奇怪的巧合，但尽管伦敦是个大城市，我凭经验也知道世界其实很小，所以我把注意力集中在格蕾丝与已婚男士的这段婚外情对她意味着什么，以及她为何对此如此兴奋。在咨询中，她向我倾诉了她与X先生之间深厚的感情，以及尽管他们的关系似乎是命中注定，她却感觉自己好像认识他很久了。她滔滔不绝地讲述着他们计划的外出约会，我静静地听着，她的情绪也从兴奋转为沉思。

‘Why is it’, she complained, ‘that every man I meet seems to be gay or married?’

“为什么，”她抱怨道，“我遇到的每个男人似乎都是同性恋或者已婚人士？”

We discussed how this affair with Mr X held considerable jeopardy for her, particularly given the recent rejection by her husband, and I wondered to myself why she was taking this risk so lightly.

我们讨论了她与 X 先生的这段婚外情对她来说有多么危险，尤其是考虑到她最近被丈夫抛弃，我不禁纳闷，她为什么如此轻易地承担这种风险。

As it turned out, the affair with Mr X fizzled out quite quickly. His work took him overseas and they agreed that their relationship couldn’t really go anywhere. But my thoughts about Grace and the partners she was choosing began to develop further as she then embarked upon a series of relationships that all ended suddenly. She’d begin to date someone in an excited and enthusiastic way but quite quickly she’d find them too keen or they’d abruptly drop her. She also began to tell me about her love life before her marriage to Dylan. All through her twenties she had avoided getting involved with anyone. She’d had many one-night stands but somehow either she or her date didn’t pursue it further. Her first proper relationship had been with Oscar, an older, clever and successful man, whom she’d met at a conference in Rome. He lived in Copenhagen so they began a long-distance affair that lasted four years. Eventually, however, that too fizzled out and soon afterwards she found out that Oscar had got married and had a child. I wondered if she and Oscar had ever discussed living together and she told me no, not really. Oscar had sometimes joked they should get married but she’d never taken him seriously. But Grace was, apparently, now ready for something serious. She talked often about her age and how her friends were becoming settled with partners and having babies. She dated furiously, bemoaning the problems of the internet and how all the men she met were jerks or boring. Mostly she’d dismiss them out of hand but occasionally she’d become excited about someone – and I would notice that this ‘someone’ always seemed a bit unsuitable or unavailable.

结果，她和X先生的这段婚外情很快就无疾而终。他的工作需要他到海外，两人都认为这段关系没有发展下去的可能。但随着格蕾丝开始一段又一段突然结束的恋情，我对她以及她选择的伴侣的看法也开始变得更加复杂。她总是兴致勃勃地开始一段新的恋情，但很快她就会发现对方过于热情，或者对方会突然甩了她。她也开始跟我谈起她嫁给迪伦之前的感情生活。在她二十多岁的时候，她一直避免和任何人发展关系。她有过很多次一夜情，但不知为何，要么是她，要么是对方，都没有进一步发展下去。她的第一段正式恋情是和奥斯卡，一个年纪稍长、聪明能干、事业有成的男人，两人是在罗马的一个会议上认识的。奥斯卡住在哥本哈根，于是他们开始了长达四年的异地恋。然而，这段恋情最终也无疾而终，不久之后，她发现奥斯卡已经结婚生子了。我好奇她和奥斯卡有没有讨论过同居，她告诉我没有，真的没有。奥斯卡有时会开玩笑说他们应该结婚，但她从来没当真。不过，格蕾丝现在显然准备好认真谈恋爱了。她经常谈起自己的年龄，说她的朋友们都找到了伴侣，生了孩子。她疯狂地约会，抱怨网络的种种问题，说她遇到的男人要么是混蛋，要么是无聊透顶。大多数时候她都会直接拒绝，但偶尔也会对某个人动心——而我注意到，这个人总是显得有点不合适，或者根本就不是她想要的。

‘The fates are against me,’ she complained, ‘I’m so unlucky.’

“命运与我作对，”她抱怨道，“我太不幸了。”

But it wasn’t about luck and it was no coincidence that she was struggling to get into a serious relationship.

但这并非运气使然，她难以建立一段认真的恋爱关系也绝非偶然。

Of course, chance and coincidence play their part in people finding love but from my perspective, it’s by no means the most powerful force at work. The romantic idea that you and your partner were destined to meet is a charming, sweet notion but, frankly, pretty unlikely, and the myth that on Halloween, with the aid of a brush, apple and candle, you will see your future husband’s ghostly image in the mirror is clearly unproved. Nevertheless, these myths and superstitions relating to finding love are powerful and enduring in all cultures. I remember, in my early teens, when buses had conductors with silver ticket machines slung around their necks, staring intently at the letters and numbers on this tiny piece of paper for clues to my future love life. How much I longed to know my destiny.

当然，机遇和巧合在人们找到爱情的过程中扮演着一定的角色，但在我看来，它们绝非最强大的力量。你和你的伴侣命中注定要相遇的浪漫想法固然美好动人，但坦白说，可能性微乎其微。而万圣节那天，借助刷子、苹果和蜡烛，就能在镜子里看到未来丈夫的鬼魂影像，这种说法显然未经证实。然而，这些与寻找爱情相关的神话和迷信在各种文化中都根深蒂固，经久不衰。我记得十几岁的时候，公交车上的售票员脖子上挂着银色的售票机，目不转睛地盯着那张小纸片上的字母和数字，试图从中寻找我未来爱情的线索。我当时是多么渴望知道自己的命运啊！

But though the fates don’t choose our partners, something nearly as mysterious is at work – our unconscious. We seem drawn to certain people, we connect, we click. We seem to like their smell, the way they move, the way they laugh. Something attracts us and whilst they may, in actuality, be beautiful, kind and clever, that mysterious something goes beyond these known and visible attributes.

虽然命运不会选择我们的伴侣，但某种同样神秘的力量在起作用——那就是我们的潜意识。我们似乎会被某些人吸引，我们之间产生共鸣，彼此心意相通。我们似乎喜欢他们的气味、举手投足、笑声。某种东西吸引着我们，尽管他们实际上可能美丽、善良、聪明，但那神秘的力量却超越了这些显而易见的特质。

There is a theory, derived from psychoanalysis, about why couples choose each other. It’s one that I find not only compelling but which has been borne out by my own clinical experience. This theory suggests that the way we’re cared for, handled, loved and nurtured in childhood shapes us. Alongside this direct experience, we also witness and observe the intimate relationships around us. We watch our mothers and our fathers love; we absorb the way our carers treat each other and these influences structure our deepest feelings about intimacy. We learn how safe it is to depend on another human and if it’s not safe, we watch our loved ones and learn ways to protect ourselves. All this can leave us with a problem, a problem that we only really confront when we get older and begin love affairs of our own.

有一种源于精神分析的理论，解释了伴侣为何会选择彼此。我发现这个理论不仅令人信服，而且也得到了我自身临床经验的证实。该理论认为，我们在童年时期所受到的关爱、呵护、呵护和养育塑造了我们。除了这种直接体验之外，我们还会观察和感知周围的亲密关系。我们观察父母如何相爱；我们吸收照顾者彼此相处的方式，这些影响塑造了我们对亲密关系最深层的感受。我们学会了依赖他人是否安全，如果并不安全，我们会观察我们所爱的人，并学习如何保护自己。所有这些都可能给我们留下一个问题，一个我们只有在长大成人、开始自己的恋爱关系时才会真正面对的问题。

We can be popular at school, do well at work and excel at sports but when we love, then the trouble, which began in childhood, comes home to roost. We find ourselves attracted to people whose early experiences dovetail or complement ours. We’re powerfully drawn to them as though, at some level, not accessible to our conscious minds, we recognise each other; we feel understood, known. Now, of course, neuroscientists and social scientists would emphasise different reasons for why we fall in love. They’d say it’s pheromones and hormones that determine who you fall for. They’d reference evolutionary biology or cite class, social status or a crossover of interests. And whilst I’m sure all of these things are factors, I’m also convinced that a compelling part of falling in love includes things that are deeply unconscious.

我们可能在学校里人缘好，工作上表现出色，运动方面也成绩斐然，但一旦坠入爱河，那些始于童年的烦恼就会迎面而来。我们会发现自己被那些早期经历与我们契合或互补的人所吸引。我们被他们深深吸引，仿佛在某种我们意识无法触及的层面，我们彼此心意相通；我们感到被理解，被认识。当然，神经科学家和社会科学家会强调我们坠入爱河的不同原因。他们会说，是信息素和荷尔蒙决定了你会爱上谁。他们会引用进化生物学，或者提及阶级、社会地位或兴趣的交集。虽然我相信所有这些都是因素，但我同样确信，坠入爱河的动人之处还包含着一些深藏于潜意识中的因素。

Young lovers lie in bed discovering each other’s lives and feel weirdly as one. From the superficial excitement at finding out you like the same colour, read the same authors and love the same TV series to listening intently to this new person’s feelings about their life, their hopes, their family – something just … resonates. Of course, attraction is also affected by looks, accents, jobs, social status, etc., but running alongside all these calculations is what, in our deepest minds, we feel about coupling and love. Grace wasn’t unlucky in love; it was no coincidence she kept on connecting with men who let her down – these men simply reflected her own uncertainty about commitment, her own deep ambivalence about letting someone into her heart.

年轻的恋人们躺在床上，探索着彼此的生活，奇妙地感受到彼此融为一体。从发现彼此喜欢相同的颜色、阅读相同的作家作品、追看同一部电视剧时产生的表面兴奋，到认真倾听对方对生活、希望和家庭的感受——某种东西……产生了共鸣。当然，吸引力也受到外貌、口音、职业、社会地位等因素的影响，但除了这些考量之外，我们内心深处对结合和爱情的感受也同样重要。格蕾丝并非情路坎坷；她总是遇到让她失望的男人并非偶然——这些男人恰恰反映了她自己对承诺的不确定，以及她内心深处对于敞开心扉的矛盾心理。

One morning she arrived at the consulting room in an agitated state and I immediately noticed how pale she looked.

一天早上，她情绪激动地来到诊室，我立刻注意到她脸色苍白。

‘My father’s coming to London. He’s been living in Sydney with his new wife for the last eight years. I haven’t seen him since he moved there. He’s coming with her … It’s going to be awful.’

“我父亲要来伦敦了。过去八年他一直和新婚妻子住在悉尼。自从他搬去那里后，我就没见过他。他要和她一起来……这太糟糕了。”

I had heard very little about her family, apart from the fact that her parents were divorced. She seemed very close to her mother but her relationship with her father was distant and awkward.

除了知道她父母离异之外，我对她的家庭知之甚少。她似乎和母亲关系很亲密，但和父亲的关系却疏远而尴尬。

‘That’s a long time not to have seen him,’ I commented.

“好久没见到他了，”我评论道。

‘He’s asked me to visit. Several times. I just never wanted to go. He’s coming back now because, apparently, her sister is ill.’

“他邀请我去探望她好几次了。我一直都不想去。现在他要再去一次，据说是因为她妹妹生病了。”

‘Her sister?’ I enquired. ‘His second wife’s sister?’

“她妹妹？”我问道。“他第二任妻子的妹妹？”

‘Third wife,’ corrected Grace.

“是第三任妻子，”格蕾丝纠正道。

She then began to tell me more about her parents’ divorce when she was eleven and her brother was seven. She told it in a way that felt as if she’d never thought about it before, as though it had been locked away inside her mind since it happened. She spoke hesitantly, with past and present muddled and the narrative jumbled and confusing. Her father and mother, she claimed, had seemed happy and never argued, so the divorce had come as a total shock.

然后，她开始跟我讲述她十一岁、弟弟七岁时父母离婚的事。她讲述的方式，仿佛从未想过这件事，仿佛它从发生之日起就被锁在她记忆深处。她说话犹豫不决，过去和现在交织在一起，叙述混乱不堪。她说，她的父母看起来一直很幸福，从未吵过架，所以父母的离婚对她来说完全是晴天霹雳。

‘I haven’t always been distanced from Dad. When I was little, we were really close. He was funny and played with me and my brother much more than Mum ever did.’

“我并非一直和爸爸关系疏远。小时候，我们非常亲密。他很幽默，而且比妈妈更经常陪我和弟弟玩。”

‘Do you have memories of when he left?’

你还记得他离开时的情景吗？

‘I was devastated, actually. I remember feeling sick and frightened. Mum told me not to cry. She always said he was a shit and didn’t deserve any tears.’

“我当时真的崩溃了。我记得我感到恶心和害怕。妈妈让我别哭。她总是说他是个混蛋，不配流眼泪。”

‘A shit?’ I questioned.

“一坨屎？”我问道。

‘Basically, he left me for another woman.’

“说白了，他是为了另一个女人抛弃了我。”

I was struck by her Freudian slip; Grace had meant to say that he’d left her mother for another woman.

我被她口误吓了一跳；格蕾丝原本想说的是他为了另一个女人抛弃了她的母亲。

‘Perhaps your father’s betrayal of your mother felt like it was a betrayal of you?’ I asked.

“或许你觉得父亲背叛母亲的行为也等同于背叛了你？”我问道。

‘I think he was probably having affairs all the time.’ She paused and then spoke very slowly, again as if recalling things for the first time. ‘I remember being taken on drives and being left in the car. I hated it. I was always scared because he’d be a long, long time. When he came back it would be dark. Then he’d take me to Toys‘R’Us before we went home.’ She frowned. ‘When I was older, he took me to Hennes to buy clothes. He bought me a lot of clothes.’

“我觉得他可能一直都有外遇。”她停顿了一下，然后又慢慢地说，仿佛是第一次回忆起这些事。“我记得他带我出去兜风，然后把我留在车里。我讨厌这样。我总是很害怕，因为他要很久很久才能回来。他回来的时候天都黑了。然后他会带我去玩具反斗城，之后才回家。”她皱起了眉头。“我长大一些后，他会带我去亨尼斯买衣服。他给我买了很多衣服。”

Grace then began to cry but instantly fought against it, pushing the tears back down until she had control.

格蕾丝开始哭泣，但她立刻努力克制住情绪，强忍住泪水，直到控制住为止。

‘Actually, I hate him now,’ she said. ‘He’s a selfish cunt. He was obviously fucking someone whilst I sat in the car. Jesus, what a bastard.’

“说实话，我现在恨死他了，”她说。“他是个自私的混蛋。我坐在车里的时候，他显然在和别人鬼混。天哪，真是个混蛋。”

‘You feel very angry, Grace. I think it feels like he betrayed you.’

“格蕾丝，你感到非常生气。我想你觉得他背叛了你。”

‘He’s just a cunt!’ Grace repeated.

“他就是个混蛋！”格蕾丝重复道。

‘You’re expressing a lot of anger but not any hurt. It sounds like you were very frightened and confused by all this as a child. Perhaps the anger protects you from these other feelings?’

“你表现出了很多愤怒，但没有表现出任何伤痛。听起来你小时候对这一切感到非常害怕和困惑。也许愤怒能保护你免受其他负面情绪的侵扰？”

Grace nodded and I saw her eyes brim with tears again.

格蕾丝点了点头，我看到她的眼眶再次盈满了泪水。

In the following weeks, we slowly began to understand more about her difficulties with intimacy and commitment. We explored how there were two contradictory feelings inside her that could easily be evoked if she began to get close to a lover. The first feeling was her fear of losing love and being rejected, and it seemed the source of this fear related to her childhood loss of her father. She’d adored him but often felt, even before he left, that her connection to him was precarious. Her father had been exciting and seductive but then he’d drop her for work or a lover, meaning that Grace had never felt truly secure.

接下来的几周，我们逐渐开始了解她在亲密关系和承诺方面遇到的困难。我们探讨了她内心两种矛盾的情感，一旦她开始与爱人亲近，这两种情感就很容易被唤起。第一种情感是害怕失去爱和被拒绝，而这种恐惧似乎源于她童年时期父亲的离世。她非常爱他，但即便在他离开之前，她也常常感到与父亲的关系岌岌可危。她的父亲曾让她感到兴奋和充满魅力，但他却会为了工作或情人而抛弃她，这意味着格蕾丝从未真正感受到安全感。

‘I think I always felt I bored him. He’d play with us but then he’d look irritated with me and he’d go out. I always felt anxious about that. That he’d leave me behind.’

“我觉得我一直让他觉得无聊。他会和我们玩，但之后他会看起来很生气，然后就出去了。我总是为此感到焦虑，害怕他会把我一个人留下。”

She told me that when he did finally leave home, she rarely saw him, though from time to time he’d turn up and sweep her off her feet, only to drop her again, leaving her bereft.

她告诉我，当他最终离开家后，她很少见到他，尽管他偶尔会突然出现，让她神魂颠倒，但之后又会抛弃她，让她伤心欲绝。

The second feeling that seemed to be interfering with making a serious commitment to a man was that, whilst she worried about being left, she also feared getting too close and could, quite easily, feel suffocated and long for her own space. She would often describe this as being ‘peopled out’. I began to wonder if unconsciously she’d married Dylan because he was ambivalent about her; that his ambivalence, because he was gay, echoed her own.

第二个似乎阻碍她与男人建立认真关系的感受是，她既担心被抛弃，又害怕走得太近，很容易感到窒息，渴望拥有自己的空间。她经常把这种感觉描述为“人际交往障碍”。我开始怀疑，她是否在潜意识里嫁给了迪伦，因为迪伦对她态度暧昧；而迪伦的暧昧，因为他是同性恋，恰好与她自己的矛盾心理相呼应。

She then began to talk a great deal about her mother and I could see how intense their relationship was. I wondered whether this was the other side of the coin. Did this intensity with her mother, which made her feel suffocated, get re-evoked in her relationships with lovers? It was clear that intimate relationships could easily make her feel claustrophobic.

她开始滔滔不绝地谈起她的母亲，我能感受到她们母女关系的亲密程度。我不禁思考，这是否是硬币的另一面？这种让她感到窒息的亲密关系，是否会在她与爱人的关系中重现？显然，亲密关系很容易让她感到幽闭恐惧。

One morning, as we drew near to the August break, Grace started her session by complaining about her holiday plans. ‘You know I told you about me going away with my friend Chloe and her brother Tom? We’ve rented this flat in Mykonos.’

一天早上，临近八月假期，格蕾丝在课上开始抱怨她的假期计划。“你们知道我跟你们说过我要和我朋友克洛伊还有她哥哥汤姆一起出去玩吗？我们在米科诺斯岛租了一套公寓。”

I nodded.

我点了点头。

‘Well, you won’t believe it, but my mother has rented an Airbnb practically right across the street. Which is ridiculous because it’s right in the middle of the old town, which she’ll hate. This is practically the first summer holiday I’ve had in ages without her. I don’t want to be mean to her but she’s not going to enjoy it anyway. She hates hot places and I don’t think she’ll like the clubbing much either!’ Her laughter died away and she paused. ‘I can’t tell her not to come, she’d be too upset.’

“哎呀，你肯定不信，我妈居然在街对面租了个Airbnb。真是太荒唐了，那地方就在老城区中心，她肯定会讨厌的。这几乎是我好久以来第一次没有她陪伴的暑假。我不想对她不好，但她反正也不会喜欢。她讨厌热的地方，而且我觉得她也不会喜欢去夜店！”她笑了笑，停顿了一下。“我不好意思不让她来，她会很难过的。”

I was struck at how intrusive her mother was. Couldn’t she see that she’d be unwelcome and that barging into her 35-year-old daughter’s holiday was a little inappropriate? This incident gave me a clearer picture of the relationship between them and I began to see how Grace could feel that it wasn’t just her father who put his own needs first. But then I also asked myself why Grace wasn’t more assertive with her mother. Why didn’t she gently explain that she wanted to go alone? It seemed as if it was impossible for her to say anything to her mother that smacked of rejection or might start an argument. It reminded me of the way her mother had instructed her not to cry over her father’s desertion and how, dutifully, Grace had therefore suppressed her feelings.

我震惊于她母亲的干涉程度。难道她看不出来自己不受欢迎，闯入35岁女儿的假期有多么不妥吗？这件事让我更清楚地了解了她们之间的关系，也开始明白格蕾丝为什么会觉得，并非只有她父亲才会把自己的需求放在第一位。但同时，我也在想，为什么格蕾丝对母亲不够强势？为什么她不委婉地解释自己想独自前往？似乎她根本无法对母亲说出任何带有拒绝意味或可能引发争吵的话。这让我想起她母亲曾告诫她不要为父亲的离去而哭泣，而格蕾丝也因此乖乖地压抑了自己的情绪。

I also began to notice the way Grace was treating me. She was mostly a very solicitous patient, enquiring how I was doing at the start of each appointment, despite my never giving more than a discouraging brief nod. It wasn’t that I minded her asking but I wanted her to understand that in therapy she didn’t need to follow these social protocols. She’d also look worried when I responded to her in a compassionate way, almost as though it was me who was hurting rather than her. If I looked concerned, she’d become agitated and reassure me she was fine. She paid her bill literally minutes after I sent it to her and she always kept an eye on the timing of the session, never leaving it to me to say that it was time to end.

我也开始注意到格蕾丝对待我的方式。她基本上是个非常体贴的病人，每次预约开始时都会问我感觉如何，尽管我最多只是敷衍地点点头。我倒是不介意她问，只是希望她明白，在治疗过程中她不需要遵守这些社交礼仪。当我以同情的态度回应她时，她也会显得很担心，好像受伤的是我而不是她。如果我表现出担忧，她就会变得焦躁不安，并向我保证她没事。她总是在我把账单发给她后几分钟就付款，而且她总是留意着治疗的时间，从来不会等到我提醒她该结束了。

It began to dawn on me that perhaps she felt I needed protecting in some way; sometimes she even seemed to treat me as though I was the needy, fragile one, not her. I recognised this as the transference – was she recreating with me the kind of relationship she had with her mother?

我开始意识到，或许她觉得我需要某种程度的保护；有时她甚至好像把我当成那个需要帮助、脆弱的人，而不是她自己。我意识到这是移情——她是不是想在我身上重现她和她母亲之间的那种关系？

Understanding the transference and countertransference is central to the way I work and, indeed, to the work of all psychoanalytic therapists. The transference refers to the way attitudes and feelings about a relationship from the past are recreated in the relationship between a patient and their therapist. Whilst countertransference refers to the feelings a patient may stir up in the therapist and how these might relate to the re-enactment of a pattern of relationship derived usually from childhood experience. In Grace’s case, it began to be evident that feelings about her mother’s fragility were being ‘transferred’ onto me and I could see that she was convinced that I needed to be handled with kid gloves. This really helped me get a sense of how deeply she feared upsetting her mother.

理解移情和反移情是我工作的核心，实际上也是所有精神分析治疗师工作的核心。移情指的是患者过去对一段关系的感受和态度如何在患者与治疗师的关系中重现。而反移情指的是患者可能在治疗师身上激起的感受，以及这些感受如何与通常源于童年经历的关系模式的重现相关联。在格蕾丝的案例中，我开始意识到她将对母亲脆弱的感受“转移”到了我身上，我能看出她坚信我需要被小心翼翼地对待。这让我深刻地体会到她内心深处有多么害怕惹母亲生气。

Then something else shone further light on childhood events that seemed to be shaping her current love life. As Grace’s curiosity about herself grew, she wanted to know more about her childhood but it seemed there were many things she couldn’t remember. It was almost as if there were gaps she couldn’t fill, and they began to worry her. Finally, she worked up the courage to have a conversation with her mother whilst on a weekend visit to her aunt in Norfolk. It was a sunny day and the three of them sat in the garden drinking Pimm’s and talking about the past. After an hour of them jointly bitching about her father, she asked her mother about her birth and her mother told her tearfully that she’d been hospitalised with postnatal depression soon after Grace was born. And this had happened again when Grace’s brother arrived, two years later.

后来，一些事情进一步揭示了童年往事，这些往事似乎正在影响着她现在的爱情生活。随着格蕾丝对自己的好奇心日益增长，她想了解更多关于自己童年的事情，但似乎有很多事情她都记不起来了。就好像有一些空白无法填补，这让她开始感到焦虑。最终，在周末去诺福克探望姨妈时，她鼓起勇气和母亲谈了谈。那天阳光明媚，她们三人坐在花园里喝着皮姆酒，聊着往事。她们一起抱怨了她父亲一个小时后，格蕾丝问起母亲关于她出生的事，母亲含泪告诉她，格蕾丝出生后不久，她就因产后抑郁症住院了。两年后，格蕾丝的弟弟出生时，同样的事情再次发生。

Was this at the root of why Grace was so protective of her mother? In my mind, I visualised a two-year-old desperately missing her mum. I imagined that Grace, in a child’s way, may have sensed her mother’s fragility and been very frightened by it. Had she then become hypersensitive to her mother’s moods? Had she tried her absolute best to prevent her mother becoming sad and leaving again? What a burden this must have been for a little toddler.

这是否就是格蕾丝如此保护母亲的根源？我脑海中浮现出一个两岁孩子无比思念母亲的画面。我想，格蕾丝或许以孩童特有的方式，感受到了母亲的脆弱，并为此感到害怕。她是否因此对母亲的情绪异常敏感？她是否竭尽全力阻止母亲再次伤心离去？这对一个蹒跚学步的孩子来说，该是多么沉重的负担啊。

Over some weeks, we talked about these aspects of her childhood and how some of the feelings she had about her mother were being repeated with me.
