Reggie and Lawrence Play Piggy in the Middle

雷吉和劳伦斯玩“中间人”游戏

As soon as Reggie and Lawrence began to talk, I felt optimistic that I could help them. They’d come, they quickly reassured me, not because they’d had any problems of their own but because they were concerned that their 25-year-old son seemed stuck.

雷吉和劳伦斯一开口，我就觉得或许能帮到他们。他们很快向我保证，他们来这里不是因为他们自己遇到了什么问题，而是因为他们担心自己25岁的儿子似乎陷入了困境。

‘Stuck?’ I enquired.

“卡住了吗？”我问道。

‘Yes, stuck at home,’ said Lawrence. ‘I think even Reggie thinks it’s time he moved on.’ Reggie, with a resigned sigh, nodded her head in agreement.

“是啊，困在家里，”劳伦斯说。“我觉得就连雷吉都觉得他该离开了。”雷吉无奈地叹了口气，点头表示同意。

As they told me more about their son, Woody, I gradually noticed how difficult it was to focus on them both. They were sitting as far apart on my couch as they could possibly get and, as they talked, I felt like a spectator at Wimbledon, my head turning from side to side as each of them played their shot. Often, they interrupted each other and disagreed, eager to tell me their ‘true’ version of events. By the end of the first session, I felt exhausted. Despite this tiredness, however, I had a good feeling that they’d found the session useful. They needed a lot of support but I was hopeful I could assist them and thereby help Woody to get on with his life.

随着他们向我讲述更多关于他们儿子伍迪的故事，我渐渐意识到要同时关注他们俩有多么困难。他们尽可能地分开坐在沙发上，我感觉自己像温布尔登网球公开赛的观众，随着他们各自击球，我的头也左右摇摆。他们经常打断对方，意见不一，急于告诉我他们各自“真实”的说法。第一次咨询结束时，我感到筋疲力尽。尽管如此，我仍然觉得这次咨询对他们很有帮助。他们需要很多支持，但我希望我能帮助他们，从而帮助伍迪继续生活下去。

At the next session, they again sat far apart. Underneath her taupe trench coat, I could see that Reggie was wearing stripy tights and an orange corduroy dress. Her colourful clothes made her look a little like a presenter on a children’s television programme. Lawrence was dressed like a farmer – thick brown trousers and a rough, tweedy jacket covering his Tattersall shirt. He was clean-shaven but his long, thinning hair was pushed back off his face and rested gently on his shoulders. They told me they were gardeners and you could see from their ruddy faces and weather-beaten hands that they spent a lot of time outdoors.

下次见面时，他们又坐得很远。透过雷吉的灰褐色风衣，我看到她穿着条纹紧身裤和橙色灯芯绒连衣裙。她这身色彩鲜艳的衣服让她看起来有点像儿童电视节目的主持人。劳伦斯则打扮得像个农民——厚厚的棕色裤子，一件粗花呢外套罩在格子衬衫外面。他刮了胡子，稀疏的长发向后梳起，自然地垂在肩上。他们告诉我他们是园丁，从他们红润的脸庞和饱经风霜的双手可以看出，他们经常在户外工作。

‘I’d like to say, Susanna, how helpful the last meeting was. I really felt you “got” the issues and, after we got home, I had a long talk with Woody that evening, which felt like a bit of a breakthrough.’

“苏珊娜，我想说，上次的会面真的很有帮助。我感觉你真的理解了这些问题，回家后，那天晚上我和伍迪进行了一次长谈，感觉这算是一个突破。”

As soon as he drew breath, Reggie interrupted Lawrence’s flow. ‘I didn’t know you spoke to Woody last week. You didn’t say. I spoke to him too. On Friday. When did you speak to him? Was it before or after?’

雷吉刚一喘口气，就打断了劳伦斯的话。“我不知道你上周跟伍迪说过话。你没说。我也跟他说过话。周五。你什么时候跟他说话的？之前还是之后？”

‘What does it matter?’ Lawrence snapped, raising his hands in the air in a gesture of exasperation. He turned to me and, in a much more reasonable voice, proceeded to tell me how he felt he’d really connected with Woody and how Woody had agreed that he’d do more in the house and perhaps come and help them on some jobs, once he finished his dissertation.

“这有什么关系？”劳伦斯厉声说道，同时无奈地举起双手。他转向我，用一种平和得多的语气告诉我，他觉得自己和伍迪的关系真的很好，伍迪也同意在完成论文后多做些家务，也许还会来帮他们做些活。

‘His dissertation?’ I enquired.

“他的论文？”我问道。

‘You did what?’ Reggie said, ignoring me. ‘Why’d you say he could work with us? You know he hates gardening and how does it help him become more independent if he’s working for us? It doesn’t, does it?’

“你干了什么？”雷吉没理我，问道，“你为什么说他可以跟我们一起工作？你知道他讨厌园艺，让他为我们工作怎么能让他变得更独立呢？根本没用，对吧？”

This back and forth continued at pace and I had to work overtime to manage the session in such a way that each of them had a say. Each of my interventions seemed to chime with them and I found myself liking them a great deal; their passion and engagement was evident. On the other hand, I confess to feeling irritated with Woody – he sounded rather selfish, lazy and entitled. He needs a firmer approach, I thought to myself, but it was clear that Reggie and Lawrence seemed to be set on taking it in turns to protect him in one way or another.

这种你来我往的对话持续进行，节奏很快，我不得不加班加点地安排谈话，确保每个人都能发表意见。我的每一次发言似乎都与他们的想法不谋而合，我发现自己非常喜欢他们；他们的热情和投入显而易见。另一方面，我承认我对伍迪感到有些恼火——他听起来相当自私、懒惰，而且自以为是。我心想，他需要更强硬的管教，但很明显，雷吉和劳伦斯似乎决心轮流以各种方式保护他。

The following session, they arrived wearing heavy boots covered in mud, which they proceeded to unlace and leave by the door, padding over to the couch in their socks. Reggie spoke first, smiling at me and asking how I was.

下一次聚会时，他们穿着沾满泥巴的厚重靴子来了，他们解开鞋带把靴子扔在门口，然后穿着袜子轻手轻脚地走到沙发旁。雷吉先开了口，他笑着问我感觉怎么样。

‘I’d like to talk about what happened on Tuesday evening,’ she said, glancing at Lawrence, who nodded his assent. ‘I think it would be helpful because it was a really good example of what goes on with Woody all the time.’

“我想谈谈周二晚上发生的事，”她说着，瞥了一眼劳伦斯，劳伦斯点头表示同意。“我觉得这会很有帮助，因为这件事很好地体现了伍迪一贯的行事风格。”

‘Was it Tuesday?’ Lawrence suddenly interrupted. ‘I think it was Wednesday, when we got back from Kingston.’

“是星期二吗？”劳伦斯突然打断道，“我想是星期三，我们从金斯顿回来的那天。”

‘It doesn’t matter which day,’ Reggie said coldly, raising her eyebrows in contempt and looking to me for agreement.

“哪一天都无所谓，”雷吉冷冷地说，轻蔑地扬起眉毛，看向我征求意见。

Before they started their usual bickering I interrupted. ‘Shall we stay with what you were going to tell me? I think you both wanted me to hear it.’ And they nodded in agreement. Lawrence was about to speak but Reggie shushed him with a fierce look and took up the reins.

在他们开始像往常一样争吵之前，我打断了他们。“我们还是继续讲你们刚才要跟我说的话吧？我觉得你们俩都想让我听到。”他们点头表示同意。劳伦斯正要开口，雷吉却狠狠地瞪了他一眼，示意他噤声，然后接管了谈话。

‘We’d just got back. From Kingston. We’ve been working on a big project down there, a great project, actually. I was knackered, we both were. And, as usual, Woody was in the dining room playing on his Xbox and the kitchen was ab-so-lute-ly filthy ! He’d obviously been in there all day; there were cups, plates, glasses. And he’d been smoking – you could smell it. And I said to him, quite nicely, “Please clear up.”’

“我们刚从金斯顿回来。我们在那边一直在忙一个大项目，真的是个很棒的项目。我累坏了，我们俩都累坏了。而且，像往常一样，伍迪在餐厅里玩他的Xbox，厨房简直脏得一塌糊涂！他显然在里面待了一整天；到处都是杯子、盘子、玻璃杯。他还抽烟——都能闻到烟味。我客气地跟他说：‘请收拾一下。’”

Lawrence huffed dismissively.

劳伦斯不屑地哼了一声。

‘I did say it nicely,’ Reggie responded, turning on Lawrence.

“我说话的语气很客气，”雷吉回应道，转身看向劳伦斯。

‘I didn’t say anything!’

“我什么都没说！”

And then they were off again, bickering about Woody’s attitude and how Reggie’s version of what happened was entirely wrong or entirely right.

然后他们又开始争论起来，争论伍迪的态度，以及雷吉对事情经过的描述是完全错误还是完全正确。

I put up my hand. ‘Stop! Let’s just try to think through together what happened.’ And they both looked at me guiltily and quietened down.

我举起手说：“停！我们一起想想到底发生了什么。”他们俩都愧疚地看着我，安静了下来。

‘I don’t want to start another fight but really, Lawrie, why won’t you ever support me? We make an agreement – we’d agreed, hadn’t we? That we’d ask him to help out more but then as soon as I challenge him, you jump in to defend him. Why? You make it seem like I’m being a bitch … or something. I don’t think I am.’

“我不想再吵架了，但劳里，你为什么从来不支持我？我们不是说好了吗？我们答应过要他多帮忙，但可我一质疑他，你就跳出来维护他。为什么？你这样说，好像我是个泼妇似的……或者别的什么。我不觉得我是。”

‘You jump on him; you know what you do. Like he’s like minding his own business and you’re on him as soon as we walk in. I don’t know, it just seems you don’t give him a chance. And then you’re on at me for not doing something or other, or not being supportive ,’ Lawrence finished, spitting out the last word contemptuously.

“你一下子就扑上去，你知道你在干什么。他明明好好的，我们一进门你就冲他嚷嚷。我不知道，你好像根本不给他机会。然后你又因为我没做什么或者没支持他而责怪我，”劳伦斯说完，最后一个字带着轻蔑的语气。

‘Is it ever the other way round?’ I asked.

“有没有反过来的情况呢？”我问道。

They looked at me puzzled.

他们疑惑地看着我。

‘Is it ever Reggie saying that you’re being too tough, too harsh? Is it ever that way round?’

“雷吉有没有说过你太严厉、太苛刻？或者反过来呢？”

‘Sometimes … yes,’ Lawrence replied hesitantly. ‘Not so much recently but definitely when he was younger. You never let me tell him off … ever. Ever! Not when he was little – no way! You’re just as bad as me,’ Lawrence concluded triumphantly.

“有时候……是的，”劳伦斯犹豫地回答。“最近不太常这样，但他小时候肯定经常这样。你从来不让我训斥他……从来没有。从来没有！他小时候绝对不行！你跟我一样坏，”劳伦斯得意洋洋地总结道。

They continued to rant at each other about who’d been the most involved and who’d been most devoted when Woody was younger. I was wondering where this would take us when Reggie began to speak in a different tone.

他们继续争论谁在伍迪小时候参与度最高、谁最尽心尽力。我正琢磨着这会把事情引向何方，这时雷吉突然换了个语气说话。

‘What you don’t know, Susanna, is that I was actually pregnant before Woody, about a year before he was born. I had a late miscarriage.’

“苏珊娜，你不知道的是，伍迪出生前大约一年，我其实怀过孕。后来流产了。”

‘It was a stillbirth, Reg, wasn’t it? Not really a miscarriage,’ Lawrence interjected.

“那是死产，雷格，对吧？不算流产，”劳伦斯插话道。

And then they told me about the son they’d lost, just a month before he was due to be born. They never found out why he’d died; the pregnancy had gone smoothly and they were both so happy and then suddenly he stopped moving. As they spoke, they seemed to relive the horror of it. Reggie sobbed and Lawrence stared glassily into the distance, and I felt tears welling in my eyes too. But after the session ended, I also wondered why Reggie had called it a miscarriage. Did it sound less traumatic? More ‘normal’, somehow?

然后他们跟我讲了他们失去儿子的事，就在预产期前一个月。他们始终没能找到孩子夭折的原因；怀孕过程很顺利，他们俩都非常幸福，然后孩子突然就停止了胎动。他们一边说着，一边仿佛又一次经历了那可怕的时刻。雷吉泣不成声，劳伦斯目光呆滞地望着远方，我的眼眶也湿润了。但咨询结束后，我一直在想，为什么雷吉会把这件事称为“流产”呢？是不是这样听起来没那么痛苦？是不是感觉更“正常”一些？

As the weeks went by, it became clearer they both struggled to be firm with Woody. We talked about how these parenting difficulties were very much shared, as they took it in turns to admonish and then indulge him. Reggie would often scold him for not doing something in the house or nag him about his coursework, but then a heartbeat later, she’d be making him a snack or doing his laundry and paying his mobile bill.

随着时间推移，越来越明显的是，他们俩都很难对伍迪采取强硬的态度。我们聊到，这些育儿难题其实是他们共同面对的，因为他们轮流训斥伍迪，然后又溺爱他。雷吉经常会责备伍迪没做家务，或者唠叨他的作业，但转眼间，她又会给他做点零食，帮他洗衣服，帮他交手机费。

At some point, as almost always happens when couples come to discuss problems with their children, Reggie and Lawrence stopped talking about Woody and started talking about themselves. There was a painful disappointment with their sex life, which had dwindled away and now they were never intimate with each other. It was unclear why they’d stopped having sex as each of them declared they missed it. Despite this, neither of them was able to take the initiative. Neither would, in the quiet, dark of the night, make the move towards the other. It was as though they were frozen, full of longing but petrified, like marble sarcophagi in their bed.

就像几乎所有夫妻在讨论孩子问题时都会发生的那样，雷吉和劳伦斯最终不再谈论伍迪，而是开始谈论自己。他们的性生活令他们感到痛苦的失望，性生活日渐减少，如今他们之间再也没有亲密接触。他们各自都说想念性生活，但却不清楚他们停止性生活的原因。尽管如此，他们谁也无法主动。在寂静的夜里，谁也不愿主动靠近对方。他们仿佛被冻住了，内心充满渴望却又僵硬如石，像两座石棺静静地躺在床上。

Though I could sense their discomfort, I decided to be more direct about their lack of love-making. I asked when it had begun to fade and whether they had thoughts about why this had happened. At this point, they started to find it problematic to attend together. One week, Lawrence had such a bad back that he couldn’t come. The next, Reggie had to visit her mother. Then Lawrence had a dental appointment, which couldn’t be rearranged, and Reggie had to take Woody to a job interview. So it went on, with me seeing each of them in turn and I confess it took me some weeks to make the link, that exploring their sex life jointly was something they were, unconsciously, resisting.

虽然我能感觉到他们的不自在，但我决定更直接地询问他们性生活不和谐的问题。我问他们性生活是从什么时候开始减少的，以及他们是否想过这是为什么。这时，他们开始觉得一起来聚会很困难。有一周，劳伦斯背痛得厉害，来不了。下一周，雷吉要去看望她母亲。然后劳伦斯有个牙医预约，时间无法更改，雷吉又要陪伍迪去面试。就这样，我轮流见他们，我承认，我花了几个星期才意识到，他们潜意识里一直在抗拒共同探索性生活这件事。

It was November and freezing cold when I finally got them back in the room together. The heating in my office had broken down so we were making do with a noisy and only partly effective blow heater.

那是十一月，天气冷得要命，我终于把他们俩弄回了同一个房间。我办公室的暖气坏了，所以我们只能用一个噪音很大、效果也不太好的电暖器凑合着用。

‘Woody’s got a job!’ Lawrence told me excitedly.

“伍迪找到工作了！”劳伦斯兴奋地告诉我。

‘He’s working for Help the Aged,’ Reggie chimed in, laughing.

“他在老年人救助会工作，”雷吉笑着插嘴道。

‘Feel sorry for the aged,’ Lawrence joked.

“真替老年人感到惋惜，”劳伦斯开玩笑说。

And then they competed to tell me more about the news and, once again, I felt my head turning repeatedly from side to side as I tried to listen to them both equally. And then, as usual, they fell to bickering.

然后他们开始争先恐后地告诉我更多新闻，我又一次感觉自己的头不停地左右转动，试图同时听他们俩说两句。然后，像往常一样，他们又开始争吵起来。

‘I don’t know why you’re even talking about it to Susanna. You were against him having a job until he got his MA,’ Lawrence said angrily.

“我真不明白你为什么还要跟苏珊娜谈这件事。你之前一直反对他找工作，直到他拿到硕士学位为止。”劳伦斯生气地说。

‘Rubbish, I took him for the interview,’ Reggie said petulantly, glancing at me. ‘ I helped with the application. You really think you’re the only one who does anything for Woody?’

“胡说，是我带他去面试的，”雷吉不高兴地说，瞥了我一眼。“我还帮他填了申请表。你真以为只有你一个人在帮伍迪？”

‘You’re always jealous of our relationship. Always. You never let me and Woody have a moment. It’s not all about you. You really know how to spoil things.’

“你总是嫉妒我们的关系。总是。你从来不让我和伍迪单独相处一会儿。这不仅仅是你的问题。你真的很会破坏事情。”

Suddenly, it occurred to me. I was Woody. Or rather, there was something similar in the way they related to me and him. They competed over me in the same way they competed over their son. It was happening right now. As they argued, both were keeping one eye on how I was reacting, whose side I would come down on, and I was finding myself having that old familiar ‘Wimbledon’ feeling as I struggled to listen and attend to them both.

我突然意识到，我就是伍迪。或者更确切地说，他们对待我和伍迪的方式有相似之处。他们争夺我的方式，就像他们争夺儿子一样。这一切此刻正在发生。他们争吵时，都时刻关注着我的反应，看我会站在哪一边。我发现自己又一次体会到了那种熟悉的“温布尔登”式的紧张感，努力倾听并关注着他们两人。

‘It seems you both feel that Woody doesn’t have a relationship with the two of you as a couple. And that means you have to compete for his love. I wonder if you feel similarly with me – you’re both constantly checking which of you I really like better? I think you believe that only one of you can get my attention, my care, and that the other is then going to be completely left out in the cold. As if you can’t imagine that I can hold you both in mind?’

“看来你们俩都觉得伍迪跟你们俩之间没有感情。这意味着你们得争夺他的爱。我不知道你们是不是也这么想——你们俩是不是总在琢磨我到底更喜欢你们俩中的一个？我觉得你们觉得只有你们其中一个才能得到我的关注和爱，另一个就会被彻底冷落。难道你们就想象不到我其实会同时想着你们俩吗？”

They stopped bickering and turned to reassuring me that it wasn’t so. They both thought I was entirely fair, they said, and this was one of the reasons they felt safe with me. But something clearly chimed with them as they then began to explore their competitiveness. They laughed as they recounted how they behaved when they played games and they acknowledged they could turn everything into a race.

他们停止了争吵，转而向我保证事情并非如此。他们说，他们都认为我非常公平，这也是他们觉得和我在一起很安全的原因之一。但随后，他们之间似乎产生了某种共鸣，开始探讨起彼此的竞争意识。他们笑着回忆起玩游戏时的情景，并承认自己能把所有事情都变成一场比赛。

‘When you were kids, did you compete with your siblings?’ I asked.

“你小时候会和兄弟姐妹比赛吗？”我问。

‘My sister was so much older that I felt more like an only child. I was definitely my father’s favourite, wasn’t I?’ Reggie began, looking to Lawrence for confirmation. ‘He always took my side. If Mum was cross, he’d always tell her off. Since he died, I’ve got much closer to my mum.’ Reggie paused. ‘I felt … feel … a bit guilty about how I treated her when I was a teenager.’ I watched her absorb what she’d just said. ‘I’d hate to think I was doing the same with Woody … I don’t want him to feel “piggy in the middle” like I did.’

“我姐姐比我大很多，所以我感觉自己更像个独生子。我肯定是我爸爸最宠爱的孩子，对吧？”雷吉说着，看向劳伦斯寻求认同。“他总是站在我这边。如果妈妈生气了，他总是会替她训斥。自从他去世后，我和妈妈的关系亲近了很多。”雷吉停顿了一下。“我……我……有点愧疚，因为我十几岁的时候那样对待她。”我看着她消化着刚才的话。“我可不想我对伍迪也那样……我不想让他像我一样，感觉自己夹在中间左右为难。”

‘Piggy in the middle?’ I echoed, seeking more.

“中间那只小猪？”我重复道，想要了解更多。

‘Yes, well, they were always fighting. My mum was always on at my dad about something or other. Usually money,’ she said ruefully. ‘I think I felt sorry for him and, because she nagged me too, he felt sorry for me.’

“是啊，他们总是吵架。我妈总是因为这样那样的事唠叨我爸，通常都是钱的事，”她懊恼地说。“我想我当时挺同情他的，而且因为我妈也唠叨我，所以他也挺同情我的。”

‘It sounds like you and your father had some kind of special bond?’ I ventured. She nodded. ‘Which excluded your mother,’ I continued.

“听起来你和你父亲之间似乎有着某种特殊的感情？”我试探性地问道。她点了点头。“这其中不包括你母亲，”我继续说道。

She nodded again and then noticed how perplexed Lawrence looked. She turned her hand in that familiar shorthand for the question ‘What?’

她再次点了点头，然后注意到劳伦斯一脸困惑。她用那个熟悉的手势比划了一下，意思是“什么？”

‘But your dad loved your mother; he was devoted to her. I never saw them argue. They seemed … tight, very close. At least, to me.’

“但是你爸爸很爱你妈妈；他非常爱她。我从没见过他们吵架。他们看起来……关系很亲密，非常亲密。至少在我看来是这样。”

‘That was after, after I left home. I think it changed once I moved out. You didn’t see them before. There’s a before and after. They fought like cat and dog.’

“那是在我离开家之后的事了。我觉得我搬出去之后一切都变了。以前你没见过他们这样。他们以前就像猫狗一样吵架。”

We talked more about Reggie’s childhood and how she was sorry she never really had a sister or brother around and then, suddenly, they began to talk about the lost baby. I’d almost forgotten about the stillbirth – it had been so many months since we’d discussed it – but now it seemed very important.

我们聊了很多关于雷吉的童年，她说她很遗憾自己从来没有兄弟姐妹在身边。然后，突然间，她们开始谈起那个夭折的孩子。我几乎都忘了那次死产——我们已经好几个月没谈起这件事了——但现在看来，它非常重要。

‘I wish we’d had two children. One isn’t quite enough to go round,’ Lawrence said, laughing ruefully. And then he talked about what it had been like for him growing up with five brothers and sisters: an experience so markedly different to Reggie’s. ‘It was great in lots of ways. I was never alone. I always had someone to play with … or fight with. I’ve always thought it’s a bit sad for Woody, he’s just got us …’

“我真希望我们有两个孩子。一个孩子根本不够，”劳伦斯苦笑着说。然后他谈起了自己和五个兄弟姐妹一起长大的经历：这和雷吉的经历截然不同。“从很多方面来说，那段时光都很棒。我从来不会感到孤单。我总有人陪我玩……或者打闹。我一直觉得伍迪有点可怜，他只有我们……”

‘But I guess it must’ve been hard at times to get attention?’ I commented. ‘Attention from your parents for instance?’

“但我猜想，有时候想要引起别人的注意一定很困难吧？”我评论道，“比如说，想要引起父母的注意？”

‘Kinda,’ Lawrence replied, looking thoughtful.

“算是吧。”劳伦斯若有所思地回答道。

It was the end of the session and it felt as though we’d got somewhere. Where, I wasn’t sure, but something was shifting. I knew that for this couple, the issues they struggled with circled around the problem of threesomes. It was as though they really believed the old adage, ‘Two’s company and three’s a crowd.’ A crowd in which you were unlikely to get seen or noticed.

咨询结束了，感觉我们好像取得了一些进展。至于进展到哪里了，我也不确定，但确实有什么东西在发生变化。我知道，对于这对伴侣来说，他们面临的问题都围绕着三人行展开。他们似乎真的相信那句老话：“两人成伴，三人成群。” 在人多的地方，你很难被人注意到。

The weeks passed and Reggie and Lawrence made slow and steady progress. They continued to bicker about who was doing what and whether Woody was pulling his weight but their fighting seemed less vicious and we had more and more reflective moments. I had the feeling that Woody was also doing better; the old arguments about him had lessened. He seemed to have a girlfriend, Maya, though neither Reggie nor Lawrence was permitted to meet her, but it was clear he was out and about more and no longer always stuck at home on his Xbox.

几周过去了，雷吉和劳伦斯的关系稳步发展。他们仍然会因为谁该做什么以及伍迪是否尽职尽责而争吵，但他们的争吵似乎不再那么激烈，我们也有了更多反思的时刻。我感觉伍迪的情况也有所好转；以前关于他的争论减少了。他似乎交了个女朋友，名叫玛雅，虽然雷吉和劳伦斯都不被允许见她，但很明显他现在更多地出门活动，不再总是宅在家里玩Xbox了。

Then, one week they came in and I knew immediately that something was wrong.

然后，一周后他们来了，我立刻就知道出事了。

Neither of them spoke for quite some time; they avoided looking at each other and even at me. We sat in silence, the clock’s ticking the only accompaniment to the deepening quiet. From outside, I could hear the sounds of children coming out of the school opposite my house.

他们俩沉默了许久，彼此避讳，甚至连我的目光也不敢看向对方。我们静静地坐着，只有时钟的滴答声伴着越来越深的寂静。从屋外，我能听到对面学校里孩子们的嬉闹声。

‘Difficult to start today?’ I eventually commented.

“今天开始很困难吗？”我最终还是问道。

Nothing. We sat longer and I could feel the tension rising. After a while, I tried again. ‘Perhaps you’re both too upset to talk?’

什么也没发生。我们又坐了一会儿，我能感觉到气氛越来越紧张。过了一会儿，我又试着开口：“也许你们俩都太难过了，说不出话来？”

This seemed to stir Reggie, who looked at me as if noticing my presence for the first time. She smiled gently and I thought she was trying to apologise for their lack of response.

这似乎触动了雷吉，她看向我，仿佛第一次注意到我的存在。她温柔地笑了笑，我想她是在为他们之前的冷漠道歉。

‘I guess we should explain.’ Lawrence’s voice almost made me jump as it punctured the heavy silence. Then he told me that there’d been an almighty row the previous evening, which had culminated in Woody packing his bags and moving out. They weren’t sure where he’d gone but they thought it was probably to his girlfriend’s. Then they became animated and talked anxiously for some minutes about what they should do. They’d tried his mobile numerous times but it was switched off and they’d rung some of his friends but they didn’t seem to know where he was. They didn’t have Maya’s number, nor did they know where she lived. As they talked, I could feel the fear rising and, as it did, they became angrier and blaming.

“我想我们应该解释一下。”劳伦斯的声音打破了沉闷的沉默，差点让我吓了一跳。他告诉我，前一天晚上他们大吵了一架，最后伍迪收拾行李搬了出去。他们不知道他去了哪里，但估计是去了他女朋友家。接着，他们激动起来，焦急地讨论了好几分钟该怎么办。他们给他的手机打了好几次电话，但都关机了；他们也给他的一些朋友打了电话，但朋友们似乎也不知道他在哪里。他们没有玛雅的电话号码，也不知道她住在哪里。随着他们的谈话，我能感觉到恐惧在不断蔓延，而恐惧也愈发强烈，他们开始互相指责。

‘If he doesn’t come back, I’ll never forgive you,’ Reggie spat.

“如果他不回来，我永远不会原谅你，”雷吉怒道。

‘I won’t be your whipping boy. You’re not going to do the usual – make it all my fault. You were the one on his back – not me. As usual. If you hadn’t gone on about the mess in the car, he wouldn’t have left. But you just couldn’t shut up. He’d already done a lot.’

“我不会做你的出气筒。你别想再像往常那样，把一切都怪到我头上。是你压在他身上，不是我。跟往常一样。如果你不一直唠叨车里的脏乱，他就不会走了。但你就是闭不上嘴。他已经做了很多坏事了。”

‘He hadn’t done a lot, that’s total rubbish. You want me to look after YOU and you want me to look after him. What am I? Mummy to you both? He doesn’t need me to mummy him anymore – isn’t that what we’ve been agreeing with Susanna? But he does need you to step up and be a proper father for Christ’s sake. Set an example, stop whining to me!’

“他没做什么，这完全是胡说八道。你想让我照顾你，又想让我照顾他。我算什么？你们俩的妈妈吗？他不再需要我像妈妈一样照顾他了——我们和苏珊娜不是一直都这么说吗？但他确实需要你承担起责任，做一个称职的父亲，看在上帝的份上。以身作则，别再跟我抱怨了！”

They made little progress that session and when they left in high dudgeon, I felt worried about them. That night, I woke in the early hours of the morning, wondering where Woody had got to and whether he was safe.

那次谈话他们进展甚微，他们气冲冲地离开时，我为他们感到担忧。那天晚上，我凌晨醒来，想知道伍迪去了哪里，他是否安全。

Weeks passed and Woody didn’t come back and nor did he contact them. He didn’t answer their messages or pick up his phone; he completely shut them out. I watched them break and it was heart-rending. Session after session, they’d weep and fight and weep and fight and all I could do was be with them in their anger and grief. Many times, I held back my own tears as they tried to come to terms with Woody’s absence. They knew he was safe; they’d heard from one of his friends that he was around and fine, living with Maya in south London. They could also see what he was posting on his social media accounts but he’d changed his phone number and didn’t respond to emails. He’d left them, abandoned them, and it felt a cruel and bitter way to leave.

几周过去了，伍迪没有回来，也没有联系他们。他不回信息，也不接电话，彻底与他们断绝了联系。我眼睁睁地看着他们崩溃，心如刀绞。一次又一次的咨询中，他们哭泣、争吵，哭泣、争吵，我只能陪伴在他们身边，感受他们的愤怒和悲伤。很多次，当他们努力接受伍迪的离去时，我强忍着泪水。他们知道他很安全；他们从他的一个朋友那里听说，他就在附近，和玛雅住在伦敦南部。他们也能看到他在社交媒体上发布的内容，但他换了手机号码，也不回复邮件。他离开了他们，抛弃了他们，这种离开的方式残酷而痛苦。

I told them that I thought Woody had felt this was the only way to separate from them, that he’d had to mobilise every bit of anger he felt to tear himself from their soft bosom. Maybe that thought helped them a little, I’m not really sure. Lawrence couldn’t sleep and the doctor prescribed sleeping pills; Reggie found it difficult to get out of bed in the mornings and the doctor prescribed anti-depressants. They were powerless to do anything and had no choice but to wait and hope and I waited and hoped with them.

我告诉他们，我觉得伍迪觉得这是离开他们的唯一办法，他必须调动所有愤怒才能挣脱他们柔软的怀抱。也许这个想法对他们有所帮助，我也不确定。劳伦斯睡不着觉，医生给他开了安眠药；雷吉早上起床很困难，医生给他开了抗抑郁药。他们无能为力，只能等待和期盼，我也和他们一起等待和期盼。

Sometimes, of course, they hated their son but it never lasted long. They reserved their deepest anger for Maya, who they decided was a witch, a bitch and worse for stealing Woody. I tried to help them see that Woody was grown and had made his own choices; for all they knew, Maya could be appealing to him to contact them.

当然，有时候他们也会恨自己的儿子，但这种恨意不会持续太久。他们最深的怒火都倾注在玛雅身上，他们认定玛雅是个女巫、是个泼妇，甚至更糟，因为她偷走了伍迪。我试图让他们明白，伍迪已经长大成人，他做出了自己的选择；说不定玛雅正在劝说伍迪联系他们呢。

For some couples, this might have brought them together but Woody had been the glue between them; without him there, what was left? They began to talk about separation, Reggie leading the way. She decided she didn’t want to work with Lawrence anymore, that she was too old for gardening, and took a job working for a friend in a local bookshop. Lawrence sulked, retreating to the office shed, where, hour after hour, he played his guitar and kept out of Reggie’s way. Their nest had emptied and they were now faced with just each other and what was left between them.

对某些夫妻来说，这或许会让他们更加亲密，但伍迪一直是维系他们关系的纽带；没有了他，他们之间还剩下什么？他们开始讨论分居，雷吉率先提出。她决定不再和劳伦斯一起工作，她觉得自己年纪大了，不适合再做园艺了，于是去朋友的当地书店找了份工作。劳伦斯闷闷不乐，躲进办公室的棚屋里，一连几个小时弹着吉他，尽量不去打扰雷吉。他们的“家”空了，现在只剩下彼此，以及他们之间仅存的一切。

There are many couples who, once they have children, lose their connection to each other. Often, this problem is linked to a feeling that intimacy between them is cruelly excluding for the children; where there is only one child, this problem can be worse. Family life becomes centred around the child and their needs but once they leave home (and in this situation, children can take a whole lot longer to do that), the couple find themselves without a relationship to fall back on.

许多夫妻在有了孩子后，彼此之间的联系就会减弱。通常，这个问题源于他们觉得彼此间的亲密关系对孩子来说是一种残酷的排斥；如果只有一个孩子，这个问题会更加严重。家庭生活围绕着孩子及其需求运转，但一旦孩子离开家（在这种情况下，孩子可能需要更长的时间才能离开家），夫妻就会发现自己失去了可以依靠的亲密关系。

Though I tried hard, during this period I felt I couldn’t reach either Lawrence or Reggie; the wound they’d suffered was scarring over and they now seemed resigned that their marriage was over too. They blamed each other for what had happened, shoving the guilt and sense of failure out of themselves into each other. They forgot what they’d shared, the life they’d built. In the sessions, they’d often reconnect but it was as if being together without Woody was too painful to bear. Nearly a year after Woody fled, Lawrence moved out to stay with his sister, Iris.

尽管我竭尽全力，但在这段时间里，我感觉自己无法与劳伦斯或雷吉沟通；他们曾经遭受的创伤已经愈合，他们似乎也接受了婚姻破裂的事实。他们互相指责对方，将内疚和失败感从自己身上转移到对方身上。他们忘记了曾经共同拥有的一切，忘记了他们共同建立的生活。在咨询中，他们常常能够重新建立联系，但仿佛没有伍迪的相处对他们来说太过痛苦。伍迪离开将近一年后，劳伦斯搬去和他的姐姐艾瑞斯住在一起。

Despite their separation, they continued to come to see me. I think I was, at that point, an anchor of sorts, in a darkening sea. Perhaps I linked them back to hope, to love and to each other?

尽管他们已经分开，但他们仍然会来看我。我想，在那时，我就像黑暗海洋中的一盏明灯。或许是我让他们重新燃起了希望，重新燃起了爱，重新燃起了彼此之间的希望？

Then, three weeks after Lawrence moved out, Woody turned up at Reggie’s door, suitcase in hand. I was fascinated by this; it seemed extraordinary that Woody would come back just as Lawrence left. What did it mean? Was it the threesome that Woody hadn’t been able to stand anymore? Was that why he’d left? Did Lawrence’s absence now leave a space for Woody to occupy, allowing him to have Reggie all to himself? Was it simply that now he wouldn’t have to be ‘piggy in the middle’? Or was it that he felt he couldn’t leave his poor mother on her own?

劳伦斯搬走三周后，伍迪提着行李箱出现在雷吉家门口。我对此感到十分好奇；伍迪偏偏在劳伦斯离开后回来，这实在太不可思议了。这究竟意味着什么？难道是伍迪再也无法忍受三人关系？难道这就是他离开的原因？劳伦斯的离开是否给伍迪留下了空间，让他可以独占雷吉？难道仅仅是因为他现在不用再“夹在中间”了？还是因为他觉得不能留下可怜的母亲独自一人？

On a bright, crisp Monday morning in April, two weeks later, Reggie and Lawrence arrived together for their session. I could hear them chatting and laughing as they came through the gate and I smiled to myself, wondering if a rapprochement was now under way.

两周后，四月一个阳光明媚、空气清新的星期一早晨，雷吉和劳伦斯一起来参加他们的会议。我听到他们走进大门时有说有笑，我不禁暗自微笑，心想他们之间是不是正在和解。

There was no hesitation today as Lawrence pulled off his battered khaki parka. ‘We’ve had a good week. Lots to tell you.’ He glanced at Reggie who nodded in agreement. ‘We talked to Woody properly. It was awkward but really, really helpful. I feel sooo relieved and you do too, don’t you, Reg?’

今天，劳伦斯毫不犹豫地脱下他那件破旧的卡其色派克大衣。“我们这周过得不错，有很多事要跟你说。”他瞥了一眼雷吉，雷吉点头表示同意。“我们和伍迪好好谈过了。虽然有点尴尬，但真的很有帮助。我感觉如释重负，你也一样，对吧，雷吉？”

‘Yeah, yeah. Shall I tell her what he said?’

“是啊，是啊。我该告诉她他说了什么吗？”

‘Absolutely,’ Lawrence answered. I was struck by how they finally seemed to be acting like a couple. ‘Well, we talked for hours last Tuesday – it was … amazing. I can’t tell you, Susanna. It felt like … being reborn,’ Reggie laughed. ‘What you said last week about us needing to sit down as a family really helped. After seeing you, we went for lunch and agreed we couldn’t let him “split” us, you know, like you described, how we needed to be a team. You saying, “Remember you’re on the same team” really rang a bell for us. Because that’s always been the problem, hasn’t it? Not knowing we were on the same side. So we went home and told him we wanted to talk to him. He looked really scared and I was scared too. I thought he might run away again.’

“当然，”劳伦斯回答道。我惊讶地发现他们终于像一对夫妻了。“嗯，上周二我们聊了好几个小时——真是……太棒了。苏珊娜，我简直无法形容。感觉就像……重生了一样，”雷吉笑着说。“你上周说的我们需要坐下来好好谈谈，这真的很有帮助。见了你之后，我们一起吃了午饭，一致认为不能让他‘拆散’我们，就像你描述的那样，我们需要像一个团队一样。你说‘记住你们是同一战线的’，这真的让我们醍醐灌顶。因为这始终是问题所在，不是吗？我们不知道我们其实是站在同一阵线上的。所以我们回家告诉他，我们想和他谈谈。他看起来很害怕，我也很害怕。我以为他会再次逃跑。”

‘I went home for dinner the next night,’ Lawrence now took up the reins excitedly. ‘I was shitting myself, to be frank, but Woody said he was sorry. He’d just needed to get away for a bit because he was fed up with us.’

“第二天晚上我回家吃晚饭，”劳伦斯兴奋地接过话茬。“说实话，我当时吓得要死，但伍迪说他很抱歉。他只是需要出去走走，因为他受够了我们。”

‘Was he able to tell you what he was fed up about?’ I asked.

“他能告诉你他到底在抱怨什么吗？”我问。

‘Us rowing. Rowing and … nagging,’ Lawrence replied. ‘He said there was no room for him. Which is ironic. That we were fighting over him all the time but he never got to speak.’

“我们划船。划船，还有……唠叨，”劳伦斯回答说。“他说没他的位置。真是讽刺。我们一直在为他争吵，但他却从来没有机会说话。”

‘Yes, and about us being too focused on the business,’ Reggie added.

“是的，还有我们过于关注业务的问题，”雷吉补充道。

‘Well, a bit. But that wasn’t the main thing. It was us rowing wasn’t it?’

“嗯，有一点。但这并不是重点。重点是我们划船，对吧？”

I could see they were about to squabble and I pointed out the irony of this, which made us all laugh. I thought about how, on numerous occasions, I’d probably had a similar experience to that which Woody had lived with daily. I felt torn between them, which made me kind of important too because they both wanted my approval and attention. But I’d also often felt powerless; their competitiveness made them so totally focused on each other that there seemed to be no room for anyone else. Except, perhaps, as a referee to their battles? I thought about the loneliness of that for a child and the invidious situation of being that ‘piggy in the middle’. Woody had clearly felt neglected and, in leaving, he’d made them feel as neglected and overlooked as he’d felt himself.

我看出他们要吵起来了，便指出这其中的讽刺意味，逗得我们都笑了。我想，很多时候，我可能也经历过伍迪每天面对的那种情况。我夹在他们中间左右为难，这让我觉得自己也很重要，因为他们都渴望得到我的认可和关注。但我也常常感到无能为力；他们的竞争让他们完全专注于彼此，似乎容不下其他人。或许，除了做他们争吵的裁判？我想到孩子在这种情况下该有多么孤独，以及夹在中间那种尴尬的处境。伍迪显然感到被忽视了，而他的离开，也让他们感受到了和他自己一样的被忽视和冷落。

Much changed after that. We did the work of understanding all these disparate threads and they began to acknowledge how difficult it was for Woody as well as for them to be in this threesome. In their inner worlds, there always seemed a danger that someone would be left out and they fought over who that would be. Each, in competing to be the best and most loved by Woody, would indulge him. But in fighting to win, Woody’s real emotional needs were overlooked. And no one won.

之后一切都发生了很大的变化。我们努力理解了所有这些看似无关的线索，他们也开始意识到，对于伍迪和他们三人来说，维持这种三人关系有多么艰难。在他们的内心世界里，似乎总有一种被冷落的危险，他们为此争吵不休。为了成为伍迪最爱的人，每个人都竭尽全力地讨好他。然而，在争夺的过程中，伍迪真正的情感需求却被忽略了。最终，没有人是赢家。

In a session not long before they stopped coming, Reggie spoke about how she’d felt anxious having sex with Lawrence ever since Woody was a baby. She worried he’d wake up and need them and they wouldn’t hear him when he cried. We explored how, deep down, they’d felt guilty about being intimate, sexually or in any way, because then they’d be excluding Woody. These Oedipal dynamics permeated the family system, shaping everything.

在他们停止来访前不久的一次咨询中，雷吉谈到自从伍迪还是婴儿时，她就一直对和劳伦斯发生性关系感到焦虑。她担心伍迪醒来需要他们，而他们却听不到他的哭声。我们探讨了他们内心深处对亲密关系（无论是性方面的还是其他方面的）感到内疚，因为那样就等于把伍迪排除在外。这种俄狄浦斯情结渗透到整个家庭系统中，影响着一切。

Then Woody moved out again to live with a friend and almost immediately Lawrence moved back in. He stayed in the spare room and both of them seemed comfortable with that. It seemed they needed to be more separate. When they ended the therapy, it was with a quiet gratitude. I thought they’d grown up a lot; they were both much more subdued, they fought much less – but then, perhaps, they shared less too?

后来伍迪再次搬出去和朋友住，劳伦斯几乎立刻就搬了回来。他住在客房里，两人似乎都觉得这样挺好。看来他们需要更多一些的私人空间。治疗结束后，他们带着一丝淡淡的感激。我觉得他们都成熟了很多；两人都变得更加沉稳，争吵也少了很多——但或许，他们之间的交流也减少了？

All couples must learn to accept the limitations of their relationship. Some couples try to manage their disappointments by avoiding things or finding comfort elsewhere. Other couples, like Reggie and Lawrence, seem to engage in a long, passionate battle to get what they want and, in some way, these battles keep couples very absorbed with each other. Most couples, as the years pass, stop most of the fighting. The natural processes of ageing make us more aware of the cost of conflict and, battle-worn, we slowly accept who our partner is and recognise that some things simply are as they are. Because of this, couples lower their expectations of each other and when that happens, there is less disappointment and more capacity to enjoy and appreciate what they have.

所有伴侣都必须学会接受彼此关系的局限性。有些伴侣会试图通过逃避或从别处寻求慰藉来应对失望。而另一些伴侣，比如雷吉和劳伦斯，似乎会为了得到自己想要的东西而展开一场漫长而激烈的斗争，某种程度上，这些斗争让他们彼此深深地沉浸其中。随着岁月的流逝，大多数伴侣都会停止大部分争吵。衰老的自然过程让我们更加意识到冲突的代价，饱经风霜的我们慢慢接受了伴侣的本来面目，并意识到有些事情就是如此。正因如此，伴侣们会降低对彼此的期望，而当这种情况发生时，失望就会减少，他们也更有能力享受和珍惜自己所拥有的一切。

# ↩

Postscript

后记

Many readers may find aspects of these cases frustrating. They may wish for more detail, more clarity and especially clearer and more certain outcomes. I am sorry for this but I can only say it is the same frustration that every psychoanalytic therapist lives with every day. One can never actually know the unconscious – if one could, it wouldn’t be unconscious, would it? All we can hope to do is take some soundings from the deep and learn to notice the waving flags that appear on the surface from time to time. Understanding is always speculation and only meaningful if it is meaningful to the patient.

许多读者可能会对这些案例的某些方面感到沮丧。他们或许希望看到更多细节、更清晰的阐述，尤其是更明确、更确定的结果。对此我深感遗憾，但我只能说，这正是每位精神分析治疗师每天都要面对的困境。我们永远无法真正了解无意识——如果可以，它就不是无意识的了，不是吗？我们所能做的，只是从深层探寻，并学会留意那些不时浮现于表面的迹象。理解始终是一种推测，只有当它对患者有意义时，才具有意义。

So many of these chapters end without any conclusion, the patients simply falling off the page and out of sight. I can’t apologise for this lack – it is exactly what I experience. I very rarely know if the therapy has led to a couple or an individual patient having a good-enough life. I don’t find out if a couple stayed together or if their children thrived. It is unfortunate but it keeps me, as much as possible, in the now and that is where feelings – the essential business of therapy – usually live. So, in order to be authentic, I’m afraid you have to cope without much of an end to the story, just as I do.

很多章节都戛然而止，没有结局，病人仿佛从纸面上消失，不见踪影。我无法为此道歉——这正是我自己的亲身经历。我很少知道治疗是否让一对伴侣或一位病人拥有了足够好的生活。我不知道一对伴侣是否继续在一起，他们的孩子是否健康成长。这很遗憾，但它让我尽可能地活在当下，而情感——治疗的核心——通常就存在于当下。所以，为了保持真诚，恐怕你也得像我一样，接受故事没有结局的现实。

Much of this book was written during the pandemic and it is clear that this global disaster has had an enormous impact on us all and on our family life. I don’t think anyone can quite know as yet what that impact means, though we are all keen to jump to conclusions. How we have fared psychologically isn’t known, though the impact on children and adolescents is beginning to look worrying.

本书大部分内容写于疫情期间，显而易见，这场全球灾难对我们所有人以及我们的家庭生活都产生了巨大影响。我认为目前尚无人能够完全了解这种影响究竟意味着什么，尽管我们都急于下结论。我们自身的心理状况如何尚不得而知，但疫情对儿童和青少年的影响已开始令人担忧。

What I have noticed is that for some couples, the pandemic has hardly been mentioned. The more distressed the couple, the less the pandemic seems to come into the sessions. I’ve begun to conclude that for most distressed patients, the inner world of feelings makes such a racket that the clamour and noise of the outside world makes hardly a sound.

我注意到，有些夫妻几乎从未提及疫情。夫妻双方越是痛苦，疫情似乎就越少出现在咨询中。我开始得出结论：对于大多数痛苦的来访者来说，内心世界的种种感受如此喧嚣，以至于外界的嘈杂几乎听不到。

致谢

I am deeply indebted to many of my colleagues and teachers at Tavistock Relationships, some of whom are sadly now dead. There are so many colleagues who have been inspirational and important to me that it’s hard to list them all, but this book stands on their shoulders and couldn’t have been written without them. Particular thanks must go to Warren Colman, Christopher Clulow, Mary Morgan, Stan Ruszczynski, David Hewison, Christel Buss-Twachtmann and Anton Obholzer. And a dedication in remembrance is due to James Fisher and Nina Cohen. All of these people were essential to my development as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist and many of the ideas in this book come directly from their mouths. A long overdue thanks is also due to Elizabeth Gee.

我由衷感谢塔维斯托克关系研究所的众多同事和老师，其中一些人不幸已经离世。有太多同事对我影响深远，激励着我，难以一一列举，但本书的完成离不开他们的贡献。在此，我特别感谢沃伦·科尔曼、克里斯托弗·克卢洛、玛丽·摩根、斯坦·鲁什琴斯基、大卫·休伊森、克里斯蒂尔·布斯-特瓦赫特曼和安东·奥布霍尔泽。谨以此书献给詹姆斯·费舍尔和尼娜·科恩，以表缅怀他们。所有这些人对我作为一名精神分析心理治疗师的成长都至关重要，本书中的许多观点都直接出自他们之口。此外，我还要向伊丽莎白·吉致以迟来的谢意。

Thank you to my good friends who’ve listened to me bang on about this book for too long. Particularly to Professor Lynda Nead, Charlotte Wickers, Jenny Riddell and Andrea Collett. And thanks must go to my sister Keren Abse for her generous support. Her home in Ogmore-by-Sea was such a welcome writing retreat.

感谢我的好朋友们，你们听我唠叨这本书已经很久了。特别感谢琳达·尼德教授、夏洛特·威克斯、珍妮·里德尔和安德里亚·科莱特。还要感谢我的妹妹凯伦·阿布斯，她给予了我慷慨的支持。她在海滨小镇奥格莫尔的家真是个理想的写作避风港。

Thank you to my husband, Paul Gogarty, without whom there simply wouldn’t be a book. He must have read all the chapters a dozen times, editing my clumsy language, offering insight and imagination and correcting my appalling punctuation and making everything work so much better. To Miren Lopategui and Nigel Richardson – I am eternally grateful for your sharp eyes and thoughtful reading of the book.

感谢我的丈夫保罗·戈加蒂，没有他，这本书根本不可能问世。他肯定把所有章节都读了不下十遍，帮我修改笨拙的语言，贡献真知灼见和丰富想象力，纠正我糟糕的标点符号，让整本书更加流畅自然。还要感谢米伦·洛帕特吉和奈杰尔·理查森——我永远感激你们敏锐的眼光和认真细致的阅读。

And to my children, Max Gogarty and Larne Abse Gogarty, and their spouses, Suzy Gregg and Adam Lane, who have been excited and patient with my bookishness. Finally, to my grandson, Rudy, who was born in the same week that I finally birthed this book. Your imminent arrival spurred me on to the finish line.

还要感谢我的孩子们，Max Gogarty 和 Larne Abse Gogarty，以及他们的配偶 Suzy Gregg 和 Adam Lane，感谢你们一直以来对我的书虫爱好给予的热情和耐心。最后，还要感谢我的孙子 Rudy，他出生的那一周，正是我完成这本书的那一周。你的即将到来激励我最终完成了它。

And lastly, but most definitely not least, a deep and enduring gratitude is owed to my patients past and present who have allowed me into their lives and from whom I’ve learnt so much.

最后，也是最重要的一点，我要深深地、持久地感谢我过去和现在的病人，感谢他们让我走进他们的生活，也感谢他们让我学到了很多东西。
